Plural treatment of "data" is applied cleanly, so the sentence stands. Consistency of number across clause and main verb is the test.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the higher costs involved, several firms proceeded with relocation plans."
"Whoever oversees the transition should account for delays typically involved in construction."
"The firm denied having deliberately overstated its reshoring progress."
"There is several reasons why completion rates remained so low."
"The initiative, which was funded over several years, aims to expand domestic capacity."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the higher costs involved, several firms proceeded with relocation plans."**

"Despite" never takes "of"; the paired idiom is "in spite of." Written "Despite of" is a fusion error. The preposition belongs only with "in spite," not with standalone "despite."

**Trap:** Cross-contamination from "in spite of." If you hear "of," you need the full "in spite of" phrase, not "despite of."

Repair to "Despite the higher costs…" or "In spite of the higher costs…," so the line fails.

**B) "Whoever oversees the transition should account for delays typically involved in construction."**

"Whoever" correctly heads the subject clause; "oversees" agrees with that indefinite singular subject, and "should account" is a natural predicate for the whole clause. The free relative occupies subject position, so no extra pronoun ("he who") is required.

The free-relative subject is formed properly, so the sentence is sound. Keep singular verb agreement with "whoever" unless a clearly plural referent is forced.

**C) "The firm denied having deliberately overstated its reshoring progress."**

After "denied," the perfect gerund "having…overstated" correctly marks a prior alleged act. Adverb placement ("deliberately") inside the gerund is natural. "Denied" + -ing (or having + past participle) is the standard pattern for rejecting a past accusation.

The verb pattern matches the meaning, so the wording holds. Prefer the gerund form after deny rather than a bare that-clause with the wrong tense.

**D) "There is several reasons why completion rates remained so low."**

Existential "there" agreement tracks the notional noun: plural "reasons" needs "There are," not "There is." The postponed subject "several reasons" controls the verb, not the dummy "there."

**Trap:** Habitual "there's" in speech before plural nouns. Formal writing restores "there are" before plural heads.

Repair to "There are several reasons…," so the sentence fails.

**E) "The initiative, which was funded over several years, aims to expand domestic capacity."**

Singular "initiative" takes singular verbs in both the relative clause ("was funded") and the main clause ("aims"). The non-restrictive clause is well attached. Commas around "which was funded…" mark extra information without changing the subject's number.

Agreement stays consistent, so the sentence is true. Match both the relative verb and the main verb to the same singular head.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "The strategy aimed to strengthen resilience by concentrating production in a single overseas facility."
"The narrowing cost gap made relocation more economically viable for several manufacturers."
"Government funding was allocated to expand domestic production capacity in strategic sectors."
"The firm's diversification strategy left it wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier."
"Automation helped offset rising domestic costs by improving overall productivity."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The strategy aimed to strengthen resilience by concentrating production in a single overseas facility."**

In this bank's supply-chain sense, resilience is built by reducing single-source exposure, not by concentrating everything in one overseas plant. The sentence uses "resilience" with the opposite strategy. Paragraph 1's single-source justin-time model is exactly the vulnerability concentrating production recreates.

**Trap:** Putting all eggs in one "efficient" basket looks decisive but is the vulnerability the passage describes. Resilience collocates with diversification, not with deeper single-facility concentration.

The collocation reverses the established meaning, so the wording fails.

**B) "The narrowing cost gap made relocation more economically viable for several manufacturers."**

"Narrowing cost gap" plus "more economically viable" tracks the passage logic that a smaller labour-cost differential makes relocation more feasible. The adjectives and nouns match ordinary usage. Paragraph 4's "more feasible by a narrowing cost differential" is the same idea in near-synonyms.

The meaning lines up with the established sense, so the sentence stands. Accept viable/feasible paraphrases when they stay tied to a narrower cost gap.

**C) "Government funding was allocated to expand domestic production capacity in strategic sectors."**

"Allocated…to expand…capacity" is the same natural funding collocation used for the CHIPS / Chips Acts. Nothing is twisted. The passage's "$52 billion in subsidies to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity" is the model for this wording.

The wording matches standard use, so it is true. Keep allocate/subsidise paired with expanding capacity, not with eliminating all cost gaps.

**D) "The firm's diversification strategy left it wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier."**

Diversification means spreading exposure across sources; "wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier" is concentration, the opposite outcome. The sentence forces contradictory poles into one strategy label. In the passage, diversification is the move toward allied third countries — the opposite of single-supplier dependence.

That clash of meanings overturns the claim. Reject any item that defines diversification as ending in sole dependence.

**E) "Automation helped offset rising domestic costs by improving overall productivity."**

"Offset…by improving…productivity" is a standard collocation and matches how the passage describes automation absorbing part of the reshoring cost gap. Paragraph 8's "offset by automation-driven productivity gains" is the direct text anchor.

The usage is natural and text-aligned, so the sentence holds. Treat offset + productivity as a valid cost-gap absorption phrase in this bank.
highlights: single-source suppliers operating under justin-time inventory models that minimised stockpiles in favour of efficiency
this shift has been made more feasible by a narrowing cost differential
allocated $52 billion in subsidies to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity
diversification toward allied or trusted third countries
offset by automation-driven productivity gains

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "Friend-shoring refers to relocating production entirely back to one's own home country."
"The company's exposure to single-source risk was reduced after diversifying its supplier base."
"The subsidy was described as sufficient to fully eliminate the cost gap between relocated and offshored production."
"Reshored production is generally described in the passage as costlier per unit than its offshored equivalent."
"The trend's long-term durability is treated in the passage as a matter of active, unresolved debate."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Friend-shoring refers to relocating production entirely back to one's own home country."**

In the passage, friend-shoring is diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, expressly contrasted with a "genuine return of production to the home country." Home-country return is reshoring proper, not friend-shoring. The definition in the claim erases that contrast and steals reshoring's meaning.

**Trap:** Any "-shoring" word can be misread as "bring it all home." Friend-shoring keeps production abroad among trusted partners.

The definition swaps friend-shoring for genuine reshoring, so the claim fails.

**B) "The company's exposure to single-source risk was reduced after diversifying its supplier base."**

Diversifying the supplier base and reducing single-source exposure are the paired meaning the passage builds from Paragraph 1's vulnerability. The causal link is ordinary and correct. Concentrated justin-time single sourcing was the fragile setup; spreading suppliers is the resilience move.

The wording matches established usage, so the sentence is true. Keep diversify and reduce single-source risk as matching collocations.

**C) "The subsidy was described as sufficient to fully eliminate the cost gap between relocated and offshored production."**

The text never says subsidies wipe out the gap; reshored production still costs "20% and 25% more per unit," with only a modest consumer share and margins/automation covering the rest. "Fully eliminate" invents a claim. Policy can accelerate capacity without erasing the unit-cost premium.

That absolute wipeout overstates what subsidies do in the passage, so the statement fails. Reject "fully eliminate" whenever the text still prices a 20–25% premium.

**D) "Reshored production is generally described in the passage as costlier per unit than its offshored equivalent."**

Paragraph 8 states reshored production costs "between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent." "Costlier per unit" is a faithful paraphrase. "Generally" here simply reflects that average estimate, not a claim that every product category matches the same exact percentage.

The cost comparison matches the text, so the claim holds. Anchor on the more-per-unit wording rather than on how much of the gap reaches consumers.

**E) "The trend's long-term durability is treated in the passage as a matter of active, unresolved debate."**

The close of Paragraph 9 says whether the reordering is durable or temporary "remains a matter of active debate among economists." "Unresolved debate" tracks that framing. The passage leaves structural reversal versus temporary shock open; it does not close the question.

The sentence mirrors the passage conclusion, so it stands. Do not upgrade the debate into a firm verdict that the shift is either permanent or finished.
highlights: diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, a practice sometimes termed "friend-shoring,"
globally dispersed, single-source suppliers
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
remains a matter of active debate among economists

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The severe economic distress described in Paragraph 1 is attributed partly to a chronic shortage of US dollars needed to purchase fuel, machinery, and raw materials.
Marshall's proposal, as described in Paragraph 2, required European governments to coordinate their reconstruction efforts jointly rather than negotiate purely bilateral aid requests.
Czechoslovakia is described as having withdrawn from the programme entirely on its own initiative, without any external pressure being involved.
The programme's total disbursement of approximately $13.3 billion was distributed over a four-year period following Congressional authorisation in April 1948.
The United Kingdom is described as having received a smaller share of total aid than France.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The severe economic distress described in Paragraph 1 is attributed partly to a chronic shortage of US dollars needed to purchase fuel, machinery, and raw materials.**

Paragraph 1 lists several causes of Europe's post-war distress, and one of them is explicit: a chronic US-dollar shortage left governments unable to buy fuel, machinery, and raw materials for rebuilding. The statement restates that causal link without adding outside claims. "Partly" is fair because the same stretch also names lagging industrial output and failed harvests beside the dollar problem, so the shortage is one named driver, not the only one.

**Tip:** When a statement names a cause plus the imports blocked by it, check that both pieces sit in the same paragraph stretch.

Match the statement's purchase list to the passage's "fuel, machinery, and raw materials" wording rather than inventing other blocked goods. That dollar-shortage wording matches Paragraph 1, so the claim lines up with the passage.

**B) Marshall's proposal, as described in Paragraph 2, required European governments to coordinate their reconstruction efforts jointly rather than negotiate purely bilateral aid requests.**

Paragraph 2 presents Marshall's Harvard proposal as conditional on joint European coordination of reconstruction, rather than each country seeking purely bilateral aid. That is exactly the contrast the statement draws. The key hinge is the condition itself: aid is offered only if governments work together, not if each files a separate bilateral ask.

Watch for paraphrase swaps such as "encouraged" versus "conditional on," since the passage makes joint coordination a requirement of the proposal. The joint-coordination condition in Paragraph 2 supports the claim as written.

**C) Czechoslovakia is described as having withdrawn from the programme entirely on its own initiative, without any external pressure being involved.**

Paragraph 2 says Czechoslovakia initially showed interest, then "was compelled by Soviet pressure to withdraw." The exit is coerced, not a free solo decision. The statement invents "own initiative" and erases the Soviet pressure the text names. Initial interest only sets the scene; the compulsion clause is what decides whether the exit was voluntary.

**Trap:** Initial interest can look like voluntary exit if you stop reading before the compulsion clause.

Any true paraphrase must keep "Soviet pressure" in view, not replace it with self-directed withdrawal. Because withdrawal is forced by Soviet pressure, the "own initiative" claim fails against the passage.

**D) The programme's total disbursement of approximately $13.3 billion was distributed over a four-year period following Congressional authorisation in April 1948.**

Paragraph 3 places Congressional authorisation in April 1948 via the Economic Cooperation Act, then states that over the following four years the programme paid out about $13.3 billion. Timing and total both match the statement. "Following" tracks the passage order: authorisation first, then the multi-year disbursement window.

Do not detach the $13.3 billion figure from the "over the following four years" span, or the statement would misplace when the money went out. The four-year, $13.3 billion sequence after April 1948 is what Paragraph 3 reports, so the claim holds.

**E) The United Kingdom is described as having received a smaller share of total aid than France.**

Paragraph 3 ranks recipients: the United Kingdom took the largest share at roughly 24%, with France next at about 20%. The statement reverses that order and treats the UK as the smaller recipient. "Largest single share… followed by France" is an explicit ranking, not an open comparison you can flip.

**Trap:** Later Austria/UK national-income percentages (Paragraph 8) are relative weight, not the same ranking as absolute shares of the aid pot.

Keep absolute shares of the total pot separate from aid-as-a-share-of-national-income figures later in the text. Because the UK outranks France at 24% versus 20%, the smaller-share claim does not match the passage.
highlights: a chronic shortage of US dollars left European governments unable to purchase the fuel, machinery, and raw materials needed to rebuild
conditional on European governments jointly coordinating their own reconstruction efforts rather than each simply requesting bilateral assistance
was compelled by Soviet pressure to withdraw its participation within weeks
Over the following four years, the programme disbursed a total of approximately $13.3 billion in grants and loans
with the United Kingdom receiving the largest single share at roughly 24% of the total, followed by France at approximately 20%

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The plan's conditions are described as extending beyond fund transfers to include tariff reduction and currency stabilisation requirements.
Institutional cooperation fostered by the OEEC is presented as having laid groundwork for later European economic integration.
The programme's containment rationale is described as being always publicly acknowledged by American officials at the time.
Communist parties in France and Italy are described in the passage as having drawn political strength partly from post-war economic hardship.
Milward argued that Western European industrial output had already reached roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began in 1948.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The plan's conditions are described as extending beyond fund transfers to include tariff reduction and currency stabilisation requirements.**

Paragraph 4 opens by saying the plan's conditions went well beyond money transfers. Recipients had to cut tariffs and trade barriers, stabilise currencies, and accept mutual oversight through the OEEC. Tariff cuts and currency stabilisation are named conditions, not optional extras. The statement's "extending beyond fund transfers" mirrors that opening contrast between cash and policy strings.

Confirm both named duties—tariff reduction and currency stabilisation—appear in the requirements list, not only in later historical commentary. Those beyond-funds requirements in Paragraph 4 make the statement a faithful paraphrase.

**B) Institutional cooperation fostered by the OEEC is presented as having laid groundwork for later European economic integration.**

Paragraph 4 reports that many historians see the OEEC-centred cooperation as laying essential groundwork for deeper European economic integration, which later produced the European Economic Community. "Groundwork" is the passage's own word for that contribution. The claim stays inside what historians "regard" as preparatory, without asserting that integration was already complete in 1948.

Keep "groundwork for… integration" tied to the OEEC cooperation sentence rather than to the mere transfer of dollars alone. The groundwork-for-integration reading matches Paragraph 4, so the claim stands.

**C) The programme's containment rationale is described as being always publicly acknowledged by American officials at the time.**

Paragraph 5 says architects framed the programme as Cold War containment "explicitly, if not always publicly." That qualifier means public acknowledgment was not constant. "Always publicly acknowledged" flips the hedge into its opposite. The passage allows explicit framing that still was not invariably public, so "always" is the fatal overstatement.

**Trap:** "Explicitly" describes how they framed the tool, not how openly they advertised it every time.

Treat "if not always publicly" as a limit on publicity, not as proof of constant public admission. Because the text says "if not always publicly," the always-public claim fails.

**D) Communist parties in France and Italy are described in the passage as having drawn political strength partly from post-war economic hardship.**

Paragraph 5 links American hopes of reducing communist appeal to France, Italy, and elsewhere, and notes that post-war economic hardship had contributed to those parties' electoral strength. Hardship is a partial cause of that strength, just as the statement says. "Contributed to" already signals a partial, not exclusive, explanation, which "partly" preserves.

Locate the hardship link in the same sentence that names France and Italy rather than inferring it from containment motives alone. That hardship-to-electoral-strength link in Paragraph 5 supports the claim.

**E) Milward argued that Western European industrial output had already reached roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began in 1948.**

Paragraph 6 attributes to Alan Milward the claim that Western European industrial output was already about 111% of its 1938 level when large-scale Marshall disbursements began flowing in 1948. Figure, baseline year, and timing all align. The statement reports Milward's argument, not a narrator's independent measurement, so attribution stays accurate.

Check that "111%," "1938," and the 1948 onset of large-scale aid all appear together before you credit the paraphrase. Milward's 111%-of-1938 output argument in Paragraph 6 is exactly what the statement reports.
highlights: Recipient governments were required to reduce tariffs and other barriers to intra-European trade, stabilise their currencies
laid essential groundwork for the deeper European economic integration that would eventually produce the European Economic Community
framed it explicitly, if not always publicly, as a tool of Cold War containment
where post-war economic hardship had contributed to their electoral strength
Western European industrial output had already recovered to roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Milward and others attributed the recovery visible by 1948 mainly to domestic factors such as currency stabilisation and rising savings rates.
Proponents of the traditional view argued that Marshall aid played no meaningful role in relieving the dollar shortage regardless of domestic recovery momentum.
In Austria, Marshall assistance amounted to as much as 14% of national income in some years, compared to under 3% in the United Kingdom.
The passage presents a single, universally agreed conclusion about whether the Marshall Plan was the decisive driver of recovery.
The ongoing historical debate about the Marshall Plan is described as paralleling later disputes over foreign aid effectiveness in other contexts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Milward and others attributed the recovery visible by 1948 mainly to domestic factors such as currency stabilisation and rising savings rates.**

Paragraph 7 says Milward and others pointed instead to domestic drivers—currency stabilisation, rising savings, and pent-up demand after wartime rationing—as more decisive for the recovery already visible by 1948. The statement correctly names that domestic attribution. "More decisive" in the text is what licenses "mainly" in the statement without inventing a new ranking.

The examples need only be representative; the passage also lists pent-up demand, so naming two of the domestic drivers is still faithful. Those domestic-factor claims in Paragraph 7 match the statement.

**B) Proponents of the traditional view argued that Marshall aid played no meaningful role in relieving the dollar shortage regardless of domestic recovery momentum.**

Paragraph 7's traditional camp argued the opposite: Marshall aid was "nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage" that would otherwise have forced import cuts, even if domestic momentum existed. "No meaningful role" erases that critical-relief claim. "Nonetheless" is the hinge: they concede domestic momentum yet still insist dollar-shortage relief mattered.

**Trap:** Critics minimise aid's driving role; traditional proponents still call dollar-shortage relief critical.

Do not swap the critics' downplaying of aid as the recovery engine for the proponents' own position on dollar relief. Because proponents call aid critical for easing the dollar shortage, the "no meaningful role" line fails.

**C) In Austria, Marshall assistance amounted to as much as 14% of national income in some years, compared to under 3% in the United Kingdom.**

Paragraph 8 contrasts relative aid burdens: Austria reached as much as 14% of national income in some programme years, while the UK figure stayed under 3% throughout. Both percentages appear as stated. The comparison is share of national income, not a claim that Austria took the largest slice of the total aid pot.

Keep "as much as 14%" and "under 3%" attached to national-income weight rather than to Paragraph 3's absolute country shares. The 14% Austria versus under-3% UK contrast is Paragraph 8's own comparison, so the claim holds.

**D) The passage presents a single, universally agreed conclusion about whether the Marshall Plan was the decisive driver of recovery.**

Paragraph 9 leaves the decisive-engine versus secondary-contribution question as "a matter of ongoing historical debate," not a settled consensus. "Single, universally agreed conclusion" invents closure the text refuses. The closing even sets two competing readings side by side instead of crowning one.

**Trap:** Strong closing sentences still can announce unresolved debate rather than a winner.

If the text still says "whether… or… remains," you cannot rewrite it as unanimous agreement. Because Paragraph 9 frames the issue as ongoing debate, the universal-conclusion claim does not match the passage.

**E) The ongoing historical debate about the Marshall Plan is described as paralleling later disputes over foreign aid effectiveness in other contexts.**

Paragraph 9 says the Marshall Plan debate "closely parallels later disputes over the effectiveness of foreign aid in other contexts and eras." The parallel is explicit, not inferred. You do not need outside knowledge of those later disputes; the passage itself asserts the likeness.

Match "parallels… foreign aid… other contexts" to that closing clause rather than stretching Paragraph 6–7's Milward quarrel alone. That parallel to later foreign-aid disputes matches Paragraph 9, so the statement stands.
highlights: currency stabilisation measures, rising savings rates, and pent-up consumer demand following years of wartime rationing, as more decisive drivers of the recovery already visible by 1948
Marshall aid was nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage

as much as 14% of national income in some years of the programme, reflecting the country's particularly acute post-war needs, whereas in the United Kingdom, a considerably larger economy, the equivalent figure remained under 3%
remains a matter of ongoing historical debate
closely parallels later disputes over the effectiveness of foreign aid in other contexts and eras

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, ordered by the paragraph each relies on, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since the OEEC was formed to administer aid collectively, it can be inferred that each participating country had equal decision-making weight regardless of its size or need.
Because the plan's conditions included trade liberalisation, the passage implies economic cooperation was valued as an end in itself, not merely as a condition for receiving aid.
If the total aid of $13.3 billion was distributed evenly across all 16 participating countries, each would have received approximately $831 million.
Because Milward cited a 111%-of-1938 output figure, the passage implies he believed the Marshall Plan had no effect whatsoever on European recovery.
Because Austria's aid represented a much higher share of its national income than the UK's, it can be inferred that Austria received a larger absolute dollar amount of aid than the UK.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the OEEC was formed to administer aid collectively, it can be inferred that each participating country had equal decision-making weight regardless of its size or need.**

Collective administration does not imply equal votes. Paragraph 3 says remaining shares were divided "according to need and negotiated allocation formulas," which already signals unequal treatment. Equal decision-making weight is an extra leap the text never authorises. Joint administration can still rest on uneven bargaining power and need-based formulas.

**Trap:** "Collectively" describes joint administration, not one-country-one-vote power.

If allocation tracks need and negotiation, equal decision weight is not a safe inference from OEEC formation alone. Need-based negotiated shares contradict equal weight, so the inference fails.

**B) Because the plan's conditions included trade liberalisation, the passage implies economic cooperation was valued as an end in itself, not merely as a condition for receiving aid.**

Paragraph 4 lists tariff cuts and related reforms as requirements recipient governments had to meet to take the aid. That frames cooperation as an attached condition of the aid relationship, not as a free-standing goal divorced from receiving funds. "End in itself" overreads the conditions clause. Historians later praise the cooperation's groundwork role, but that still does not turn the original requirements into an independent ideal separate from aid.

Ask whether the text presents liberalisation as a duty tied to receiving funds or as a free-standing celebration of cooperation for its own sake. Conditions-for-aid wording does not license an independent "end in itself" motive, so the implication fails.

**C) If the total aid of $13.3 billion was distributed evenly across all 16 participating countries, each would have received approximately $831 million.**

Paragraph 2 names sixteen Western European participants; Paragraph 3 gives a total of about $13.3 billion. Splitting that total evenly yields roughly $831 million apiece ($13,300 million ÷ 16). The statement is a correct hypothetical arithmetic check, even though the passage itself describes uneven allocation. The "if" keeps the claim inside a counterfactual, so it does not deny the UK's larger real-world share.

**Tip:** Hypothetical even-split maths can still be true while the actual distribution was unequal.

Use the stated headcount and total only for the division; do not import Paragraph 3's unequal ranking into the hypothetical. The even-split calculation from the given total and sixteen countries is arithmetically sound, so the claim holds as stated.

**D) Because Milward cited a 111%-of-1938 output figure, the passage implies he believed the Marshall Plan had no effect whatsoever on European recovery.**

Milward uses the 111% figure to argue recovery was already substantially underway before large-scale aid could have driven it—a claim about timing and relative driving force. Paragraph 9's framing of the debate likewise allows "economically secondary" significance rather than absolute zero impact. "No effect whatsoever" escalates relative-weight criticism into total denial. Showing recovery before aid flowed undercuts "decisive engine," not every possible contribution.

**Trap:** "Already recovering before aid drove it" is not the same slogan as "aid did nothing at all."

Stay with Milward's timing-and-driver argument in Paragraph 6 rather than rewriting it as blanket nullity. The 111% citation questions aid as the decisive driver, not every effect, so the zero-effect implication fails.

**E) Because Austria's aid represented a much higher share of its national income than the UK's, it can be inferred that Austria received a larger absolute dollar amount of aid than the UK.**

A high share of a smaller economy's income need not mean a larger absolute cheque. Paragraph 3 already states the United Kingdom took the largest single share of total aid (~24%). Paragraph 8's 14% versus under 3% is about relative weight of aid in national income, not absolute dollars. Percentage-of-income and percentage-of-total-aid answer different questions.

**Trap:** Confusing "share of national income" with "share of the aid pot" flips Austria above the UK incorrectly.

When absolute ranking is already given for the UK, do not overturn it with Austria's higher income-share figure. The UK's largest absolute share overturns inferring a bigger Austrian dollar total from the higher income percentage.
highlights: according to need and negotiated allocation formulas
Recipient governments were required to reduce tariffs and other barriers to intra-European trade, stabilise their currencies
disbursed a total of approximately $13.3 billion in grants and loans
suggesting that the region's recovery was substantially underway before the aid could plausibly have driven it
with the United Kingdom receiving the largest single share at roughly 24% of the total

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The dollar shortage described in Paragraph 1 helps explain why relieving that shortage is presented in Paragraph 7 as a key argument for the plan's importance.

Because the plan's conditions fostered cooperation (Paragraph 4) and later integration is credited to this cooperation, it follows that the Marshall Plan alone caused the eventual creation of the European Economic Community.
The four-year disbursement period described in Paragraph 3 overlaps with the period in which Milward argues output had already reached 111% of its 1938 level.
Because containment motives are described as not always public (Paragraph 5), the passage implies American officials universally concealed this rationale from all European governments at all times.
The variation in aid's share of national income across countries (Paragraph 8) is consistent with the passage's earlier point that allocation followed need rather than equal division (Paragraph 3).
tactical_explanations:
**A) The dollar shortage described in Paragraph 1 helps explain why relieving that shortage is presented in Paragraph 7 as a key argument for the plan's importance.**

Paragraph 1 makes the dollar shortage a core reason Europe could not buy rebuilding imports. Paragraph 7's traditional proponents then call Marshall aid critical precisely because it relieved that shortage. Linking the early problem to the later defence of the plan is a fair cross-paragraph reading. The same bottleneck—scarce dollars for essential imports—reappears as the stake proponents say aid eased.

Syntheses are safe when both paragraphs name the same constraint rather than when you invent a new causal chain. The shortage-to-relief bridge across Paragraphs 1 and 7 supports the synthesis.

**B) Because the plan's conditions fostered cooperation (Paragraph 4) and later integration is credited to this cooperation, it follows that the Marshall Plan alone caused the eventual creation of the European Economic Community.**

Paragraph 4 credits institutional cooperation with laying "essential groundwork" for later integration toward the EEC. Groundwork is a contributing foundation, not sole causation. "Alone caused" upgrades a supporting role into exclusive authorship the text never claims. Even the historians' view stops at preparatory groundwork, not unique creation of the Community.

**Trap:** "Laid groundwork for X" is weaker than "alone caused X."

Keep the causal verb as weak as the passage's "groundwork" wording; do not promote it to sole cause. Sole-cause wording overstates Paragraph 4's groundwork claim, so the inference fails.

**C) The four-year disbursement period described in Paragraph 3 overlaps with the period in which Milward argues output had already reached 111% of its 1938 level.**

Paragraph 3 starts large-scale disbursement after April 1948 and runs about four years. Paragraph 6 places Milward's 111%-of-1938 output claim at the moment those large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948. The timelines meet at that 1948 onset. Overlap here means the aid window and Milward's benchmark share the 1948 starting point, not that every later aid year is identical to that output claim.

Anchor both paragraphs on "large-scale disbursements… in 1948" before you judge the timelines. The shared 1948 start of large-scale aid correctly links Paragraphs 3 and 6, so the overlap claim holds.

**D) Because containment motives are described as not always public (Paragraph 5), the passage implies American officials universally concealed this rationale from all European governments at all times.**

"If not always publicly" means disclosure was uneven or incomplete, not permanent universal secrecy toward every European government. "Universally concealed… at all times" inflates a hedge into absolute concealment. A motive can be explicit among architects yet still not constantly public without amounting to total concealment forever.

**Trap:** "Not always public" still allows some public or semi-public framing.

Do not upgrade a publicity hedge into a claim about every audience and every moment. The absolute-concealment gloss overstates Paragraph 5's qualifier, so the implication fails.

**E) The variation in aid's share of national income across countries (Paragraph 8) is consistent with the passage's earlier point that allocation followed need rather than equal division (Paragraph 3).**

Paragraph 3 divides remaining shares by need and negotiated formulas, not equal slices. Paragraph 8's wide gap—Austria up to 14% of national income versus the UK under 3%—illustrates uneven relative weight aligned with differing need. The two paragraphs push the same uneven-allocation logic. Austria's "particularly acute post-war needs" in Paragraph 8 even echoes the need-based language of Paragraph 3.

Consistency here means both passages reject equal division; it does not require identical statistics in both places. Need-based allocation plus the Austria/UK income-share gap fit together, so the consistency claim holds.
highlights: Marshall aid was nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage
laid essential groundwork for the deeper European economic integration
by the time large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948
if not always publicly
according to need and negotiated allocation formulas

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the dollar shortage not been relieved, several governments would have restricted imports of essential goods."
"The committee recommended that each government submits an annual report on its progress."
"The number of countries participating in the programme continue to be debated by historians."
"Neither the aid nor the accompanying conditions were welcomed unanimously by every government."
"Having stabilised its currency, the government was able to attract renewed investor confidence."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the dollar shortage not been relieved, several governments would have restricted imports of essential goods."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with inversion: Had + past participle replaces If + had. The main clause keeps would have + past participle (would have restricted), which pairs correctly with that unreal past condition. The negative Had… not… still belongs to the same unreal-past family as If the shortage had not been relieved.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… not… still needs would have (not would alone) in the result clause.

Check both halves: inverted past perfect in the condition and would have + past participle in the result. The Had… would have pattern is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The committee recommended that each government submits an annual report on its progress."**

After recommend that, formal English expects the subjunctive base form: submit, not the present indicative submits. The plural sense of governments does not override that mandative pattern. Each government is singular in form, but the real issue is mood: mandative that-clauses take the bare infinitive, not third-person -s.

**Trap:** Present -s after that can look like ordinary agreement while the subjunctive wants the bare verb.

Other triggering verbs in the same family include demand, insist, and suggest that. Mandative recommend that needs submit, so the line fails — "The committee recommended that each government submit an annual report on its progress."

**C) "The number of countries participating in the programme continue to be debated by historians."**

The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb because number is the grammatical head. Continue should be continues; the plural countries only modify the of-phrase. Contrast a number of, which often takes a plural verb; here the determiner is the number, so singular agreement holds.

**Trap:** Do not let the nearest plural noun steal agreement from the number.

Strip the of-phrase mentally and test The number… continues. Singular the number needs continues, so this is false — "The number of countries participating in the programme continues to be debated by historians."

**D) "Neither the aid nor the accompanying conditions were welcomed unanimously by every government."**

With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here conditions is plural, so were is the right match. The earlier singular aid does not control the verb once nor introduces a plural partner. If the nearer noun had been singular, the verb would flip to was; proximity, not the first noun, decides.

When you reverse the order to neither the conditions nor the aid, expect a singular verb instead. Proximity agreement with plural conditions makes were correct, so the sentence holds.

**E) "Having stabilised its currency, the government was able to attract renewed investor confidence."**

The perfect participle Having stabilised attaches to the government, which is the logical agent that stabilised the currency. Subject and -ing meaning align, so there is no dangling modifier. Its currency also points back to the same government, reinforcing the agent match.

A dangling version would begin with Having stabilised… and then switch to an incompatible subject such as investor confidence rose. The government is the right agent after Having stabilised, so the wording is sound.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the aid been disbursed than reconstruction efforts visibly accelerated."
"The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, were finalised before the programme began."
"Each of the participating governments have agreed to the oversight conditions."
"By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies will have already recovered significantly."
"The figures, which were compiled across sixteen countries, indicate considerable variation in need."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the aid been disbursed than reconstruction efforts visibly accelerated."**

No sooner… than correctly pairs with past-perfect inversion (had the aid been disbursed) and a simple-past follow-on clause. The correlative is than, not when, which matches the template. Inversion after No sooner is required in this formal pattern: had + subject + past participle.

Replacing than with when is a common slip that breaks the correlative pair. No sooner had… than… is formed correctly, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, were finalised before the programme began."**

Along with… is parenthetical; the true subject remains singular allocation. The verb must be was finalised, not were. Extra plural nouns after along with do not pluralise the head. The commas mark the along with phrase as an add-on, not as a second subject joined by and.

**Trap:** Comma-wrapped along with phrases often trick agreement toward the nearer plural.

As with as well as and together with, keep agreement with the head noun before the insert. Singular allocation needs was, so the line fails — "The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, was finalised before the programme began."

**C) "Each of the participating governments have agreed to the oversight conditions."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows. Have agreed should be has agreed; governments is only the of-phrase object. Each makes the subject notionally singular: every government considered one by one.

Nearby plurals after of are the usual distraction; test Each… has without the of-phrase. Each of requires has agreed, so this is false — "Each of the participating governments has agreed to the oversight conditions."

**D) "By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies will have already recovered significantly."**

By the time the programme concluded fixes a past reference point, so the main event needs past perfect (had already recovered), not future perfect will have. Future perfect looks forward from now, which clashes with a finished programme. Sequence-of-tense: a past time clause wants a past-perfect result already complete before that point.

**Trap:** By the time often invites future perfect when the time clause is past, not future.

Save will have for By the time the programme concludes (future), not concluded. A past conclusion point needs had already recovered, so the sentence fails — "By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies had already recovered significantly."

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across sixteen countries, indicate considerable variation in need."**

Figures is treated as plural throughout: were compiled in the relative clause and indicate in the main clause. Plural agreement is consistent and grammatical. The non-restrictive which-clause adds compiling detail without changing the plural head.

If the subject were The figure, both verbs would need singular forms; here plurality stays aligned. Plural figures with were / indicate matches cleanly, so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."
"Whoever administers the fund should account for the differing needs of each recipient."
"The government denied having deliberately delayed its currency stabilisation measures."
"There is several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."
"The programme, which was authorised in 1948, aimed to accelerate European recovery."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."**

Despite never takes of. Either drop of (despite the conditions) or switch to in spite of. Despite of is a common blend of the two patterns. The noun phrase the conditions attached is fine; only the preposition pairing is wrong.

**Trap:** In spite of needs of; despite stands alone before a noun phrase.

Remember the short rule: despite + noun; in spite of + noun. Despite of is ungrammatical, so the line fails — "Despite the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."

**B) "Whoever administers the fund should account for the differing needs of each recipient."**

Whoever correctly heads the subject clause (whoever administers the fund), and should account is a well-formed modal predicate for that subject. The relative sense of whoever as "the person who" fits the advising tone. Administers is singular because whoever is treated as a singular indefinite subject.

Whomever would be wrong here because the pronoun is the subject of administers, not an object. Whoever + singular verb + should account is sound, so the sentence stands.

**C) "The government denied having deliberately delayed its currency stabilisation measures."**

After deny, a perfect gerund (having + past participle) reports a prior act as the content of the denial. Having deliberately delayed places the delay before the denying, which is the intended time relation. Denied delaying would also be possible, but the perfect gerund makes the earlier timing especially clear.

Keep the -ing form after deny; a bare that-clause with a finite past is a different pattern. Denied having… is the right pattern for a prior act, so the wording holds.

**D) "There is several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."**

Existential there agrees with the notional subject that follows. Several reasons is plural, so the verb must be are, not is. There itself is a dummy; number comes from reasons, not from there.

**Trap:** There is feels default in speech even when a plural noun is coming.

Glance ahead to the noun after the verb before choosing is or are. Plural reasons needs There are, so this is false — "There are several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."

**E) "The programme, which was authorised in 1948, aimed to accelerate European recovery."**

The non-restrictive relative which was authorised modifies singular programme, and the main verb aimed agrees with that same singular subject. Relative and main clauses stay aligned. Commas mark the which-clause as extra information about the already-identified programme.

That was authorised would be more restrictive in feel; which with commas fits a known programme dated to 1948. Singular programme with was / aimed is consistent, so the sentence is sound.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "The policy was framed explicitly as a tool of containment, aiming to reduce the appeal of rival ideologies."
"Pent-up demand refers to consumer spending that has already been fully satisfied over a long period."
"The dollar shortage left governments unable to purchase the imports their reconstruction required."
"The historians' dispute centres on the relative weight assigned to domestic versus external factors."
"Containment, in this context, refers to actively expanding the political influence of a rival power."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The policy was framed explicitly as a tool of containment, aiming to reduce the appeal of rival ideologies."**

Framed as a tool of containment to reduce a rival's appeal matches both ordinary political English and the passage's own wording about containment aims. The collocation framed… as a tool of containment is natural and accurate. Reduce the appeal tracks the passage's hope of reducing communist parties' political draw.

You are checking usage and sense, not inventing a new historical claim beyond the passage vocabulary. That containment-tool framing uses the word in its established sense, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Pent-up demand refers to consumer spending that has already been fully satisfied over a long period."**

Pent-up demand is demand that has built up and remains unsatisfied, ready to be released when constraints ease. "Already fully satisfied" is the opposite of that meaning. The passage's "pent-up consumer demand following years of wartime rationing" points to stored-up, not exhausted, spending pressure. Rationing blocked spending; the demand waited, it was not used up.

**Trap:** Pent-up can sound like "a long history of spending" if you ignore the blocked/unreleased idea.

If spending is already satisfied, call it met demand, not pent-up demand. Satisfied spending is not pent-up demand, so the definition fails.

**C) "The dollar shortage left governments unable to purchase the imports their reconstruction required."**

Dollar shortage here means a lack of US dollars for buying needed imports—the same causal shape Paragraph 1 uses when Europe cannot purchase fuel, machinery, and raw materials. The verb left… unable to purchase fits the established sense. Shortage names the missing means of payment, not a shortage of the goods themselves inside Europe.

Collocation check: shortage left X unable to purchase is the passage's own causal pattern. That shortage-blocks-imports reading is standard, so the wording holds.

**D) "The historians' dispute centres on the relative weight assigned to domestic versus external factors."**

Relative weight is a natural collocation for how much importance each factor receives in an explanation. Paragraph 8's own phrase "The relative weight of the aid" uses the same idiom for comparative importance. Centres on correctly introduces the focal issue of that dispute.

Weight here means explanatory importance, not physical heaviness or a single numerical share. Relative weight for competing causal factors is correct usage, so the sentence stands.

**E) "Containment, in this context, refers to actively expanding the political influence of a rival power."**

Containment means checking or limiting a rival's spread of influence, not expanding it. Expanding a rival's reach is roughly the inverse of Cold War containment as the passage frames it. The passage's tool-of-containment framing aims to reduce communist appeal, which is limiting, not enlarging, rival influence.

**Trap:** Containment and expansion can both appear in geopolitics talk, but they pull in opposite directions.

If the definition flips limit into expand, reject it even when the topic words sound familiar. Expanding rival influence is not containment, so the definition fails.
highlights: framed it explicitly, if not always publicly, as a tool of Cold War containment
pent-up consumer demand following years of wartime rationing
a chronic shortage of US dollars left European governments unable to purchase the fuel, machinery, and raw materials needed to rebuild
The relative weight of the aid also varied considerably by recipient
as a tool of Cold War containment

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "The programme's disbursements were conditional on recipient governments meeting certain requirements."
"A country's aid representing a high share of its national income implies that country needed proportionally more support."
"Multilateral cooperation refers to a single country acting entirely independently of all others."
"The recovery was described as already gathering momentum before large-scale aid had fully arrived."
"Historians who dispute a plan's decisive role are, by definition, claiming the plan had absolutely no effect at all."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The programme's disbursements were conditional on recipient governments meeting certain requirements."**

Conditional on correctly means "depending on" fulfilment of requirements. Paragraph 2 uses the same structure when Marshall's proposal is conditional on joint European coordination. The collocation matches established usage. Disbursements… conditional on keeps the money tied to prior compliance, which is the ordinary aid-condition sense.

If the sentence said regardless of requirements, it would break both the collocation and the passage logic. Conditional on + requirements is sound, so the sentence stands.

**B) "A country's aid representing a high share of its national income implies that country needed proportionally more support."**

Paragraph 8 links Austria's high aid-to-income share to particularly acute post-war needs, while a larger economy like the UK stays under 3%. Reading a high national-income share as a signal of proportionally greater need follows that framing. Proportionally is doing the work: the claim is about relative burden, not about beating the UK in absolute dollars.

Keep this sense distinct from Paragraph 3's largest absolute share ranking for the United Kingdom. That income-share reading of relative need fits the passage's contrast, so the claim holds.

**C) "Multilateral cooperation refers to a single country acting entirely independently of all others."**

Multilateral means involving several parties acting together. A single country acting entirely alone is unilateral independence—the opposite. The passage praises multilateral cooperation precisely as joint, many-sided practice. Multi- marks many participants, not many choices for one actor.

**Trap:** Multi- can be misread as "many options for one actor" instead of "many actors."

Pair multilateral with joint coordination language from the passage, not with solo policy. Solo independence is not multilateral cooperation, so the definition fails.

**D) "The recovery was described as already gathering momentum before large-scale aid had fully arrived."**

Paragraph 9's secondary-contribution framing speaks of "a recovery already gathering its own momentum," and Milward's camp places substantial recovery before large-scale 1948 disbursements. Gathering momentum ahead of full aid arrival is faithful wording. The sentence reports how the recovery is described in the debate, not a new causal verdict you must invent.

Match gathering momentum to Paragraph 9's phrasing and the pre-aid timing in Paragraph 6. Already gathering momentum before major aid matches the passage's debate terms, so the sentence stands.

**E) "Historians who dispute a plan's decisive role are, by definition, claiming the plan had absolutely no effect at all."**

Disputing a decisive role questions degree of importance—whether the plan was the main engine—not every possible effect. Paragraph 9 even allows an "economically secondary contribution," which still grants some role. "Absolutely no effect" collapses graded disagreement into total denial. By definition overreaches: the debate vocabulary itself includes secondary, not null, contributions.

**Trap:** Decisive versus secondary is about weight, not presence versus absence.

If the text still allows politically significant or economically secondary effects, zero-effect is too strong. Challenging a decisive role is not the same as claiming zero effect, so the definition fails.
highlights: conditional on European governments jointly coordinating their own reconstruction efforts
as much as 14% of national income in some years of the programme, reflecting the country's particularly acute post-war needs
market-oriented reconstruction and multilateral cooperation
a recovery already gathering its own momentum
Whether the Marshall Plan should be understood primarily as the decisive engine of Western European recovery, or as a politically significant but economically secondary contribution

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Choice architecture is described as a strategy that works by restricting the available options rather than redesigning their presentation.
Nudging is described as a strategy that redesigns the context of a choice without removing any options from the menu.
Under opt-in enrolment, average retirement plan participation in the cited 2015 study was around 61%, rising to approximately 91% under opt-out enrolment.
The underlying menu of retirement plan options is described as changing substantially when employers switched from opt-in to opt-out enrolment.
The gap between opt-in and opt-out organ donation consent rates is attributed in the passage primarily to differing cultural attitudes toward donation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Choice architecture is described as a strategy that works by restricting the available options rather than redesigning their presentation.**

Paragraph 1 draws the opposite contrast: proponents exploit choice architecture "not by restricting options, but by redesigning the context in which choices are made." Restricting the menu is exactly what nudging is said to avoid. The paragraph introduces choice architecture as being about "the specific way choices are presented," which is a claim about presentation, not about availability.

**Trap:** Flipping the "not X but Y" contrast is a classic false reading.

When a passage uses a "not… but…" frame, the item writer only has to swap the two halves to manufacture a plausible-sounding falsehood, so read that construction slowly and note which side the author actually endorses. The claim reverses Paragraph 1's wording, so it fails — the passage keeps options open and redesigns context instead.

**B) Nudging is described as a strategy that redesigns the context of a choice without removing any options from the menu.**

Paragraph 1 defines nudging as redesigning the choice context without restricting options, and Paragraph 2 confirms the retirement menu "remaining unchanged" while enrolment still shifted. The definition and the worked example therefore point in the same direction rather than pulling against each other.

**Tip:** Pair the general definition with the concrete "menu…unchanged" proof.

True statements in this format usually combine a definition from one paragraph with an illustration from another, so confirming both halves is quicker than hunting for a single perfect sentence. The statement tracks both the strategy and the unchanged menu, so it matches the passage.

**C) Under opt-in enrolment, average retirement plan participation in the cited 2015 study was around 61%, rising to approximately 91% under opt-out enrolment.**

Paragraph 2 states opt-in participation "averaged around 61%" and that under automatic opt-out enrolment it "rose to approximately 91%." The statement simply restates those figures in order. Both the hedging words ("around," "approximately") and the direction of movement are preserved, which is what a faithful restatement should do.

**Tip:** Check that each number stays attached to its own enrolment system.

Number items are usually falsified by switching which figure belongs to which condition, so match each percentage to its label before deciding. The numbers line up with Paragraph 2, so the claim holds.

**D) The underlying menu of retirement plan options is described as changing substantially when employers switched from opt-in to opt-out enrolment.**

Paragraph 2 says participation rose "despite the underlying menu of retirement options remaining unchanged." The menu stays the same; only the default enrolment rule changes. That contrast is the entire point of the example, since holding the options fixed is what isolates the default as the active ingredient.

**Trap:** "Changed substantially" invents a rewrite of options the text expressly denies.

The word "despite" is the grammatical signal here: it marks the menu as the thing that did not change while participation did. The claim fails because the passage says the menu remained unchanged.

**E) The gap between opt-in and opt-out organ donation consent rates is attributed in the passage primarily to differing cultural attitudes toward donation.**

Paragraph 3 attributes the consent gap "not to differing cultural attitudes toward donation but to the powerful effect of the default option itself." Culture is named only to be rejected. Mentioning an explanation in order to dismiss it is not the same as endorsing it, and the passage is explicit about which side it lands on.

**Trap:** The passage's "not…but…" construction flips cleanly into a false cultural claim.

Whenever you can find the candidate explanation in the text, check whether it appears after "not" before you accept it as the author's view. The statement fails because the text credits the default, not culture.
highlights: not by restricting options, but by redesigning the context
despite the underlying menu of retirement options remaining unchanged

participation in a 2015 study of US employers averaged around 61%. When employers instead switched to automatic, opt-out enrolment — in which employees are enrolled by default unless they actively choose to leave — participation in the same study rose to approximately 91%
despite the underlying menu of retirement options remaining unchanged
not to differing cultural attitudes toward donation but to the powerful effect of the default option itself

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The cafeteria experiment found that placing fruit at eye level increased its selection while removing dessert from the menu entirely.
"Libertarian paternalism" is described as preserving the formal freedom to choose an alternative outcome, even while steering people toward a particular one.
Critics of nudging argue that exploiting cognitive biases sits comfortably alongside genuine respect for individual autonomy.
A 2022 meta-analysis found an average nudge effect of approximately 8.7 percentage points, which fell to approximately 1.4 percentage points after adjusting for publication bias.
The adjustment for publication bias is described as increasing confidence that nudges are more powerful than the original literature suggested.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The cafeteria experiment found that placing fruit at eye level increased its selection while removing dessert from the menu entirely.**

Paragraph 4 reports fruit rose ~25% at eye level and dessert fell ~15% when moved to a less convenient spot, "again without removing any option from the menu." Dessert was relocated, not deleted. The word "again" links this small-scale case back to the earlier examples, all of which keep the full set of choices intact.

**Trap:** "Removing…entirely" smuggles a ban that the passage explicitly refuses.

Half-true items like this pair one accurate detail (the fruit result) with one fabricated detail (the removal), and a single wrong clause is enough to sink the whole statement. The claim fails because no option was removed from the menu.

**B) "Libertarian paternalism" is described as preserving the formal freedom to choose an alternative outcome, even while steering people toward a particular one.**

Paragraph 5 defines the approach as paternalistic (steering toward assumed interests) yet libertarian because it "preserves the formal freedom to choose otherwise." Steering plus retained exit is the whole point of the label. The two halves of the term are meant to sit in tension, which is exactly what the statement reproduces.

**Tip:** For hyphenated or paradoxical labels, check that both halves survive in the restatement.

A statement that keeps only the steering or only the freedom would misdescribe the concept, but this one keeps both. That definition matches the statement, so the claim holds.

**C) Critics of nudging argue that exploiting cognitive biases sits comfortably alongside genuine respect for individual autonomy.**

Paragraph 5 says critics argue that exploiting biases such as status quo bias and loss aversion "sits uneasily with genuine respect for individual autonomy." "Comfortably" reverses "uneasily." Everything else in the statement is copied faithfully, which is what makes the single swapped adverb easy to skim past.

**Trap:** Softening "uneasily" into "comfortably" flips the critics' stance.

Critics are, by definition, raising an objection, so an item that has them endorsing the practice should trigger suspicion before you even locate the line. The claim fails because critics say the practice sits uneasily with autonomy.

**D) A 2022 meta-analysis found an average nudge effect of approximately 8.7 percentage points, which fell to approximately 1.4 percentage points after adjusting for publication bias.**

Paragraph 6 gives both figures in order: ~8.7 percentage points on average, then ~1.4 after adjusting for publication bias. The statement copies that before/after pair. It also keeps the causal ordering intact, with the adjustment coming after the headline figure rather than before it.

**Tip:** For before/after numbers, verify the sequence as well as the values.

A common falsification is to keep both numbers but reverse which one is the corrected estimate. The figures match Paragraph 6, so the claim holds.

**E) The adjustment for publication bias is described as increasing confidence that nudges are more powerful than the original literature suggested.**

After the adjustment, Paragraph 6 says the published literature "may have substantially overstated how powerful typical nudges actually are." Correction shrinks the estimated effect; it does not boost confidence that nudges are stronger. The direction of the numbers alone settles this, since 1.4 is well below 8.7.

**Trap:** "More powerful" inverts the "overstated" verdict.

"Overstated" means the earlier figure was too high, so any statement built on the idea that nudges turned out stronger is running against the passage's arithmetic and its conclusion. The claim fails because the bias adjustment weakens, not strengthens, the typical-effect story.
highlights: again without removing any option from the menu
preserves the formal freedom to choose otherwise
sits uneasily with genuine respect for individual autonomy

average behaviour-change effect of approximately 8.7 percentage points. However, once the analysis was adjusted to account for publication bias — the tendency for studies with small or null effects to go unpublished — the estimated average effect size fell to approximately 1.4 percentage points
the published literature may have substantially overstated how powerful typical nudges actually are

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: By 2022, more than 200 dedicated behavioural insights units were reported to be operating across over 60 countries.
The UK's Behavioural Insights Team was founded before the term "sludge" was introduced by Thaler in the passage's account.
"Sludge," as defined in the passage, refers to friction that encourages a desired action rather than discouraging it.
Ethicists are described as generally viewing retirement savings defaults as more ethically contentious than sludge practices that benefit the nudging institution.
The passage concludes by presenting nudging's effectiveness and ethical status as a settled, noncontroversial matter.
tactical_explanations:
**A) By 2022, more than 200 dedicated behavioural insights units were reported to be operating across over 60 countries.**

Paragraph 7 reports exactly that scale: "by 2022, more than 200 dedicated behavioural insights units were reported to be operating across over 60 countries." The statement keeps both the date and the two "more than / over" thresholds in place rather than converting them into exact counts.

**Tip:** Preserved hedges ("more than," "over," "reported") are a sign of a faithful restatement.

When an item reproduces a sentence almost word for word, your job is simply to confirm no quantifier or date has been quietly nudged. The statement restates Paragraph 7's figures, so it matches the passage.

**B) The UK's Behavioural Insights Team was founded before the term "sludge" was introduced by Thaler in the passage's account.**

Paragraph 7 places the UK team's founding in 2010; Paragraph 8 says Thaler "later drew a related distinction" introducing "sludge." On the passage's timeline, 2010 precedes that later distinction. Note that the ordering comes from the word "later" rather than from a second date, so the text supplies the sequence without supplying a year.

**Tip:** Chronology items hinge on "founded in 2010" versus "later."

Relative time markers count as evidence just as much as explicit dates do, provided you anchor them to the event they follow. The founding precedes the sludge distinction in the text, so the claim holds.

**C) "Sludge," as defined in the passage, refers to friction that encourages a desired action rather than discouraging it.**

Paragraph 8 defines sludge as "friction deliberately or carelessly introduced into a process to discourage a desired action." Encouraging is the opposite of that definition. The illustration given — an unnecessarily complicated cancellation procedure — makes the obstructive intent unmistakable.

**Trap:** Swapping encourage/discourage reverses the sludge concept.

If a definition item feels almost right, test it against the example the passage attaches to the term, since the example usually exposes the reversal immediately. The claim fails because sludge is friction that discourages, not encourages, a desired action.

**D) Ethicists are described as generally viewing retirement savings defaults as more ethically contentious than sludge practices that benefit the nudging institution.**

Paragraph 8 says ethicists generally treat individual-benefiting defaults such as retirement savings as "less ethically contentious" than institution-benefiting sludge. "More" flips "less." The underlying principle is who gains from the intervention, and interventions that benefit the person being nudged draw the milder judgement.

**Trap:** Comparative polarity (less vs more) is the whole trap.

With comparison items, identify which side the passage ranks higher before reading the statement, so a swapped comparative stands out at once. The claim fails because retirement defaults are treated as less, not more, contentious.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting nudging's effectiveness and ethical status as a settled, noncontroversial matter.**

Paragraph 9 leaves the question "open and actively contested" among economists and policymakers. Nothing in the close presents the debate as settled. The final paragraph in fact sets out two rival characterisations — an effective, defensible tool versus an overstated policy fashion — without choosing between them.

**Trap:** "Settled" claims rarely survive a concluding paragraph built on "whether… or…".

A closing sentence that lays out competing possibilities is signalling unresolved debate, not consensus. The claim fails because the passage ends on an open, contested question.
highlights: by 2022, more than 200 dedicated behavioural insights units were reported to be operating across over 60 countries
Following the founding of the UK's Behavioural Insights Team in 2010
friction deliberately or carelessly introduced into a process to discourage a desired action
less ethically contentious than nudges or sludge practices that primarily benefit the nudging institution
remains an open and actively contested question

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, ordered by the paragraph each relies on, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since opt-out enrolment increased retirement participation without changing the menu of options, it can be inferred that the default option itself, not the options available, drove the change.
If participation rose from 61% to 91% under opt-out enrolment, this represents an increase of exactly 30 percentage points.

Because organ donation consent rates differ sharply between opt-in and opt-out countries, it follows that opt-out countries must have citizens who are, on average, more altruistic than those in opt-in countries.
Because critics question whether "libertarian paternalism" understates manipulation, the passage implies critics believe nudges leave individuals with no meaningful choice whatsoever.
Since the meta-analysis found a smaller effect after adjusting for publication bias, it can be inferred that nudges have no measurable effect on behaviour at all.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since opt-out enrolment increased retirement participation without changing the menu of options, it can be inferred that the default option itself, not the options available, drove the change.**

Paragraph 2 holds the menu fixed while only the enrolment default changes, and participation still jumps. With options held constant, the default is the factor the passage leaves you to credit. This is the same logic Paragraph 3 states outright for organ donation, where the default is named as the operative cause.

**Tip:** Same menu + different default → infer the default drove the shift.

A safe inference only rearranges what the text already supplies; here it identifies the one variable the passage reports as changing. That inference is licensed by Paragraph 2, so the claim holds.

**B) If participation rose from 61% to 91% under opt-out enrolment, this represents an increase of exactly 30 percentage points.**

Paragraph 2's 61% → 91% shift is "an increase of roughly 30 percentage points." 91 − 61 = 30, so "exactly 30" matches the arithmetic the passage itself frames as roughly 30. The passage hedges because its own inputs are averages, but the subtraction of the two stated figures is unambiguous.

**Tip:** Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages, not a percentage change.

Had the statement claimed a roughly 49% relative increase, that would be a different calculation entirely, so keep the unit straight. The arithmetic matches the cited figures, so the claim holds.

**C) Because organ donation consent rates differ sharply between opt-in and opt-out countries, it follows that opt-out countries must have citizens who are, on average, more altruistic than those in opt-in countries.**

Paragraph 3 rejects cultural-attitude explanations and credits "the powerful effect of the default option itself." Inferring greater altruism reimports the explanation the text rules out. Because the mechanism is administrative rather than attitudinal, the consent gap says nothing about the generosity of the populations involved.

**Trap:** Sharp rate gaps invite personality stories the passage explicitly refuses.

An inference that requires a claim the author has already denied is not an inference at all. The inference fails because the passage attributes the gap to defaults, not altruism.

**D) Because critics question whether "libertarian paternalism" understates manipulation, the passage implies critics believe nudges leave individuals with no meaningful choice whatsoever.**

Critics worry about exploitation of bias "regardless of how easy the opt-out technically remains." Their concern is about manipulative steering, not about zero remaining choice — the text still stresses that the exit stays open. The phrase "regardless of" concedes that the opt-out exists while arguing that its existence does not settle the ethics.

**Trap:** "Understates manipulation" is not "leaves no choice."

Overstating a critic's position into an absolute is one of the most common inference traps, so check whether the text supports the extreme version or only the moderate one. The claim overreaches; critics contest autonomy under residual opt-out, not total absence of choice.

**E) Since the meta-analysis found a smaller effect after adjusting for publication bias, it can be inferred that nudges have no measurable effect on behaviour at all.**

Paragraph 6's adjusted estimate is still "approximately 1.4 percentage points" — smaller, not zero. A reduced positive average is not evidence of no measurable effect.
