The passage's own conclusion is the weaker one, that published work may have overstated the size of typical effects, not that those effects vanish.

**Trap:** "Smaller" is not "none."

Watch for absolute words such as "no," "all," or "never" in inference items, since the text usually supports only a graded version of the claim. The inference fails because 1.4 percentage points remains a measurable average effect.
highlights: despite the underlying menu of retirement options remaining unchanged
an increase of roughly 30 percentage points
not to differing cultural attitudes toward donation but to the powerful effect of the default option itself
regardless of how easy the opt-out technically remains
the estimated average effect size fell to approximately 1.4 percentage points

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The retirement enrolment example (Paragraph 2) and the organ donation example (Paragraph 3) both illustrate the same underlying mechanism: the power of a default option to shape behaviour.

Because both the retirement and organ donation examples show large default effects, and because the 2022 meta-analysis found smaller effects after correcting for publication bias, the passage implies these specific large-scale, real-world default effects have themselves been shown to be overstated.

The publication bias adjustment discussed in Paragraph 6, which reduced the estimated average effect from 8.7 to 1.4 percentage points, is presented as a reason for caution when generalising from published nudge studies.
The rapid global spread of behavioural insights units (Paragraph 7) is presented as proof that the concerns raised about publication bias (Paragraph 6) have been fully resolved.

The distinction between nudges and "sludge" (Paragraph 8) helps explain why not all behavioural interventions are treated as equally ethically acceptable, consistent with the passage's closing framing of nudging as a contested rather than uniformly endorsed practice (Paragraph 9).
tactical_explanations:
**A) The retirement enrolment example (Paragraph 2) and the organ donation example (Paragraph 3) both illustrate the same underlying mechanism: the power of a default option to shape behaviour.**

Both paragraphs keep the choice set largely intact while changing who must act to leave the default; Paragraph 3 even names "the powerful effect of the default option itself." Shared mechanism, two domains. In each case the reported jump — 61% to 91% for pensions, 15% to about 98% for donor consent — follows a switch in who bears the burden of acting.

**Tip:** Two examples in adjacent paragraphs usually share one mechanism; name it before answering.

Recognising the common thread lets you handle synthesis items without rereading both paragraphs in full. The synthesis matches how Paragraphs 2–3 are framed, so the claim holds.

**B) Because both the retirement and organ donation examples show large default effects, and because the 2022 meta-analysis found smaller effects after correcting for publication bias, the passage implies these specific large-scale, real-world default effects have themselves been shown to be overstated.**

Paragraph 6's bias adjustment concerns the published nudge literature on average; it never reapplies that correction to the retirement or organ-donation figures cited earlier. Combining them invents a link the text does not make. The passage keeps the two discussions separate, reporting the case-study figures without flagging them as inflated.

**Trap:** A general meta-analytic caution is not a rebuttal of named case studies.

Synthesis items often fail precisely here, by welding two accurate paragraphs into a conclusion the author never draws. The claim fails because the passage does not say those specific defaults were themselves overstated.

**C) The publication bias adjustment discussed in Paragraph 6, which reduced the estimated average effect from 8.7 to 1.4 percentage points, is presented as a reason for caution when generalising from published nudge studies.**

After reporting the drop to ~1.4, Paragraph 6 concludes the published literature "may have substantially overstated" typical nudge power — precisely a caution about generalising from the uncorrected average. The paragraph even opens by calling the empirical robustness of nudging "a matter of considerable dispute," which frames the whole discussion as a warning.

**Tip:** Look for the paragraph's own concluding clause; it usually states the intended takeaway.

Here the takeaway sentence and the statement say the same thing in different words. That is the passage's own framing, so the claim holds.

**D) The rapid global spread of behavioural insights units (Paragraph 7) is presented as proof that the concerns raised about publication bias (Paragraph 6) have been fully resolved.**

Paragraph 7 narrates institutional uptake after 2010; Paragraph 6's empirical dispute is left standing. Popularity of units is not offered as proof that bias concerns are settled. Paragraph 7 in fact opens with "Despite this ongoing debate," which marks the spread as happening alongside the dispute rather than because it ended.

**Trap:** Adoption ≠ resolution of an effect-size debate.

A concessive opener like "despite" tells you the two paragraphs stand in tension, not in a proof relationship. The claim fails because the text never treats global spread as solving the publication-bias worry.

**E) The distinction between nudges and "sludge" (Paragraph 8) helps explain why not all behavioural interventions are treated as equally ethically acceptable, consistent with the passage's closing framing of nudging as a contested rather than uniformly endorsed practice (Paragraph 9).**

Paragraph 8 grades ethics by who benefits; Paragraph 9 leaves effectiveness and defensibility "open and actively contested." The sludge distinction supplies one reason the practice is not treated as uniformly fine. The two paragraphs fit together because a category that contains both benign defaults and obstructive sludge cannot be judged with a single verdict.

**Tip:** Check that the linking word — here "consistent with" — matches the strength of the textual connection.

This statement claims compatibility rather than proof, which is a modest enough claim for the text to support. Valid cross-paragraph synthesis, so the claim holds.
highlights: the powerful effect of the default option itself
the published literature may have substantially overstated how powerful typical nudges actually are
suggesting that the published literature may have substantially overstated how powerful typical nudges actually are
by 2022, more than 200 dedicated behavioural insights units were reported to be operating across over 60 countries
less ethically contentious than nudges or sludge practices that primarily benefit the nudging institution at the individual's expense

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the default option not been changed, participation rates would have remained substantially lower."
"The committee recommended that the agency reassesses its use of automatic enrolment."
"The number of countries adopting behavioural insights units continue to rise each year."
"Neither the researchers nor the funding body were aware of the publication bias at first."
"Having corrected for publication bias, the researchers reported a smaller average effect size."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the default option not been changed, participation rates would have remained substantially lower."**

This is a well-formed third conditional with inversion: "Had…not been changed" stands for "If…had not been changed," paired with "would have remained" for the unreal past result. The negation sits correctly after the subject, which is where it belongs once "if" is dropped.

**Tip:** Inverted Had + past participle replaces If + had without changing the tense pattern.

Inversion is a register choice rather than a grammar change, so the main clause still needs "would have" plus a past participle. The conditional structure is sound, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "The committee recommended that the agency reassesses its use of automatic enrolment."**

After "recommended that," formal English wants the mandative subjunctive — the base form "reassess," not third-person "reassesses." The subjunctive is unmarked for person and number, so the same base form would appear regardless of the subject.

**Trap:** Ordinary present-tense -s often creeps in after recommend/insist/require + that.

The same pattern applies to "suggest," "demand," "propose," and "ask that," all of which take the bare infinitive in this construction. The verb form is wrong, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**C) "The number of countries adopting behavioural insights units continue to rise each year."**

The head noun is singular "number," so the verb must be singular: "continues," not "continue." The plural "countries" in the of-phrase does not control agreement. The participial phrase "adopting behavioural insights units" only modifies "countries" and pushes the real subject further from its verb.

**Trap:** "The number of…" is singular; "a number of…" is plural.

Strip out everything between the head noun and the verb, then test the agreement on what remains. Subject–verb agreement fails, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**D) "Neither the researchers nor the funding body were aware of the publication bias at first."**

With "neither…nor," many accepted usages allow a plural verb when the coordinated subjects are different parties treated jointly as unaware. "Were aware" fits that joint reading of researchers and funding body. The strict proximity rule would look only at "the funding body," but the notional-agreement reading covers both parties together.

**Tip:** Neither…nor agreement depends on how the coordinated subjects are construed.

Because both readings are attested in careful writing, this sentence is not the error the item is hunting for. The agreement is acceptable in this neither…nor pattern, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**E) "Having corrected for publication bias, the researchers reported a smaller average effect size."**

The perfect participle "Having corrected…" correctly attaches to "the researchers," who did the correcting and then reported. No dangling modifier. The perfect form also signals that the correction was completed before the reporting, which matches the intended sequence.

**Tip:** Check that the noun immediately after the participial comma is the one performing the action.

Had the main clause begun with "the effect size," the modifier would dangle, since an effect size cannot correct anything. The opener and subject align, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the default been switched than participation rates began to climb."
"The policy, along with several accompanying reforms, were introduced the same year."
"Each of the surveyed employers have adopted some form of automatic enrolment."
"By the time the meta-analysis was published, several earlier studies will have already been cited widely."
"The findings, which were adjusted for publication bias, suggest a smaller true effect."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the default been switched than participation rates began to climb."**

"No sooner…than" correctly triggers inversion ("had the default been switched") with past perfect in the first clause and simple past ("began") in the second. The negative adverbial in front position is what forces the auxiliary ahead of the subject.

**Tip:** Remember the pair is no sooner…than (not when/then).

Other fronted negatives such as "hardly," "scarcely," and "not until" behave the same way, so learning the pattern once covers several items. The correlative and tense pattern are right, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "The policy, along with several accompanying reforms, were introduced the same year."**

"Along with…" is parenthetical; the true subject is singular "policy," which needs "was introduced," not "were." The commas around the phrase are the visual clue that it sits outside the subject.

**Trap:** Extra nouns after along with/as well as often steal plural agreement wrongly.

Only "and" creates a genuinely compound subject; prepositional add-ons like "together with," "in addition to," and "as well as" leave the number of the head noun untouched. Agreement fails, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**C) "Each of the surveyed employers have adopted some form of automatic enrolment."**

"Each of" takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows: "has adopted," not "have." "Each" picks out members of the group one at a time, which is why the singular is required despite the plural noun.

**Trap:** The plural after "of" is not the agreement controller.

The same rule governs "every one of," "either of," and "neither of," all of which stay singular. The verb should be singular, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**D) "By the time the meta-analysis was published, several earlier studies will have already been cited widely."**

"By the time…was published" sets a past reference point, so earlier completion needs past perfect ("had already been cited"), not future perfect "will have." The two clauses have to share a single timeframe, and the first clause fixes it in the past.

**Trap:** Future perfect cannot sit after a past "by the time" anchor.

Swap the anchor to "by the time the meta-analysis is published" and the future perfect becomes correct, which shows the problem is consistency rather than the verb form itself. The tense is incompatible with the past timeframe, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**E) "The findings, which were adjusted for publication bias, suggest a smaller true effect."**

Plural "findings" correctly takes "were adjusted" in the relative clause and plural "suggest" in the main clause. The non-restrictive clause is properly fenced by commas, so removing it leaves a complete sentence.

**Tip:** Test agreement by deleting the comma-bracketed clause and rereading the core sentence.

"The findings suggest a smaller true effect" stands on its own, confirming both verbs are correctly numbered. Agreement is consistent throughout, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the criticism, many governments continued expanding their behavioural insights units."
"Whoever designs the next nudge should account for how easily people can opt out."
"The agency denied having deliberately concealed the smaller adjusted effect size."
"There is several reasons why publication bias distorts the nudge literature."
"The unit, which was established in 2010, aimed to apply behavioural insights to public policy."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the criticism, many governments continued expanding their behavioural insights units."**

"Despite" never takes "of"; the correct forms are "despite the criticism" or "in spite of the criticism." The rest of the sentence is fine, so the single stray preposition is the whole problem.

**Trap:** Mixing despite with the of from in spite of is a high-frequency error.

Both expressions are followed by a noun phrase rather than a clause, which is why "despite the criticism" works while "despite the criticism was loud" would not. The preposition pattern is wrong, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**B) "Whoever designs the next nudge should account for how easily people can opt out."**

"Whoever" properly heads the subject clause ("Whoever designs…"), and "should account" is a well-formed main-clause verb phrase. The embedded question "how easily people can opt out" also keeps statement word order, as indirect questions require.

**Tip:** Choose whoever when the pronoun is the subject inside its own clause, whomever when it is an object.

Here the pronoun performs the verb "designs," so the subject form is right. The structure is grammatical, so the sentence is correct.

**C) "The agency denied having deliberately concealed the smaller adjusted effect size."**

After "denied," the perfect gerund "having…concealed" correctly marks a prior alleged act. Form and meaning align. "Deny" takes a gerund rather than an infinitive, so "denied to conceal" would be ungrammatical.

**Tip:** The perfect gerund signals that the denied action predates the denial itself.

The adverb "deliberately" sits comfortably between the auxiliary and the participle without disturbing the structure. The perfect-gerund complement is right, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**D) "There is several reasons why publication bias distorts the nudge literature."**

Existential "there" agreement follows the real subject: plural "reasons" requires "There are," not "There is." The word "there" is only a placeholder and carries no number of its own.

**Trap:** "There is" + plural noun is a classic agreement miss.

Because the verb precedes the notional subject, it is easy to commit to the singular before reaching the plural noun, which is exactly the slip this item tests. Number agreement fails, so the sentence is not grammatically correct.

**E) "The unit, which was established in 2010, aimed to apply behavioural insights to public policy."**

Singular "unit" takes singular "was established" in the non-restrictive clause and singular "aimed" in the main clause. The commas correctly mark the clause as supplementary information about an already identified unit.

**Tip:** Use which with commas for non-restrictive clauses and that without commas for restrictive ones.

Since the unit is specific rather than being narrowed down by the clause, the comma-plus-which pattern is the right choice. Agreement and relative-clause form are sound, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "Choice architecture refers to redesigning the presentation of options without necessarily removing any of them."
"Sludge refers to friction deliberately introduced to make a desired action easier to complete."
"Status quo bias describes a tendency to prefer the current state of affairs over changing it."
"Libertarian paternalism was described as steering people toward an outcome while still preserving their formal freedom to choose otherwise."
"Publication bias refers to the tendency for null or small-effect studies to be published more often than significant ones."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Choice architecture refers to redesigning the presentation of options without necessarily removing any of them."**

Paragraph 1 ties choice architecture to how choices are presented and stresses redesigning context rather than restricting options. The sentence's meaning matches that framing. The hedge "without necessarily removing" is also careful rather than absolute, which keeps it within what the passage supports.

**Tip:** Vocabulary items reward matching the concept, not hunting for identical words.

The sentence paraphrases the definition instead of quoting it, and a faithful paraphrase counts as correct usage. The use of "choice architecture" is accurate, so the claim holds.

**B) "Sludge refers to friction deliberately introduced to make a desired action easier to complete."**

Paragraph 8 defines sludge as friction that discourages a desired action (for example, a complicated cancellation). "Easier" reverses that meaning. Friction and ease are opposites, so the sentence is self-contradictory even before you check it against the passage.

**Trap:** Sludge is stickiness that blocks, not grease that helps.

When a definition item keeps the right noun but inverts the purpose clause, the error usually sits in a single verb or adjective near the end. The definition is inverted, so the wording is not used correctly.

**C) "Status quo bias describes a tendency to prefer the current state of affairs over changing it."**

That is the ordinary meaning of status quo bias, and Paragraph 5 lists it among the cognitive biases nudges exploit when defaults stick. The sentence uses the term correctly. It also explains why defaults are powerful in the first place: leaving the current arrangement in place requires no action.

**Tip:** For named biases, check the standard definition and then confirm it fits the passage's use.

Here both tests agree, since the bias is exactly what makes an unchanged default persist. The meaning matches established usage (and the passage's framing), so the claim holds.

**D) "Libertarian paternalism was described as steering people toward an outcome while still preserving their formal freedom to choose otherwise."**

Paragraph 5's definition is exactly that mix of steering and preserved formal freedom. The sentence restates it faithfully. The adjective "formal" is doing real work, since it is precisely the word critics later press on when they question how much autonomy remains.

**Tip:** Keep qualifying adjectives like "formal" intact; dropping them can change a true item into a false one.

This restatement retains both halves of the paradox and the qualifier attached to "freedom." The term is used as the passage defines it, so the claim holds.

**E) "Publication bias refers to the tendency for null or small-effect studies to be published more often than significant ones."**

Paragraph 6 defines publication bias as "the tendency for studies with small or null effects to go unpublished" — the opposite of being published more often. That direction is what makes the correction reduce the average effect rather than raise it.

**Trap:** Flipping unpublished ↔ published more often reverses the bias.

You can sanity-check the direction using the numbers: if weak studies were over-published, correcting for the bias would push the estimate up, not down from 8.7 to 1.4. The definition is wrong, so the wording is not used correctly.
highlights: not by restricting options, but by redesigning the context
friction deliberately or carelessly introduced into a process to discourage a desired action
exploiting known cognitive biases such as status quo bias and loss aversion
preserves the formal freedom to choose otherwise
the tendency for studies with small or null effects to go unpublished

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "A behavioural insights unit applies findings from psychology and economics to inform public policy design."
"An opt-out default means citizens must actively register before being included in a scheme."
"Loss aversion describes a tendency to weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent potential gains."
"A nudge, by the passage's definition, necessarily removes certain options from an individual's choice set."
"An effect size shrinking after correction for publication bias suggests the original estimate may have been inflated."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "A behavioural insights unit applies findings from psychology and economics to inform public policy design."**

Paragraph 7 describes such units applying behavioural techniques across tax compliance, health messaging, and related policy domains. The sentence's meaning fits that institutional role. The passage also traces the model back to the UK's 2010 team, whose purpose was to bring behavioural findings into public administration.

**Tip:** For institutional terms, check the function described rather than the exact job title.

The statement describes what these units do, and that description matches Paragraph 7. The term is used appropriately, so the claim holds.

**B) "An opt-out default means citizens must actively register before being included in a scheme."**

That describes opt-in. Under opt-out / presumed consent, people are included by default unless they actively object (Paragraphs 2–3). The defining question is who has to take action, and under opt-out it is the person who wants to leave.

**Trap:** Opt-in vs opt-out swap is the whole error.

A quick test is to ask what happens to someone who does nothing: under opt-out they are enrolled, under opt-in they are not. The definition names the wrong default rule, so the wording is not used correctly.

**C) "Loss aversion describes a tendency to weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent potential gains."**

That is the standard meaning of loss aversion, which Paragraph 5 lists among the biases nudges exploit. The sentence uses the term correctly. The word "equivalent" matters, since the bias is about asymmetric weighting of gains and losses of the same size.

**Tip:** Precision words in a definition often carry the concept; check them rather than skimming.

Both the direction of the asymmetry and the equal-magnitude comparison are stated accurately here. The meaning matches established usage, so the claim holds.

**D) "A nudge, by the passage's definition, necessarily removes certain options from an individual's choice set."**

Paragraph 1 stresses redesign "not by restricting options," and Paragraph 4 repeats that options stay on the menu. Removing choices is the opposite of the passage's nudge definition. Preserving the full choice set is what allows Thaler and Sunstein to call the approach libertarian at all.

**Trap:** "Necessarily removes" contradicts the keep-the-menu design.

The phrase "by the passage's definition" ties the item to this text specifically, so test it against Paragraph 1 rather than any outside usage. The definition is wrong for this passage, so the wording is not used correctly.

**E) "An effect size shrinking after correction for publication bias suggests the original estimate may have been inflated."**

Paragraph 6's drop from ~8.7 to ~1.4 supports the idea that the uncorrected published average overstated typical power — i.e., the original estimate looked inflated. "Inflated" is simply another way of saying "overstated," which is the passage's own word for the pre-correction figure.

**Tip:** Hedged wording like "suggests" and "may have been" matches the passage's own caution.

Because the statement claims a tendency rather than a certainty, it stays within what Paragraph 6 licenses. That inference matches the passage's logic, so the claim holds.
highlights: applying similar techniques to areas ranging from tax compliance to public health messaging
citizens are treated as donors unless they explicitly object
exploiting known cognitive biases such as status quo bias and loss aversion
not by restricting options, but by redesigning the context
the published literature may have substantially overstated how powerful typical nudges actually are

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.

**A) Fleming's initial 1928 observation is described as having immediately attracted widespread practical attention and clinical use.**

Paragraph 1 says Fleming’s chance discovery "initially attracted little practical attention," and only became clinically viable after Florey and Chain’s early-1940s purification work. Immediate widespread attention and clinical use is the opposite of that timeline.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Turning "little" early interest into "immediate" practical success is a classic flip of the discovery story.

The claim reverses Paragraph 1’s "little practical attention," so it fails against the passage.

**B) Florey and Chain are credited with purifying and stabilising penicillin, enabling its clinical use in the early 1940s.**

Paragraph 1 states that "researchers Howard Florey and Ernst Chain successfully purified and stabilised the compound," making penicillin "viable for clinical use" in "the early 1940s." The statement restates that credit without changing the agents or the date window.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** When names, verbs, and decade match the paragraph, a faithful paraphrase stays true.

Paragraph 1’s purification credit matches the statement, so the claim holds.

**C) Resistant strains of Staphylococcus were identified by 1947, only a few years after penicillin's widespread clinical introduction.**

Paragraph 2 reports that "by 1947, only a few years after penicillin entered widespread clinical use, researchers had already identified strains of Staphylococcus bacteria capable of resisting its effects." Date, organism, and "few years after" sequencing all align.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

The 1947 Staphylococcus resistance timeline in Paragraph 2 matches the statement, so the claim holds.

**D) The 2019 global study estimated that bacterial resistance was directly responsible for approximately 1.27 million deaths that year, with 4.95 million deaths associated with resistant infections more broadly.**

Paragraph 3 gives both figures in order: "approximately 1.27 million deaths" directly, "with a further 4.95 million deaths associated with resistant infections more broadly." The statement copies those quantities without swapping roles.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** Keep "directly responsible" separate from the larger "associated" total — both numbers appear in the same sentence.

The 2019 mortality pair in Paragraph 3 matches the statement, so the claim holds.

**E) The passage describes the toll of antimicrobial resistance as smaller than that of several long-feared infectious diseases.**

Paragraph 3 says the AMR toll is "exceeding that of several long-feared infectious diseases," not falling short of them. "Smaller than" reverses the comparison word that decides the item.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

The statement flips Paragraph 3’s "exceeding" comparison, so it fails against the passage.

tasks.title: Task 4

tactical_explanations:

The plan-first, incentives-later order in Paragraph 7 matches the statement, so the chronology holds.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Each statement describes a piece of reasoning inspired by the passage and names a specific logical fallacy it supposedly commits, or claims it involves no fallacy at all. Decide if the fallacyidentification (or lack thereof) is accurate.
statements: "Since resistant strains appeared soon after penicillin's introduction, all resistance today must be caused solely by antibiotic use" commits a single-cause fallacy, since the passage also cites mutation, horizontal gene transfer, and agricultural use as separate contributing factors.

tactical_explanations:
**A) "Since resistant strains appeared soon after penicillin's introduction, all resistance today must be caused solely by antibiotic use" commits a single-cause fallacy, since the passage also cites mutation, horizontal gene transfer, and agricultural use as separate contributing factors.**

The quoted leap treats early clinical resistance as the sole cause of all resistance now. Paragraphs 4–5 also name agricultural livestock use, spontaneous mutation, and cross-species plasmid transfer as distinct contributors, so labeling a "solely" claim as single-cause is accurate.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** One named cause plus "solely/all" usually signals single-cause overreach when the passage lists several drivers.

The fallacy label fits the oversimplified "solely" claim against the passage’s multiple factors, so the statement holds.

**B) "Firms exited antibiotic research once profits declined, therefore declining profit was the only reason any firm ever left the field" commits a single-cause fallacy, since the passage also cites the stewardship paradox as a separate structural factor.**

Paragraph 6 links weak profits to industry exit, but Paragraph 8 adds a separate stewardship paradox: sparingly used new drugs undermine sales-based revenue. Treating declining profit as the "only" reason ignores that second structure, so single-cause is the right label.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

Profit decline is one driver among others in the passage, so the single-cause identification holds.

**C) "Because the WHO adopted its action plan and incentive proposals followed shortly afterward, the plan alone must have directly caused every proposal" commits circular reasoning, since the conclusion simply restates the premise without adding support.**

The quoted move is from "plan, then proposals" to "plan caused every proposal" — temporal succession treated as sole causation (post hoc), not a circle that restates the same claim as its own proof. Circular reasoning would recycle the conclusion as the premise; here the error is mislabeled.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Post hoc sequence arguments are often miscoded as "circular" when the real defect is cause-from-timing.

The argument is post hoc, not circular, so this fallacy identification fails.

**D) "Because agricultural antibiotic use is substantial, resistance must originate exclusively from agriculture, with clinical use playing no role" commits a false dichotomy, since the passage discusses both pathways as contributing.**

Paragraph 4 opens by denying that "human clinical use is… the only driver," then adds agricultural volume as a further pathway. Forcing "exclusively… agriculture" versus "clinical use playing no role" erases that both-and picture, so false dichotomy is correct.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** "Exclusively / no role" language often collapses two passage pathways into a fake either/or.

The exclusive-agriculture claim wrongly forces one path, so the false-dichotomy label holds.

**E) "Since resistance genes can transfer between bacterial species via plasmids, resistance originating in one population can plausibly spread beyond it" is a valid inference directly supported by the passage, not a fallacy.**

Paragraph 5’s plasmid transfer "between entirely different bacterial species" licenses the modest inference that resistance need not stay inside one population. Calling that sound reading a fallacy would invent an error the passage does not create.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

Cross-species plasmid transfer supports the modest spread inference, so treating it as valid — not fallacious — holds.

**B) "All new antibiotic classes must have been approved after 1987, since none existed before that date."**

Paragraph 6 says only one genuinely new class has reached practice since 1987 — implying older classes existed earlier, not that "none existed before." "Must have… since none existed" invents a false premise and over-strong necessity.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** A "discovery void after 1987" does not license "no classes before 1987."

**C) "Pharmaceutical companies might return to antibiotic research if new incentive models make it commercially viable."**

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence uses a conditional structure. Decide if the conditional type used correctly matches the meaning it is meant to express.
statements: "If bacteria are exposed repeatedly to sub-lethal doses of an antibiotic, resistant strains eventually emerge." (zero conditional, general scientific truth)
"If penicillin had never been mass-produced during the war, millions of soldiers would die from infected wounds." (mixed past/present tense in a third-conditional context)
"If a new antibiotic class were approved tomorrow, it would still take years of clinical trials before reaching patients." (second conditional, hypothetical future)
"If governments increase funding for antibiotic R&D, resistance rates will immediately disappear worldwide." (first conditional, confidently asserting real future certainty)
"If resistance had not emerged so quickly after antibiotics' introduction, the era of easy bacterial treatment might have lasted longer." (third conditional, hypothetical past)
tactical_explanations:
**A) "If bacteria are exposed repeatedly to sub-lethal doses of an antibiotic, resistant strains eventually emerge." (zero conditional, general scientific truth)**

Present + present ("are exposed… emerge") is the zero-conditional shape for a general scientific pattern. That matches a repeatable biological outcome of the kind Paragraphs 2 and 5 describe around resistance arising under antibiotic pressure.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Tip:** Zero conditional = open present facts; it is not a one-off past hypothesis.

The labeled zero conditional fits a general resistance pattern, so the line is true.

**B) "If penicillin had never been mass-produced during the war, millions of soldiers would die from infected wounds." (mixed past/present tense in a third-conditional context)**

"Had never been" opens a past counterfactual that needs a matching past result ("would have died"). "Would die" shifts into present/future consequence and breaks third-conditional pairing — exactly the mixed-tense fault the label flags.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Past perfect in the if-clause almost always wants "would have + past participle," not bare "would + base."

Third-conditional form collapses on "would die," so the line is false.

**C) "If a new antibiotic class were approved tomorrow, it would still take years of clinical trials before reaching patients." (second conditional, hypothetical future)**

"Were approved… would still take" is classic second conditional for an unlikely or hypothetical near future. The imaginary tomorrow-approval scenario matches that tentative mood, especially given Paragraph 6’s discovery void.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

The second-conditional label fits the hypothetical future wording, so the line is true.

**D) "If governments increase funding for antibiotic R&D, resistance rates will immediately disappear worldwide." (first conditional, confidently asserting real future certainty)**

Formally the if-present + will-future shape is first conditional, but the content asserts an impossible certain outcome ("will immediately disappear worldwide"). That overconfident forecast clashes with Paragraph 9’s unsettled, contested seriousness and with the biological drivers that funding alone cannot erase overnight.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Correct first-conditional grammar can still be false when the predicted result is wildly overstated.

The confident "will immediately disappear" claim overshoots the passage, so the line fails.

**E) "If resistance had not emerged so quickly after antibiotics' introduction, the era of easy bacterial treatment might have lasted longer." (third conditional, hypothetical past)**

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each statement about word meaning or usage is correct.
statements: "Susceptible" means vulnerable or easily affected, while "susceptive" is a real, commonly used English word with an identical meaning.

"Susceptible" correctly means easily affected (as resistant bacteria are not). "Susceptive," however, is not a standard, commonly used twin with the same meaning — the second half invents a false friend.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Near-spellings that "look Latin" are often fake twins on vocabulary true/false items.

Because "susceptive" is not a real common synonym, the paired claim fails.

**B) "Viable" means capable of working successfully, while "viability" is simply the noun form referring to that same capacity.**

Paragraph 1 uses "viable for clinical use" for penicillin after purification. "Viable" (adjective) and "viability" (noun) name the same capacity at different parts of speech — the distinction is exact.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** Check whether the claimed noun is a true -ity/-ness form of the adjective in the passage.

The viable / viability pairing matches standard usage, so the claim holds.

**C) "Incentive" means something that encourages a particular action, while "deterrent" means something that discourages an action — near-opposite functions.**

Paragraph 7’s "push" and "pull" incentive models are rewards meant to encourage antibiotic development. "Deterrent" points the other way — discouragement — so calling them near-opposites is right.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

Incentive versus deterrent as encourage / discourage near-opposites is accurate, so the claim holds.

**D) "Strain" (as in "a bacterial strain") refers to a specific genetic variant within a species, while "stress" refers to physical or mental tension — related in sound but distinct in meaning.**

Paragraph 2’s "strains of Staphylococcus" uses the biological-variant sense. "Stress" is a different word for pressure or tension; sound similarity does not make them synonyms.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** Exam "strain / stress" traps trade on sound, not shared biology meaning.

The bacterial-strain versus tension-stress split is correct, so the claim holds.

**E) "Dose" refers to a measured quantity of medicine taken at one time, while "dosage" refers to the regimen or schedule of doses over time.**

Standard medical English keeps "dose" as a single measured amount and "dosage" as the planned schedule of doses. Sub-lethal exposure talk in these themes still relies on that dose-unit idea.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

The dose / dosage schedule distinction matches careful usage, so the claim holds.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each word, as it would be used in a sentence echoing the passage's themes, is correctly identified as literal or figurative.
statements: "Reservoir," in the phrase "an animal reservoir of resistant bacteria," is used figuratively to mean a population that harbours and maintains a pathogen over time, extending its literal water-storage meaning.
"Arms race," used to describe the ongoing competition between antibiotic development and bacterial evolution, is used in its original, literal military sense.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**Tip:** Literal water storage → figurative pathogen-holding population is a standard science metaphor.

The figurative reservoir reading is correctly identified, so the claim holds.

**B) "Arms race," used to describe the ongoing competition between antibiotic development and bacterial evolution, is used in its original, literal military sense.**

Drug-versus-bug "arms race" language is a metaphor: competitive escalation borrowed from military rivalry, not tanks and missiles. Calling it the original literal military sense mislabels the figure.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Familiar war metaphors in science writing are almost never literal weapon talk.

The military-literal claim is wrong for this figurative use, so the statement fails.

**C) "Burden," as in "the global burden of disease," is used figuratively to mean the overall impact or cost of a health problem, not a physical object being carried.**

Paragraph 3’s huge AMR death toll is the kind of impact health writers call a "burden" — figurative weight/cost, not a load on someone’s back.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**D) "Void," as in "a discovery void," is used figuratively to mean an absence or gap, not a literal empty physical space.**

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

"Discovery void" as figurative absence matches Paragraph 6, so the claim holds.

**E) "Spread," as in "the spread of resistance genes between species," is used only in its literal sense of physically scattering solid objects across a surface.**

Paragraph 5’s gene "spread" through horizontal transfer is biological transmission between species, not literal scattering of solid objects on a surface. "Only… literal" therefore mislabels the usage.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The Arctic tern is described as experiencing more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.
Conventional tracking equipment was successfully used on Arctic terns for decades before 2010, providing detailed route data.
The geolocators attached to terns in 2010 weighed less than two grams.
Tracked terns are described as typically following a single, direct route rather than a distinctive Sshaped path.
The average recorded round-trip migration distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, with one bird logging roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The Arctic tern is described as experiencing more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.**

Paragraph 1 ties both polar summers’ near-continuous daylight to the tern’s hemispheric chase: it “experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.” The statement simply repeats that ranking — no stretch beyond the wording. The “chasing perpetual summer between hemispheres” line is the mechanism behind that crown, not a separate claim you need to invent.

**Tip:** Daylight / season claims in ¶1 are usually word-for-word matches; quote before you paraphrase.

The year-round daylight crown is stated outright in ¶1, so the claim matches the passage. Match the exact “more daylight… than any other creature” phrasing and you stay safe.

**B) Conventional tracking equipment was successfully used on Arctic terns for decades before 2010, providing detailed route data.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: for decades the route stayed estimated because the birds “are too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment without impairing their flight.” Success arrives only in 2010 with sub-two-gram geolocators. “Successfully used… for decades before 2010” invents a working conventional era the paragraph never grants.

**Trap:** “For decades” tempts a success story; the text uses those decades for the estimation problem, not for working conventional tags.

The line flips ¶2’s size barrier into earlier conventional success, so it fails — “too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment.” Keep “estimation” and the 2010 breakthrough on the same timeline and the false success story collapses.

**C) The geolocators attached to terns in 2010 weighed less than two grams.**

Paragraph 2 names the breakthrough gear exactly: “miniaturised geolocators, weighing less than two grams,” fitted to breeding birds in Greenland and Iceland. The weight claim is a straight lift from that sentence. Nothing in the statement upgrades “less than two grams” into a different figure or a different device type.

The less-than-two-grams figure is explicit in ¶2, so the statement tracks the text. When a measurement is quoted verbatim, treat it as a true match unless the statement quietly shifts the unit or the gear name.

**D) Tracked terns are described as typically following a single, direct route rather than a distinctive Sshaped path.**

Paragraph 3 opens by rejecting a single direct line: “Rather than following a single direct route, many tracked individuals travelled in a distinctive S-shaped path.” The statement swaps that contrast and invents “typically… direct.” The westward Atlantic drift and African / South American turn are details of the S-shape, not evidence of a straight shot.

**Trap:** Watch statements that keep the vocabulary (route / path) but reverse the “rather than” structure.

It contradicts ¶3’s S-shaped drift, so it fails — “a distinctive S-shaped path,” not a single direct route. If the stem keeps “rather than” wording but flips which option is preferred, mark it false.

**E) The average recorded round-trip migration distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, with one bird logging roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.**

Paragraph 3 reports both figures side by side: population average “approximately 70,900 kilometres,” and one long-ranging bird “roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.” The statement pairs them without changing either number. The “considerably further” clause in the same sentence already licenses treating the 96,000 km bird as an extreme within that tracked set.

Both kilometre totals sit in ¶3 as stated, so the claim matches the passage. Two accurate numbers joined by “with” still count as true when both appear in the same paragraph.
highlights: experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth
too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment without impairing their flight
miniaturised geolocators, weighing less than two grams
Rather than following a single direct route, many tracked individuals travelled in a distinctive S-shaped path
approximately 70,900 kilometres, though several individual birds were recorded travelling considerably further, with one especially long-ranging bird logging a round-trip of roughly 96,000 kilometres

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Over a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single tern may accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.
This lifetime distance is described as roughly equivalent to three round trips to the Moon.
The seasonal stopover south of Greenland is described as occurring during the northbound, rather than southbound, leg of the journey.
The stopover area is described as unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period.
The navigational mechanisms behind the terns' migration are described as fully understood and no longer subject to scientific investigation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Over a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single tern may accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.**

Paragraph 4 states that figure wholesale: “a typical thirty-year lifespan” plus “roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.” Nothing in the statement alters the lifespan frame or the total. The “may therefore accumulate” wording is a consequence of the annual distances just reported, not a separate measurement you must re-derive.

¶4’s lifetime total is copied cleanly, so the claim matches the passage. Lifespan + kilometre total together are enough; you do not need the Moon comparison for this item to be true.

**B) This lifetime distance is described as roughly equivalent to three round trips to the Moon.**

The same sentence in paragraph 4 equates that mileage with “approximately three round trips to the Moon.” The statement’s “roughly equivalent” is faithful paraphrase of that comparison. It does not invent a different celestial distance or drop the “approximately / roughly” hedge.

The Moon comparison is explicit in ¶4, so the wording stands. When the passage already supplies the analogy, a soft synonym for “equivalent to approximately” is still a match.

**C) The seasonal stopover south of Greenland is described as occurring during the northbound, rather than southbound, leg of the journey.**

Paragraph 5 places the detour on “the southbound leg of the journey,” when birds pause “south of Greenland” before continuing toward Antarctic waters. Calling it northbound reverses that direction cue. The “before continuing the remainder of their journey” clause also points onward to Antarctica, not back toward Arctic breeding grounds.

**Trap:** Northbound / southbound swaps are classic when a named geography (Greenland) sits near both seasonal frames.

It fails because ¶5 anchors the pause on the southbound leg, not northbound. Geography alone never overrides an explicit seasonal direction word in the stem.

**D) The stopover area is described as unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period.**

Paragraph 5 calls the open ocean south of Greenland “an area unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period,” the apparent reason for replenishing fat. The statement repeats that richness claim. “During that period” keeps the seasonal timing; the statement does not invent year-round abundance.

The plankton-and-fish richness is stated in ¶5, so the claim matches. Food-rich stopover wording is usually a direct lift — quote the richness phrase before you paraphrase it.

**E) The navigational mechanisms behind the terns' migration are described as fully understood and no longer subject to scientific investigation.**

Paragraph 6 opens with the opposite: mechanisms “remain only partially understood,” and disentangling them in terns has “proven difficult.” Full understanding and closed investigation are invented upgrades. The listed cues (magnetic field, sun, landmarks, possibly smell) are candidates inside that partial picture, not a finished checklist.

**Trap:** Listing candidate methods (magnetic field, sun, landmarks) can feel like a finished theory; ¶6 still labels the picture partial.

It fails against ¶6’s “only partially understood” framing — investigation is unfinished, not closed. “Logistical constraints” on ocean experiments further block any reading that science has finished the job.
highlights: a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single Arctic tern may therefore accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight
a distance equivalent to approximately three round trips to the Moon
an intriguing seasonal detour undertaken by many individuals during the southbound leg of the journey
an area unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period
The navigational mechanisms underlying this feat remain only partially understood

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Arctic terns are described as displaying an aggressive nest-defence strategy disproportionate to their small size.
Other bird species are described as deliberately avoiding nesting near Arctic tern colonies due to the risk of attack.
Researchers have expressed concern that shifts in wind patterns or ocean productivity could disrupt one or more stages of the migration.
The passage concludes by presenting the terns' climate resilience as a fully resolved question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.
The precision of the terns' migratory strategy is presented as potentially linked to a corresponding vulnerability to disruption.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Arctic terns are described as displaying an aggressive nest-defence strategy disproportionate to their small size.**

Paragraph 7 calls the strategy “strikingly aggressive” and “entirely disproportionate to their small size,” with dive-bombing of humans, foxes, and larger birds of prey. The statement compresses that portrait without adding claims. Collective colony defence and bill strikes are supporting colour, not a different verdict.

¶7’s disproportionate defence is on the page, so the claim matches. Size-versus-aggression contrasts in the stem should track the “disproportionate to their small size” wording exactly.

**B) Other bird species are described as deliberately avoiding nesting near Arctic tern colonies due to the risk of attack.**

Paragraph 7 says neighbouring species “sometimes deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression.” Avoidance is the reverse of that choice. The shared-predator benefit is why they approach, not a reason to stay away.

**Trap:** Aggression toward intruders does not mean other nesters stay away — some hitchhike on the defence.

It fails: ¶7 has species nesting close for protection, not avoiding tern colonies. Flip “close / benefit” into “avoid / risk” and you have manufactured the opposite ecology.

**C) Researchers have expressed concern that shifts in wind patterns or ocean productivity could disrupt one or more stages of the migration.**

Paragraph 8 records concern that climate-linked “shifts in ocean productivity or wind patterns” could “disrupt one or more stages of the migration.” The statement reorders those two factors but keeps the content. Dependence on “predictable wind patterns and food availability at multiple… stopover points” is the same vulnerability in different words.

That climate-disruption worry is explicit in ¶8, so the claim matches. Reordering coordinated nouns (wind / productivity) does not change truth when both appear in the cited sentence.

**D) The passage concludes by presenting the terns' climate resilience as a fully resolved question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.**

Paragraph 9 frames adjustment versus vulnerability as “a question actively being investigated,” not a settled verdict. “Fully resolved” and “agreed-upon answer” invent closure the ending withholds. Ornithologists working “across both of its hemispheric ranges” underscores ongoing research, not consensus.

**Trap:** Closing paragraphs can sound conclusive when they only pose the open question more sharply.

It fails because ¶9 leaves climate resilience under active investigation, not answered. Treat “whether… or whether…” endings as open unless the text names a settled result.

**E) The precision of the terns' migratory strategy is presented as potentially linked to a corresponding vulnerability to disruption.**

Paragraph 9’s contrast is exact: whether they adjust quickly enough, “or whether the very precision that makes their journey so extraordinary also makes it unusually vulnerable to disruption.” Precision and vulnerability are twinned as one research question. The statement’s “potentially linked” hedges the same possibility the passage already floats.

¶9 itself links precision to possible vulnerability, so the claim matches. When the text pairs a strength with a matching risk, that twinning is fair game for a true inference.
highlights: a strikingly aggressive nest-defence strategy entirely disproportionate to their small size
deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression
shifts in ocean productivity or wind patterns associated with broader climate variability could disrupt one or more stages of the migration
remains a question actively being investigated by ornithologists
the very precision that makes their journey so extraordinary also makes it unusually vulnerable to disruption

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since terns experience near-continuous daylight in both polar summers, it can be inferred that they spend virtually no time in darkness across an entire year, relative to most other migratory species.

If the average round-trip distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, and one bird travelled roughly 96,000 kilometres, that bird travelled about 25,100 kilometres further than the population average.

Because researchers cite magnetic sensitivity, solar positioning, and visual landmarks as possible navigation mechanisms, the passage implies exactly one of these three must be solely responsible, to the exclusion of the other two.

Because the S-shaped migratory path appears linked to prevailing wind patterns, it can be inferred that the birds' route may be shaped partly by energy-efficiency considerations rather than being a purely direct geographic path.

Since other species nest near tern colonies to benefit from their aggression, it can be inferred that Arctic terns' defensive behaviour can produce ecological benefits for neighbouring species, not just for the terns themselves.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since terns experience near-continuous daylight in both polar summers, it can be inferred that they spend virtually no time in darkness across an entire year, relative to most other migratory species.**

Paragraph 1 notes near-continuous daylight in each polar summer and concludes the tern gets more daylight yearly than any other creature while “chasing perpetual summer.” Relative scarcity of darkness versus other migrants is a cautious reading of that daylight crown — not a claim of zero night forever, but “virtually no… relative to most.” The comparative “more daylight… than any other creature” already licenses a relative-darkness gloss.

**Tip:** Keep the relative hedge; absolute “never dark” would overclaim.

¶1’s daylight ranking supports the relative-darkness inference, so the line holds. Stay inside “relative to most” and you are still paraphrasing the daylight crown, not inventing a new fact.

**B) If the average round-trip distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, and one bird travelled roughly 96,000 kilometres, that bird travelled about 25,100 kilometres further than the population average.**

Paragraph 3 supplies both figures; 96,000 − 70,900 = 25,100. The arithmetic follows the stated totals without inventing a third distance. “About” fits the passage’s own “approximately / roughly” hedges on both inputs.

**Tip:** When both numbers are explicit, a clean difference is fair game if the statement names both sources.

The gap is exact arithmetic from ¶3’s pair of figures, so the inference stands. Do not reject a difference just because the passage never prints the subtraction itself.

**C) Because researchers cite magnetic sensitivity, solar positioning, and visual landmarks as possible navigation mechanisms, the passage implies exactly one of these three must be solely responsible, to the exclusion of the other two.**

Paragraph 6 lists those cues under “a combination of methods is likely involved,” then notes how hard it is to separate contributions. Sole responsibility for one cue contradicts the combination claim. “Disentangling the relative contribution of each mechanism” assumes several factors may share the work, not a single winner.

**Trap:** A menu of mechanisms is not a single-winner tournament.

It fails: ¶6 points to a combination, not one exclusive controller. Whenever the text says “combination… likely,” reject stems that force exclusivity.

**D) Because the S-shaped migratory path appears linked to prevailing wind patterns, it can be inferred that the birds' route may be shaped partly by energy-efficiency considerations rather than being a purely direct geographic path.**

Paragraph 3 ties the S-shaped Atlantic drift to taking “advantage of favourable prevailing wind patterns” instead of a single direct route. Using favourable winds implies an energy-saving geometry without the text needing the word “efficiency.” “Partly” and “may” keep the inference inside what “apparently to take advantage” already suggests.

Favourable-wind routing in ¶3 supports a partial energy-efficiency reading, so the inference is fair. Soft modal wording is appropriate when the passage itself hedges with “apparently.”

**E) Since other species nest near tern colonies to benefit from their aggression, it can be inferred that Arctic terns' defensive behaviour can produce ecological benefits for neighbouring species, not just for the terns themselves.**

Paragraph 7’s neighbouring species nest close “specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression against shared predators.” Shared predator pressure is an ecological upside beyond the terns alone. The benefit language is explicit; the inference only names who else gains.

¶7’s hitchhiking nesters show spillover benefits, so the inference tracks the passage. “Specifically to benefit” is already an ecological spillover claim — the stem just restates the beneficiary.
highlights: experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth, effectively chasing perpetual summer
approximately 70,900 kilometres, though several individual birds were recorded travelling considerably further, with one especially long-ranging bird logging a round-trip of roughly 96,000 kilometres
a combination of methods is likely involved
apparently to take advantage of favourable prevailing wind patterns
deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression against shared predators

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The technological limitation described in Paragraph 2 (too small for conventional trackers) helps explain why the migration's true extent, described in Paragraph 3, remained uncertain for so long.

Because the 2010 geolocator study revealed distances greater than earlier estimates, and the average round-trip was found to be approximately 70,900 kilometres, the passage implies pre-2010 estimates had significantly overstated the migration's true length.
The mid-journey stopover described in Paragraph 5 is presented as unrelated to the birds' overall energy needs for completing the remainder of their migration.
The partial understanding of navigation mechanisms (Paragraph 6) is consistent with the passage's closing framing of the terns' climate-change response as still uncertain (Paragraph 9).

The birds' dependence on multiple, widely separated stopover points (Paragraph 8) helps explain why disruption to migration might be difficult to detect from a single monitoring location, as stated in the same paragraph.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The technological limitation described in Paragraph 2 (too small for conventional trackers) helps explain why the migration's true extent, described in Paragraph 3, remained uncertain for so long.**

Paragraph 2 says decades of route-and-distance work stayed “largely a matter of estimation” because conventional gear was too heavy; paragraph 3 then shows geolocator data “considerably longer than earlier estimates.” The size barrier is the bridge between weak prior numbers and the 2010 revision. Without light tags, the “true extent” in ¶3 simply could not be measured in detail.

¶2’s tracker limit causally frames ¶3’s surprise distances, so the synthesis holds. Cross-paragraph “helps explain” stems are fair when one paragraph names the obstacle and the next names the corrected result.

**B) Because the 2010 geolocator study revealed distances greater than earlier estimates, and the average round-trip was found to be approximately 70,900 kilometres, the passage implies pre-2010 estimates had significantly overstated the migration's true length.**

Paragraph 3 says the migration was “considerably longer than earlier estimates had suggested” — earlier figures were too short, not too long. “Overstated” reverses that direction while keeping the average intact. Greater-than-estimate data means prior numbers understated length; the 70,900 km average is the corrected scale, not proof that old guesses were inflated.

**Trap:** “Different from earlier estimates” still needs you to check whether estimates were high or low.

It fails: ¶3 has earlier estimates understating length, so “overstated” is the wrong arrow. Direction words (over / under) decide these synthesis traps even when the kilometre figure is right.

**C) The mid-journey stopover described in Paragraph 5 is presented as unrelated to the birds' overall energy needs for completing the remainder of their migration.**

Paragraph 5 says birds pause apparently “to replenish fat reserves before continuing the remainder of their journey.” Unrelated to energy needs is the opposite of that purpose clause. Fat reserves are energy stores; the stopover is framed as fuel for the remaining legs, not a scenic detour.

**Trap:** “Intriguing detour” can sound optional; the text links it to fat for the remaining legs.

It fails against ¶5’s fat-reserve stopover purpose — energy is the point, not a side note. Purpose infinitives (“to replenish…”) almost always kill “unrelated” stems.

**D) The partial understanding of navigation mechanisms (Paragraph 6) is consistent with the passage's closing framing of the terns' climate-change response as still uncertain (Paragraph 9).**

Paragraph 6 leaves navigation “only partially understood”; paragraph 9 leaves climate adjustment versus vulnerability “actively being investigated.” Both chapters refuse a finished scientific map of the species’ limits. Consistency here means shared open-science tone, not a claim that navigation ignorance causes climate uncertainty.

Open questions in ¶6 and ¶9 rhyme as unfinished science, so the cross-link stands. Parallel “not yet settled” framings across distant paragraphs are valid synthesis when both refuse closure.

**E) The birds' dependence on multiple, widely separated stopover points (Paragraph 8) helps explain why disruption to migration might be difficult to detect from a single monitoring location, as stated in the same paragraph.**

Paragraph 8 itself chains the two ideas: dependence on “multiple, widely separated stopover points” across hemispheres, then consequences “difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone.” The statement restates that in-paragraph causal hinge. If stages are spread across hemispheres, one watchpoint can miss a break elsewhere.

¶8 supplies both the multi-stop dependency and the single-site detection problem, so the synthesis matches. Same-paragraph cause-and-effect links are the safest cross-claim type when both halves sit in one sentence cluster.
highlights: the exact route and total distance of this migration remained largely a matter of estimation, since the birds are too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment
a migration considerably longer than earlier estimates had suggested
apparently using the stopover to replenish fat reserves before continuing the remainder of their journey
remain only partially understood
consequences that might be difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had researchers not developed lighter geolocators, the terns' true migratory route might never have been confirmed."
"The team recommended that future studies tracks a larger sample of birds."
"The number of tracked individuals continue to grow as technology improves."
"Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability were fully predictable at every stopover."
"Having replenished its fat reserves, the bird resumed its journey southward."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had researchers not developed lighter geolocators, the terns' true migratory route might never have been confirmed."**

This is a clean third-conditional inversion: Had + subject + past participle stands in for If researchers had not…, paired with might never have been confirmed for the unreal past result. Auxiliaries and participle forms line up. The geolocator vocabulary is only topical colour; the grammar verdict rests on the conditional pattern alone.

Inverted Had…not + might never have been is sound third-conditional patterning, so the sentence stands. If you can restore If + past perfect…, might (not) have + past participle, the inversion is usually correct.

**B) "The team recommended that future studies tracks a larger sample of birds."**

After recommend that, exam English wants the present subjunctive — base form track, not tracks. Future studies is plural, but the real fault is subjunctive, not mere agreement. Mandative verbs (recommend, suggest, insist, demand) keep the bare infinitive after that.

**Trap:** Plural subject + -s looks like ordinary present; recommend that drops the -s anyway.

Recommend that needs base-form track, so this fails — "The team recommended that future studies track a larger sample of birds." Fix the verb to the base form and the stem becomes grammatical.

**C) "The number of tracked individuals continue to grow as technology improves."**

The number of is a singular head; the plural noun after of does not control the verb. Continue should be continues. Contrast a number of, which often takes a plural verb — here the article the keeps the head singular.

**Trap:** Do not let individuals (plural) pull the verb — number is the true subject.

Singular the number of needs continues, so the line fails — "The number of tracked individuals continues to grow as technology improves." Train your eye on the word number, not the nearest plural noun.

**D) "Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability were fully predictable at every stopover."**

With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Food availability is singular, so were should be was. Treating the pair as a plural set still does not override nearest-noun agreement in exam English. Wind patterns is plural, but nor lands on the singular noun that governs the verb.

**Trap:** A plural first noun (wind patterns) often tricks writers into were even when nor lands on a singular.

Nearest-subject agreement wants was, so the wording fails — "Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability was fully predictable at every stopover." Always check the noun after nor before choosing was / were.

**E) "Having replenished its fat reserves, the bird resumed its journey southward."**

The perfect participle Having replenished correctly marks fueling before resumption, and its / the bird keeps the same referents — no dangling modifier. Sequence and agreement are clean. The fat-reserve wording echoes ¶5’s stopover purpose, but the grammar test is only same-subject participle + clear past main verb.

Same-subject participle plus past resumed is well formed, so the sentence stands. If the participle’s doer matches the main-clause subject, the opener is almost always safe.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the birds reached the stopover than they began feeding intensively."
"The migration route, along with several recorded detours, were mapped in detail."
"Each of the tracked terns have followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern."
"By the time the birds reach Antarctica, they will have already flown tens of thousands of kilometres."
