"The data, which were collected using miniaturised geolocators, reveal a far longer migration than expected."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the birds reached the stopover than they began feeding intensively."**

No sooner…than correctly forces inversion (had before the subject) and pairs past perfect with a simple-past follow-on. Than (not when) is the right linker. The stopover feeding scene is topical only; the pattern itself is what makes the sentence grammatical.

**Tip:** Front the auxiliary: No sooner had…, not No sooner the birds had…

Inverted No sooner had…than… is textbook form, so the sentence stands. Swap than for when and the correlative would break even if the inversion looked right.

**B) "The migration route, along with several recorded detours, were mapped in detail."**

Along with… is a parenthetical add-on; the grammatical subject remains singular migration route. Were should be was. Commas around the along with phrase are a reminder that those detours are not part of a plural compound subject.

**Trap:** Material after along with / as well as / together with does not make a singular head plural.

Singular route controls the verb, so this fails — "The migration route, along with several recorded detours, was mapped in detail." Cover the along with… phrase with your finger and re-agree the verb with what remains.

**C) "Each of the tracked terns have followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when of is followed by a plural noun. Have followed should be has followed. Each, every, and either behave the same way: the verb stays singular.

**Trap:** Terns (plural) sits next to the verb and tempts have; each still rules.

Each of needs has followed, so the line fails — "Each of the tracked terns has followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern." Ignore the plural after of and lock the verb to each.

**D) "By the time the birds reach Antarctica, they will have already flown tens of thousands of kilometres."**

By the time + present reach sets a future boundary; will have already flown is future perfect for miles completed before that arrival. The aspect matches the deadline. Already sits naturally inside the future-perfect verb group for work finished ahead of that point.

Future perfect after by the time fits completed flight before arrival, so the wording stands. Present in the by the time clause + will have + past participle is the standard exam pairing.

**E) "The data, which were collected using miniaturised geolocators, reveal a far longer migration than expected."**

Here data is treated as plural: were collected in the relative clause and reveal in the main clause agree. Consistent plural handling is acceptable exam English for scientific data. Switching to was / reveals mid-sentence would be the inconsistency to punish, not this matched plural pair.

Plural data with were / reveal stays consistent, so the sentence stands. Keep both verbs plural (or both singular) once you choose a data agreement style.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs."
"Whoever analyses the tracking data should account for individual variation between birds."
"The team denied having deliberately overstated the average migration distance."
"There is several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation."
"The colony, which was studied over several breeding seasons, showed consistent defensive behaviour."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs."**

Despite never takes of; the of belongs to the twin phrase in spite of. Either drop of after despite or switch to in spite of. The logistical-challenges content is fine; only the preposition pattern is broken.

**Trap:** Despite of is a high-frequency blend of despite + in spite of.

Despite of is ungrammatical, so the line fails — "Despite the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs." Remember: despite + noun phrase; in spite of + noun phrase — never mix the two.

**B) "Whoever analyses the tracking data should account for individual variation between birds."**

Whoever is a free relative meaning “the person who,” correctly heading the subject clause; analyses (BrE singular) and should account are well formed. Whoever / whomever choice is not the issue here because the form is subject of analyses.

Whoever as clausal subject with a matching singular verb is sound, so the sentence stands. Treat whoever… as a singular noun clause unless the exam forces a clearly plural reading.

**C) "The team denied having deliberately overstated the average migration distance."**

Deny + perfect gerund (having overstated) correctly places the alleged overstatement before the denial. Deliberately is a clean adverb inside the gerund phrase. Deny that they overstated would also work; deny having + past participle is the compact equivalent for a prior act.

Denied having + past participle is the right pattern for a prior act, so the wording stands. Perfect gerunds after deny / admit / regret signal that the event already happened before the speaking verb.

**D) "There is several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation."**

Existential there agrees with the real subject that follows; several mechanisms is plural, so is must become are. Paragraph 6’s “combination of methods” vocabulary only sets the topic; agreement still follows the plural noun after there.

**Trap:** There is feels fixed; always check the noun after it.

Plural mechanisms need There are, so this fails — "There are several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation." Read There + verb + noun as verb agreeing with that noun, not with there.

**E) "The colony, which was studied over several breeding seasons, showed consistent defensive behaviour."**

The non-defining which-clause agrees with singular colony (was studied), and the main verb showed likewise stays singular. Punctuation and agreement are tidy. Commas mark extra information about the same singular subject rather than a plural compound.

Singular colony with was / showed is consistent, so the sentence stands. Keep relative-clause and main-clause verbs locked to the same singular head.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "A geolocator is a small device used to record and transmit an animal's approximate location over time."
"Prevailing wind patterns refers to the specific winds that occur only once, on a single unrepeated occasion."
"A stopover, in migratory biology, refers to a site where travelling animals pause to rest and replenish energy reserves."
"Olfactory cues refers to information gathered through an animal's sense of smell."
"A breeding colony refers to a group of animals that reproduce and nest together in the same area."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "A geolocator is a small device used to record and transmit an animal's approximate location over time."**

That matches how the passage’s 2010 tags work: tiny devices that let movements be “tracked in detail.” Location-logging over time is the established sense, not a navigational compass itself. Weight under two grams is a passage detail about these devices, not a required part of the dictionary definition.

The definition fits standard scientific use (and ¶2’s trackers), so the wording is sound. Device + location over time is enough; do not demand every passage adjective appear in the gloss.

**B) "Prevailing wind patterns refers to the specific winds that occur only once, on a single unrepeated occasion."**

Prevailing means dominant or usual over a period — the opposite of a one-off gust. Paragraph 3’s “favourable prevailing wind patterns” are habitual routes, not single-event winds. A one-time breeze cannot be “prevailing” in ordinary or scientific English.

**Trap:** Sounding like “the winds that prevail today” can be twisted into “once only”; the adjective means typically dominant.

Once-only winds invert prevailing’s meaning, so this use fails. If the gloss erases the habitual / dominant sense, reject it even when wind vocabulary from the passage is present.

**C) "A stopover, in migratory biology, refers to a site where travelling animals pause to rest and replenish energy reserves."**

That is the standard migratory sense, and paragraph 5’s Greenland pause to “replenish fat reserves” is exactly that kind of site. Rest-and-refuel, not permanent residence. The definition’s “energy reserves” maps cleanly onto the passage’s “fat reserves.”

Stopover as a refueling pause matches established migratory usage, so the definition stands. Keep temporary pause + refuel in the gloss; breeding-colony permanence would be the wrong category.

**D) "Olfactory cues refers to information gathered through an animal's sense of smell."**

Olfactory = smell-related; cues are sensory signals. Paragraph 6 lists “possibly olfactory cues” beside visual landmarks as candidate navigation inputs — smell-based information, not taste or sound. The “possibly” in the passage hedges certainty of use, not the meaning of the term.

Smell-based information is the right sense of olfactory cues, so the wording stands. Word-family knowledge (olfactory → smell) is enough even before you reread ¶6.

**E) "A breeding colony refers to a group of animals that reproduce and nest together in the same area."**

That is the ordinary biology sense; paragraph 7’s “Breeding colonies” that dive-bomb intruders are communal nesting groups, not solitary nests. Collective defence in ¶7 presupposes that communal grouping.

Communal breed-and-nest group matches breeding colony, so the definition is sound. Shared place + reproduction/nesting is the core; aggression is a behaviour of some colonies, not part of the definition itself.
highlights: favourable prevailing wind patterns
visual landmarks and possibly olfactory cues

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "Dive-bombing, as a defensive behaviour, refers to a bird making a fast, aggressive downward attack toward a threat."
"A round-trip distance refers to the total distance travelled in only one direction, excluding the return journey."
"Perpetual summer, as used figuratively here, refers to continuously experiencing summer-like daylight conditions by moving between hemispheres."
"Logistical constraints refers to practical difficulties that make carrying out a plan or experiment more difficult."
"A monitoring location refers to a fixed point from which researchers observe and record data over time."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Dive-bombing, as a defensive behaviour, refers to a bird making a fast, aggressive downward attack toward a threat."**

That matches ordinary bird-behaviour use and paragraph 7’s colonies that “collectively dive-bomb intruders,” striking heads with bills. Fast downward aggression toward a threat is exact. Collective colony action is extra colour; the verb itself still names the attack style.

Defensive downward attack is the right sense, so the wording stands. Keep “downward / aggressive / toward a threat” in the gloss and you stay aligned with both dictionary and passage use.

**B) "A round-trip distance refers to the total distance travelled in only one direction, excluding the return journey."**

Round-trip means out and back combined. Paragraph 3’s “average round-trip distance” and the 96,000 km “round-trip” are full migrations, not one-way legs. Excluding the return flips the meaning. Lifetime totals in ¶4 also build from those full round-trips, not half-routes.

**Trap:** Round can tempt “one circuit in one direction”; the compound still includes the return.

One-way-only denies round-trip’s out-and-back sense, so this use fails. If the gloss drops the return leg, it contradicts both ordinary English and the passage figures.

**C) "Perpetual summer, as used figuratively here, refers to continuously experiencing summer-like daylight conditions by moving between hemispheres."**

Paragraph 1’s “effectively chasing perpetual summer between hemispheres” is figurative daylight strategy, not literal endless calendar summer in one place. The gloss tracks that metaphor. Hemispheric movement is essential; a bird staying put cannot “chase” summer in the passage’s sense.

Chasing daylight summers across hemispheres matches ¶1’s figurative perpetual summer, so the wording stands. Honour the figurative / daylight framing and you will not over-literalise the metaphor.

**D) "Logistical constraints refers to practical difficulties that make carrying out a plan or experiment more difficult."**

Logistics = practical organisation of a task; constraints are limiting factors. Paragraph 6 cites “obvious logistical constraints” on ocean-crossing navigation experiments — feasibility barriers, not theoretical ones. Crossing oceans with experimental birds is the practical hurdle the phrase points to.

Practical feasibility limits fit logistical constraints, so the definition stands. Keep “practical / carrying out” in the gloss; pure theory limits would be the wrong register.

**E) "A monitoring location refers to a fixed point from which researchers observe and record data over time."**

That is standard field-science sense; paragraph 8’s worry that disruption may be “difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone” assumes fixed watchpoints gathering observations. “Single… alone” only makes sense if each location is a discrete observational site.

A fixed observational site matches monitoring location, so the wording is sound. Fixed point + observe/record over time is the definition; the climate-disruption worry merely uses that term.
highlights: collectively dive-bomb intruders
The average round-trip distance recorded across the tracked population was approximately 70,900 kilometres
effectively chasing perpetual summer between hemispheres
poses obvious logistical constraints
difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The Wright brothers' first flight covered approximately 37 metres in about 12 seconds, at a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour.
The First World War is described as having transformed aviation into a strategically significant military technology.
Piston engines are described as having offered unlimited power-to-weight ratios, unconstrained by any technological limitation.
Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic flight covered approximately 5,800 kilometres in roughly 33.5 hours.
By the late 1920s, cruising speeds for advanced aircraft are described as having increased to more than ten times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The Wright brothers' first flight covered approximately 37 metres in about 12 seconds, at a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour.**

Paragraph 1 pins down the Kitty Hawk hop with exact figures: "just 37 metres in approximately 12 seconds" and "a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour." The statement simply restates those quantities without stretching them. Notice that altitude and construction materials sit nearby in the same paragraph but are not part of this claim, so you only need the three measurement slots. Matching "approximately / roughly" hedging to the passage's own wording confirms nothing has been upgraded into a sharper figure.

**Tip:** When several numbers sit in one paragraph, check each figure against the same sentence cluster rather than mixing later decades.

The distance, duration, and speed all match Paragraph 1, so the claim is true.

**B) The First World War is described as having transformed aviation into a strategically significant military technology.**

Paragraph 2 says the outbreak of the First World War "transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology." That is an explicit causal claim, not an inference you have to invent. The verb "transformed" and the destination phrase "strategically significant military technology" appear together, so the statement is a near-paraphrase rather than a stretch. Later detail about engines and speed is supporting colour, not a substitute for this wartime hinge.

Wartime development is framed as the hinge that made aviation strategically important, so the statement is true.

**C) Piston engines are described as having offered unlimited power-to-weight ratios, unconstrained by any technological limitation.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: aircraft "remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines." "Unlimited" and "unconstrained" invent a capability the text never grants. The passage's "fundamentally limited" and "relatively low" are the hard constraints; any gloss that erases those limits reverses the engineering point. Keep the wartime progress sentences separate — improved reliability and speed still sit under that piston ceiling.

**Trap:** Swap "low" or "limited" for unbound praise and the item flips while still sounding technical.

The statement reverses the piston-engine limitation named in Paragraph 2, so it is false.

**D) Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic flight covered approximately 5,800 kilometres in roughly 33.5 hours.**

Paragraph 3 places Lindbergh's 1927 flight at "approximately 5,800 kilometres… in roughly 33.5 hours." The statement copies those two measurements without changing the year or the route scale. The New York–Paris framing in the passage supplies the same journey the numbers describe, so you are not borrowing a different flight's stats. Ignore the later cruising-speed comparison; this item only asks whether distance and duration match.

Both distance and duration match Paragraph 3, so the claim is true.

**E) By the late 1920s, cruising speeds for advanced aircraft are described as having increased to more than ten times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk.**

Paragraph 3 says cruising speeds rose to roughly 200 km/h, "more than four times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk" — not ten times. The multiplier is the distortion. The absolute figure (~200 km/h) and the "more than four times" comparison both sit in the same sentence, so inventing "ten times" cannot be rescued by the 200 km/h detail alone. Cross-check against Kitty Hawk's ~48 km/h if you want: four times tracks; ten times does not.

**Trap:** Exam writers often swap a faithful multiple (four) for a flashier one (ten) while keeping the rest of the sentence intact.

The passage caps the gain at more than four times Kitty Hawk's speed, so the "ten times" claim is false.
highlights: just 37 metres in approximately 12 seconds
transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology
remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines
covered approximately 5,800 kilometres between New York and Paris in roughly 33.5 hours
more than four times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Jet propulsion was first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War.
The de Havilland Comet's structural failures were later traced to metal fatigue around its window frames.
The Comet's introduction increased typical intercontinental journey times compared to propellerdriven aircraft it replaced.
The Boeing 747 entered commercial service in 1969, capable of carrying more than 400 passengers at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour.
The Boeing 747's entry into service occurred more than 66 years after the Wright brothers' first flight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Jet propulsion was first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War.**

Paragraph 4 dates the first demonstration of practical jet propulsion in "operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War." The statement restates that timing and setting. "Operational military aircraft" is the key setting phrase — not a lab prototype alone — and "closing years" keeps the timeline at war's end rather than mid-war or postwar. Later commercial jets (Comet, 747) come after this military debut, so they do not redefine "first demonstrated."

The wartime military debut matches Paragraph 4, so the claim is true.

**B) The de Havilland Comet's structural failures were later traced to metal fatigue around its window frames.**

Paragraph 5 attributes the Comet's "catastrophic structural failures" to damage "later traced to metal fatigue around window frames." Cause and location are named directly. The diagnosis comes after the failures and grounding, which is why the passage says "later traced" — the statement preserves that forensic order. Industry-wide redesign standards are a consequence of that finding, not a rival cause.

The fatigue diagnosis around the window frames matches Paragraph 5, so the statement is true.

**C) The Comet's introduction increased typical intercontinental journey times compared to propellerdriven aircraft it replaced.**

Paragraph 5 says the Comet cut typical journey times "by roughly half" versus the propeller-driven aircraft it replaced. "Increased" flips the direction of the change. "By roughly half" is a reduction magnitude; any paraphrase that turns cutting into lengthening contradicts the same comparison clause. The later fatigue story does not rewrite the earlier speed benefit the text already recorded.

**Trap:** Direction traps (cut vs increase, half vs double) often leave the rest of the wording untouched.

The passage says times were cut roughly in half, so the "increased" claim is false.

**D) The Boeing 747 entered commercial service in 1969, capable of carrying more than 400 passengers at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour.**

Paragraph 6 packs the same trio: entry "By 1969," "more than 400 passengers," and "cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour." The statement gathers those facts without altering them. Altitude near 13,000 metres appears in the same sentence but is extra detail this claim does not need — and does not distort. Keep the 747 facts separate from Concorde's later Mach speeds in Paragraph 7.

Year, capacity, and cruise speed all match Paragraph 6, so the claim is true.

**E) The Boeing 747's entry into service occurred more than 66 years after the Wright brothers' first flight.**

Paragraph 6 clocks the 747's arrival as "less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk," not more than. The comparison word is inverted. From 1903 to 1969 is under that 66-year ceiling the passage states; flipping to "more than" invents a longer gap the text rejects. Do not mix this chronology line with Concorde's 1976 entry or 2003 retirement.

**Trap:** "Less than" versus "more than" on the same number is a classic chronology trap.

The passage says less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk, so the "more than" wording is false.
highlights: first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War
later traced to metal fatigue around window frames
cutting typical journey times on major intercontinental routes by roughly half compared to the propeller-driven aircraft it replaced
capable of carrying more than 400 passengers across oceans at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour
less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Concorde cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound.
Concorde is described as having become commercially self-sustaining despite its high operating costs.
Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s.
Typical cruising speeds are described as having increased substantially since the 1960s, alongside efficiency improvements.
The passage concludes by presenting aviation's future trajectory as a settled question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Concorde cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound.**

Paragraph 7 states that Concorde "cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound." Both the figure and the Mach comparison are explicit. The London–New York time under 3.5 hours is supporting effect, not a substitute for the speed claim. Keep Concorde's Mach numbers distinct from the 747's ~900 km/h cruise in Paragraph 6.

Speed and the "more than twice sonic" claim match Paragraph 7, so the statement is true.

**B) Concorde is described as having become commercially self-sustaining despite its high operating costs.**

Paragraph 7 lists high costs, limited seating, and regulatory limits, then says the aircraft "never became commercially self-sustaining." The statement claims the opposite outcome. Admitting costs while asserting success still collides with the explicit "never" verdict. Retirement in 2003 is the endpoint of that commercial failure frame, not evidence that the type paid its own way.

**Trap:** Admitting high costs while asserting commercial success looks balanced but contradicts the verdict in the text.

The passage says Concorde never became commercially self-sustaining, so the claim is false.

**C) Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s.**

Paragraph 8 gives the efficiency figure almost verbatim: modern wide-bodies "consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s." The comparison baseline is 1960s aircraft, and the metric is fuel per passenger-kilometre — not total fleet burn or raw speed. Engine design, aerodynamics, and composites are named as the sources of that gain, which reinforces rather than replaces the 80% claim.

The 80% fuel saving matches Paragraph 8, so the statement is true.

**D) Typical cruising speeds are described as having increased substantially since the 1960s, alongside efficiency improvements.**

Paragraph 8 credits big efficiency gains while saying "typical cruising speeds have remained essentially unchanged since the 1960s." Speed growth is the false half of the claim. The passage explicitly pivots improvement "away from raw speed and toward efficiency," so pairing efficiency truth with invented speed growth still fails. Flat cruise speed is the contrasting fact that overturns "increased substantially."

Efficiency improved while cruise speed stayed flat; the "increased substantially" part fails, so the statement is false.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting aviation's future trajectory as a settled question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.**

Paragraph 9 leaves the long-run trajectory as "a question aviation historians and engineers continue to debate," not a settled consensus. The paragraph stages two live options — ongoing self-sustaining acceleration versus contingent breakthroughs whose easiest gains are already captured — and refuses to crown either. A closing tone can feel weighty without delivering a verdict; here the text stops at the debate itself.

**Trap:** Closing paragraphs often sound decisive; check whether the text actually declares a verdict or only frames a debate.

The ending is an open debate, not an agreed answer, so the statement is false.
highlights: cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound
never became commercially self-sustaining
consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s
typical cruising speeds have remained essentially unchanged since the 1960s
a question aviation historians and engineers continue to debate

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since the Wright Flyer's speed was roughly 48 km/h and cruising speeds reached roughly 200 km/h by the late 1920s, the increase over that period was approximately 152 km/h in absolute terms.

Because jet engines offered a different power-to-weight relationship than piston engines, it can be inferred that this shift enabled performance levels previously structurally impossible, not merely marginally improved ones.
Because Concorde was retired in 2003, it can be inferred that supersonic commercial flight was technologically infeasible, rather than economically unsustainable.
Since fuel efficiency improved by roughly 80% while cruising speeds stayed flat, it can be inferred that recent aviation progress has been concentrated in efficiency rather than raw speed.
Because the Comet was grounded following structural failures, it can be inferred that jet-powered commercial aviation was permanently abandoned as a result.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the Wright Flyer's speed was roughly 48 km/h and cruising speeds reached roughly 200 km/h by the late 1920s, the increase over that period was approximately 152 km/h in absolute terms.**

Paragraph 1 gives ~48 km/h at Kitty Hawk; Paragraph 3 gives ~200 km/h by the late 1920s. Subtracting yields 152 km/h, so the arithmetic inference is licensed by those two figures. The item asks for an absolute difference, not the "more than four times" multiplier also in Paragraph 3 — both readings can be true from the same numbers. Do not pull in jet-era speeds from later paragraphs; the endpoints named here are Wright and late-1920s cruise.

**Tip:** Absolute-difference items are fair when both endpoints are stated; inventing a start or end speed is not.

Both speeds appear in the passage and 200 − 48 = 152, so the inference is true.

**B) Because jet engines offered a different power-to-weight relationship than piston engines, it can be inferred that this shift enabled performance levels previously structurally impossible, not merely marginally improved ones.**

Paragraph 4 says jet engines offered a "fundamentally different relationship between power and weight" and enabled speeds and altitudes "structurally impossible for earlier aircraft designs." That supports a leap beyond marginal improvement. "Fundamentally different" plus "structurally impossible" is stronger language than a small upgrade, so the inference tracks the passage's own intensity. Paragraph 2's piston limits supply the contrast that makes the leap consequential.

The "structurally impossible" wording backs the stronger performance claim, so the inference is true.

**C) Because Concorde was retired in 2003, it can be inferred that supersonic commercial flight was technologically infeasible, rather than economically unsustainable.**

Paragraph 7 blames retirement on "Persistently high operating costs, limited seating capacity, and regulatory restrictions," and notes the type flew until 2003. Cost and regulation, not technical impossibility, explain the end. Years of service at over 2,100 km/h already show the technology worked in operation; the commercial model did not. Inferring "technologically infeasible" from a retirement date alone ignores the reasons the text lists.

**Trap:** Retirement date ≠ technological failure — successful operations can still die for commercial reasons.

The text frames economics and regulation, not infeasibility, so this inference is false.

**D) Since fuel efficiency improved by roughly 80% while cruising speeds stayed flat, it can be inferred that recent aviation progress has been concentrated in efficiency rather than raw speed.**

Paragraph 8 opens by saying improvement shifted "away from raw speed and toward efficiency," then backs that with ~80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre and unchanged cruise speeds. The inference restates the paragraph's own axis. Safety and environmental performance are named alongside efficiency, which still sits on the non-speed side of the shift. Flat typical cruise speed since the 1960s is the explicit counterweight to any raw-speed progress story.

The efficiency-over-speed framing is explicit in Paragraph 8, so the inference is true.

**E) Because the Comet was grounded following structural failures, it can be inferred that jet-powered commercial aviation was permanently abandoned as a result.**

Paragraph 5 says the type was only "temporarily grounded," and Paragraph 6 shows jet commercial flight continuing with the 747. "Permanently abandoned" overreaches a temporary pause. "Reshaped aircraft design standards industry-wide" signals reform after the failures, not an exit from jets. The 1969 747 service entry is direct evidence that commercial jets resumed and scaled up.

**Trap:** Temporary grounding language gets inflated into permanent industry exit.

The grounding was temporary and jets continued afterward, so permanent abandonment is false.
highlights: achieved a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour
structurally impossible for earlier aircraft designs to survive
Persistently high operating costs, limited seating capacity, and regulatory restrictions
commercial aviation's central axis of improvement has shifted away from raw speed and toward efficiency
temporarily grounded the type

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The power-to-weight limitations described in Paragraph 2 help explain why jet propulsion, introduced later in Paragraph 4, represented such a consequential leap forward.

Because Concorde's cruising speed exceeded 2,100 km/h and the Boeing 747's exceeded 900 km/h, Concorde's speed was more than double that of the 747's, consistent with figures given in Paragraphs 6 and 7.
The Comet's early structural failures (Paragraph 5) are presented as having permanently ended commercial jet aviation, contradicting the continued development described in Paragraph 6.
The shift toward efficiency described in Paragraph 8 is consistent with the passage's closing suggestion that aviation's easiest technological gains may already have been captured (Paragraph 9).
Because cruising speeds stagnated after Concorde's retirement, the passage implies no further aviation technology development has occurred since 2003.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The power-to-weight limitations described in Paragraph 2 help explain why jet propulsion, introduced later in Paragraph 4, represented such a consequential leap forward.**

Paragraph 2 stresses piston engines' "relatively low power-to-weight ratios"; Paragraph 4 calls jets a "fundamentally different relationship between power and weight" and the "most consequential single leap." Linking those points is exactly the synthesis the chronology invites. The earlier ceiling makes the later "structurally impossible" performance gains intelligible rather than ornamental. You are not inventing a cause the text withholds; you are joining two stated engineering contrasts across paragraphs.

The piston limit sets up why the jet leap mattered, so the cross-paragraph claim is true.

**B) Because Concorde's cruising speed exceeded 2,100 km/h and the Boeing 747's exceeded 900 km/h, Concorde's speed was more than double that of the 747's, consistent with figures given in Paragraphs 6 and 7.**

Paragraph 6 places the 747 above 900 km/h; Paragraph 7 places Concorde above 2,100 km/h. Dividing those floors (2,100 / 900) is more than 2, so "more than double" follows the stated minima. Because both figures are lower bounds ("exceeding"), the inequality still holds: anything above 2,100 is more than twice anything that only just clears 900. Do not confuse this with Concorde's "more than twice the speed of sound," which is a different comparison in Paragraph 7.

**Tip:** Floor comparisons ("exceeding X") still support "more than double" when the smaller floor times two sits below the larger floor.

Both speeds come from the passage and Concorde's exceeds twice the 747's, so the synthesis is true.

**C) The Comet's early structural failures (Paragraph 5) are presented as having permanently ended commercial jet aviation, contradicting the continued development described in Paragraph 6.**

Paragraph 5 only says the Comet was "temporarily grounded" and design standards were reshaped; Paragraph 6 then shows the 747 entering service. Nothing claims commercial jets ended for good. The supposed contradiction only appears if you rewrite "temporarily" as permanent abandonment — which the passage never does. Continued jet airliner development after 1952 is the through-line Paragraph 6 documents.

The text records a temporary pause, not a permanent end to jet aviation, so the claim is false.

**D) The shift toward efficiency described in Paragraph 8 is consistent with the passage's closing suggestion that aviation's easiest technological gains may already have been captured (Paragraph 9).**

Paragraph 8 shows progress pivoting to efficiency after speed plateaued; Paragraph 9 floats the idea that the "easiest gains have already been captured." Those beats harmonize rather than collide. Flat cruise speeds plus incremental materials and engine work fit a story where the dramatic early leaps are harder to repeat. Paragraph 9 still frames a debate, but the efficiency pivot is compatible with the "easiest gains captured" side of that debate.

Efficiency-focused late gains mesh with the "easiest gains already captured" debate, so the synthesis is true.

**E) Because cruising speeds stagnated after Concorde's retirement, the passage implies no further aviation technology development has occurred since 2003.**

Paragraph 8 places the post-Concorde story in fuel, safety, and environmental gains — including ~80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre — not a freeze of all technology. Flat cruise speed is not "no further development." Incremental work on engines, aerodynamics, and lightweight composites is explicitly still in motion. Treating one stagnant metric as a total freeze ignores the efficiency axis the paragraph names as central.

**Trap:** One stagnant metric (speed) is stretched into a claim that nothing else advanced.

Efficiency and materials kept improving after Concorde, so "no further development" is false.
highlights: remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines
cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour
temporarily grounded the type
whose easiest gains have already been captured
Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had jet engines not been developed, commercial aviation would have remained substantially slower for decades longer."
"Engineers recommended that the design undergoes further structural testing before certification."
"The number of transatlantic routes served by jet aircraft continue to expand each decade."
"Neither the engine reliability nor the structural materials were sufficiently advanced in the early 1910s."
"Having identified the source of metal fatigue, engineers redesigned the aircraft's window frames."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had jet engines not been developed, commercial aviation would have remained substantially slower for decades longer."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with optional inversion: Had + past participle stands for If…had not…, and the result clause correctly uses would have + past participle. Auxiliaries and negatives land in the right places. The content echoes the passage's jet-leap story without changing the grammar test: form, not historical trivia, decides the item. Watch that the if-clause stays past perfect (had…been developed) while the result stays would have + V3.

**Tip:** Inverted Had…not… is exam-safe when the result stays would have + V3.

The inverted third conditional is well formed, so the sentence is true.

**B) "Engineers recommended that the design undergoes further structural testing before certification."**

Recommend that triggers the mandative subjunctive: the verb after that should be the bare base form undergo, not present indicative undergoes. The singular design does not change that rule. Demand / insist / recommend / suggest that… all prefer the bare stem in formal exam English. Comet-era structural testing vocabulary from the passage is only thematic colour; the error is purely the indicative ending.

**Trap:** Subject–verb agreement habits can trick you into undergoes after a singular noun — ignore that and keep the base form.

After recommended that you need undergo, so the wording is false — "…that the design undergo…."

**C) "The number of transatlantic routes served by jet aircraft continue to expand each decade."**

The number of… is a singular subject even when the noun after of is plural, so the verb must be continues, not continue. Routes do not control the agreement. Strip the of-phrase mentally: "The number… continues." A plural verb would only fit if the head were numbers or a true plural subject. Lindbergh / Atlantic route vocabulary keeps the sentence on-theme but does not rescue the agreement error.

**Trap:** A long plural of-phrase often steals the verb; stay locked on number.

Singular the number needs continues, so the sentence is false — "…continues to expand…."

**D) "Neither the engine reliability nor the structural materials were sufficiently advanced in the early 1910s."**

With neither…nor, the verb typically agrees with the nearer subject. Here the nearer noun is plural structural materials, so were is the right choice. If the nearer noun were singular (reliability alone after nor), was would be expected instead. The early-1910s content aligns with Paragraph 2's wartime-era limits without changing the proximity rule.

Proximity agreement with plural materials licenses were, so the sentence is true.

**E) "Having identified the source of metal fatigue, engineers redesigned the aircraft's window frames."**

The -ing clause Having identified… correctly modifies engineers, who both identify and redesign. There is no dangling participle attached to the wrong noun. The perfect participle Having identified… also orders the actions: diagnosis first, redesign second — matching the Comet fatigue → redesign logic in Paragraph 5. A dangling version would leave a non-agent (frames, fatigue) as the implied subject of Having identified.

The participle attaches to the logical agent engineers, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the aircraft entered service than structural concerns began to emerge."
"The airframe, along with several related components, were redesigned after the incident."
"Each of the surveyed engineers have proposed a similar structural fix."
"By the time the aircraft is retired, it will have already flown for several decades."
"The figures, which were compiled across several test flights, indicate consistent fuel savings."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the aircraft entered service than structural concerns began to emerge."**

No sooner…than is a correlative inversion pattern: No sooner + had + subject + past participle, then than + simple past. Both halves are correctly formed here. The Comet-like timeline (service, then structural concerns) is thematic only; correctness hinges on had-inversion plus than, not when. Swapping in when or dropping the past perfect would break the exam pattern.

**Tip:** Remember the partner is than, not when; and the first clause uses past perfect with inversion.

The No sooner…than inversion is textbook-correct, so the sentence is true.

**B) "The airframe, along with several related components, were redesigned after the incident."**

Along with… is parenthetical; the grammatical subject remains singular the airframe, so the verb should be was redesigned, not were. The plural components do not inherit agreement. The same trap appears with as well as / together with / in addition to — companions after commas do not create a plural subject. Redesign-after-incident wording nods to Comet history but does not change the agreement rule.

**Trap:** Comma-wrapped companions with along with / as well as look like compound subjects but leave the first noun in charge.

Singular airframe needs was, so the wording is false — "…was redesigned…."

**C) "Each of the surveyed engineers have proposed a similar structural fix."**

Each of… takes a singular verb regardless of the plural noun that follows, so have proposed should be has proposed. Engineers is only the of-phrase. Parallel traps include every / either / neither as heads that stay singular. Structural-fix vocabulary fits the passage theme; the error is solely the plural verb after each.

**Trap:** Plural engineers after each of is a classic lure into have.

Each needs has proposed, so the sentence is false — "…has proposed…."

**D) "By the time the aircraft is retired, it will have already flown for several decades."**

By the time + present (future reference) pairs cleanly with future perfect will have flown for an action completed before that future point. The already fits the completed-before-retirement sense. Concorde's decades of service before 2003 are thematic colour; the grammar point is future perfect relative to a future-marked by-clause. Present perfect or simple future would miss that "completed before" relation.

Future perfect before a future retirement marker is exact, so the sentence is true.

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across several test flights, indicate consistent fuel savings."**

Plural figures correctly takes were compiled inside the non-restrictive which-clause and plural indicate in the main clause. Relatives and main verbs stay aligned. Commas around which… mark extra information without changing number agreement. Fuel-savings wording echoes Paragraph 8's efficiency theme but the test is plural consistency, not content recall.

Plural agreement holds in both the relative and the main verb, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 2, "novelty" means something new and unfamiliar, here describing aviation's early, fragile status before wartime development.
As used in Paragraph 3, "unimaginable" means extremely easy to predict or anticipate in advance.
As used in Paragraph 5, "absorbed" (in "commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap") means physically consumed as fuel, in a literal chemical sense.
As used in Paragraph 7, "self-sustaining" means capable of continuing to operate profitably without ongoing external financial support.
As used in Paragraph 9, "contingent" means guaranteed to occur regardless of any prior conditions or circumstances.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 2, "novelty" means something new and unfamiliar, here describing aviation's early, fragile status before wartime development.**

Paragraph 2 contrasts a "fragile novelty" with later "strategically significant military technology," so novelty names something new and not yet established — not a finished arsenal. Paired with fragile, the word marks early weakness and unfamiliarity rather than a toy or souvenir sense. The wartime transformation sentence is the gloss's best anchor: novelty is what aviation was before it became strategic.

That contextual sense matches "new and unfamiliar," so the meaning is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 3, "unimaginable" means extremely easy to predict or anticipate in advance.**

Paragraph 3 calls Lindbergh's journey "almost unimaginable" to the Wright brothers: something scarcely conceivable, not something easy to foresee. The proposed gloss flips the word. The "almost" intensifier still points toward difficulty of conception, not effortless prediction. Keeping the 5,800 km / 33.5-hour facts intact does not rescue an antonym gloss.

**Trap:** Opposite-meaning distractors often keep the surrounding history intact.

Unimaginable means hard to conceive, not easy to predict, so the gloss is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 5, "absorbed" (in "commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap") means physically consumed as fuel, in a literal chemical sense.**

"Commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap" is figurative: the industry took in and applied the advance. Nothing in the sentence treats fuel chemistry. The subject is commercial aviation as a sector, and the object is a technological leap — not kerosene or propellant. A literal soak-up reading would misfit both the subject and the abstract object.

**Trap:** Everyday concrete senses of absorb (soak up as fuel) do not fit technological-leap metaphors.

The usage means integrated the leap, not burned fuel, so the literal gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 7, "self-sustaining" means capable of continuing to operate profitably without ongoing external financial support.**

Paragraph 7 says Concorde "never became commercially self-sustaining" after listing costs, capacity, and regulations — commercial viability without perpetual external support is exactly the failed condition. The adverb commercially narrows the word to money and market survival, not biological or ecological self-maintenance. High operating costs and limited seating are the clues that "self-sustaining" here is a profit/support test.

The profitable-without-ongoing-subsidy reading fits the commercial frame, so the meaning is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "contingent" means guaranteed to occur regardless of any prior conditions or circumstances.**

Paragraph 9 speaks of "historically contingent breakthroughs" — gains that depend on particular historical conditions — the opposite of "guaranteed regardless." Historically is the tell: contingent here means dependent on circumstance, not inevitable. That sense pairs with the debate over whether easiest gains are already captured, which only makes sense if breakthroughs were situational rather than automatic.

Contingent here means dependent on circumstances, so the "guaranteed" gloss is false.
highlights: transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology
a journey that would have been almost unimaginable to the Wright brothers
Commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap with striking speed
never became commercially self-sustaining
a series of specific, historically contingent breakthroughs

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "sustained" means brief and immediately interrupted, describing a flight that lasted only a fraction of a second.
As used in Paragraph 4, "consequential" means having significant importance or far-reaching effects.
As used in Paragraph 6, "envelope" (in "performance envelope") means a physical paper container used to hold documents.
As used in Paragraph 8, "incremental" means occurring suddenly, in one single large step rather than gradually.
As used in Paragraph 2, "fragile" means strong and highly resistant to damage or failure.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "sustained" means brief and immediately interrupted, describing a flight that lasted only a fraction of a second.**

Paragraph 1 praises the first "sustained, controlled flight" lasting about 12 seconds — maintained in the air under control, not instantly cut off after a fraction of a second. Twelve seconds is short by modern standards, yet still a maintained interval, which is why sustained pairs with controlled. The gloss's "fraction of a second" invents a duration the passage does not use.

**Trap:** The flight was short by modern standards, but sustained still means kept going, not aborted instantly.

Sustained means maintained over time, so the "immediately interrupted" gloss is false.

**B) As used in Paragraph 4, "consequential" means having significant importance or far-reaching effects.**

Paragraph 4 calls jet propulsion "The most consequential single leap," then explains structural-scale performance gains. Consequential here means weighty in effect, not trivial. "Most…single leap" already signals ranking by impact; the following speeds-and-altitudes sentence supplies the far-reaching effects. Do not confuse consequential with consecutive (sequential) — the passage is about importance, not mere sequence.

Important / far-reaching matches the leap framing, so the meaning is true.

**C) As used in Paragraph 6, "envelope" (in "performance envelope") means a physical paper container used to hold documents.**

"Performance envelope" is engineering jargon for the range of speeds, altitudes, and capabilities an aircraft can handle — figurative, not stationery. Paragraph 6 ties the phrase to scale and performance that would have seemed fantasy at Kitty Hawk, which only fits an operational-range reading. A paper-wrapper gloss would make the surrounding speed and altitude numbers nonsense.

**Trap:** Everyday paper-envelope senses collide with technical compounds like performance envelope.

The phrase names an operational range, not a paper wrapper, so the gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "incremental" means occurring suddenly, in one single large step rather than gradually.**

Paragraph 8 credits "decades of incremental improvement" — small, cumulative steps across engine design, aerodynamics, and materials — the opposite of one sudden leap. "Decades of" already blocks a single-step reading; incremental names the gradual method inside that span. That gradualism is set against earlier dramatic leaps (jets, Concorde) in the passage's broader arc.

Incremental means gradual step-by-step change, so the sudden-single-step gloss is false.

**E) As used in Paragraph 2, "fragile" means strong and highly resistant to damage or failure.**

Paragraph 2 calls early aviation a "fragile novelty," contrasting weakness before wartime strengthening. Fragile means delicate / easily broken, not tough. The transformation into "strategically significant military technology" only lands if fragile first marked vulnerability. A "strong and resistant" gloss is a straight antonym of the contrast the sentence builds.

Fragile is the opposite of highly damage-resistant, so the gloss is false.
highlights: the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered heavier-than-air aircraft
The most consequential single leap
a scale and performance envelope that would have seemed like pure fantasy
decades of incremental improvement in engine design, aerodynamics, and lightweight composite materials
transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 3, "culminating" means beginning or starting a process, rather than reaching its final or highest point.
As used in Paragraph 5, "catastrophic" means minor and easily corrected without significant consequence.
As used in Paragraph 7, "persistently" means occurring only once, briefly, and then never recurring.
As used in Paragraph 8, "axis" (in "central axis of improvement") means the main focus or primary direction around which change has occurred.
As used in Paragraph 9, "trajectory" means the path or course of development that something follows over time.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 3, "culminating" means beginning or starting a process, rather than reaching its final or highest point.**

Paragraph 3 says interwar change was "culminating in Charles Lindbergh's solo transatlantic flight" — Lindbergh is framed as a climax of that period, not its opening shot. Culminating in X presents X as the high point toward which prior change builds. The interwar "further transformation" leads into Lindbergh, so a "beginning" gloss reverses the sentence's direction.

Culminating means reaching a high point, not starting, so the gloss is false.

**B) As used in Paragraph 5, "catastrophic" means minor and easily corrected without significant consequence.**

Paragraph 5 speaks of "catastrophic structural failures" that grounded the type and reshaped industry standards — disastrous scale, not a minor fix. Temporary grounding plus industry-wide redesign standards are consequences that only fit a severe reading. "Minor and easily corrected" would erase both the fatalities implied by catastrophic failure and the regulatory aftermath the text records.

Catastrophic means disastrously severe, so the "minor" reading is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 7, "persistently" means occurring only once, briefly, and then never recurring.**

"Persistently high operating costs" means costs that stayed high over time. That ongoing sense contradicts "only once…never recurring." The adverb modifies how long the costs stayed high, not how dramatic a single spike was. Pair that with limited seating and regulatory limits as ongoing commercial pressures, not one-off events.

**Trap:** Intensity words (high costs) can distract from the temporal adverb persistently.

Persistently means continuing over time, so the one-off gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "axis" (in "central axis of improvement") means the main focus or primary direction around which change has occurred.**

Paragraph 8 says commercial aviation's "central axis of improvement" shifted toward efficiency, safety, and environment — a figurative main direction of change, not a geometric line or physical spindle. Central axis of X is a metaphor for the organizing priority of X. The shift "away from raw speed" only makes sense if axis names that priority, not a literal axle.

Main-focus / primary-direction matches the figurative axis, so the meaning is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "trajectory" means the path or course of development that something follows over time.**

Paragraph 9 debates "the century-long trajectory from Kitty Hawk to modern wide-body jets" — the developmental path over time, not a one-off event. Century-long already marks duration; trajectory names the course across that span. The debate over acceleration versus contingent breakthroughs is a debate about that path's shape, which confirms the developmental-course sense.

Path-over-time is exactly how trajectory is used, so the meaning is true.
highlights: culminating in Charles Lindbergh's solo transatlantic flight in 1927
a series of catastrophic structural failures
Persistently high operating costs
commercial aviation's central axis of improvement has shifted away from raw speed and toward efficiency
the century-long trajectory from Kitty Hawk to modern wide-body jets

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's opening claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The potato was domesticated in the Andean highlands roughly 8,000 years ago from thousands of wild tuber varieties.
Chuño is described as a freeze-drying preservation technique allowing potatoes to be stored for years.
European suspicion of the potato was linked partly to its membership in the nightshade family.
The potato was widely eaten as a staple food throughout Europe almost immediately after its introduction in the 1500s.
Frederick the Great's "Potato Order" was issued in 1756, mandating cultivation in Prussia.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The potato was domesticated in the Andean highlands roughly 8,000 years ago from thousands of wild tuber varieties.**

Paragraph 1 places domestication in the high Andean plateaus of present-day Peru and Bolivia and says indigenous peoples cultivated the potato "from thousands of wild tuber varieties over roughly 8,000 years." The statement keeps place, timescale, and wild-source breadth intact. "Highlands" is a fair stand-in for those high plateaus, and "roughly 8,000 years ago" tracks the same span the passage uses for cultivation from wild stock. Nothing in the claim invents a different region or a shorter breeding history.

**Tip:** Dates and quantities that paraphrase the same span still count as true.

The claim matches the opening origin facts, so it is true.

**B) Chuño is described as a freeze-drying preservation technique allowing potatoes to be stored for years.**

Still in Paragraph 1, the text names chuño as "a freeze-drying process" that "allowed potatoes to be stored for years at high altitude without spoiling." Both the method type and the long storage claim line up. The statement does not need the altitude detail to stay accurate; "for years" already matches the passage's storage claim. Treat chuño as the named technique the text defines, not as a later European invention.

The statement restates Paragraph 1's definition of chuño, so it is true.

**C) European suspicion of the potato was linked partly to its membership in the nightshade family.**

Paragraph 2 says the plant "belonged to the nightshade family, whose relatives include several toxic species," and that this background helped fuel deep suspicion (and even leprosy blame). The family link is explicit, not invented. "Linked partly" correctly leaves room for other reasons; the passage never says nightshade kinship was the only cause. Match the wording to that causal hint rather than upgrading it into a sole explanation.

**Tip:** "Linked partly" is weaker than "only cause," so it survives here.

The nightshade link is stated in Paragraph 2, so the claim is true.

**D) The potato was widely eaten as a staple food throughout Europe almost immediately after its introduction in the 1500s.**

Paragraph 2 records introduction in the mid-1500s, then undercuts any "immediate staple" story: "for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food." The statement flips chronology and diet status. Arrival and widespread eating are separated by about two centuries of mainly decorative cultivation, so "almost immediately" and "widely eaten as a staple" both fail. Do not let the mid-1500s date alone sell an early dietary takeover.

**Trap:** Arrival date ≠ immediate culinary adoption.

The claim fails: the passage says ornamental use dominated for about two centuries, not immediate staple eating.

**E) Frederick the Great's "Potato Order" was issued in 1756, mandating cultivation in Prussia.**

Paragraph 3 states that "Frederick the Great of Prussia issued a formal \"Potato Order\" in 1756 mandating cultivation." Ruler, year, place, and mandatory cultivation all match. The statement does not invent a different monarch or a voluntary campaign; it stays inside the decree the passage names. When a claim reprints a dated formal order nearly word for word, treat it as a straight match.

The claim tracks Paragraph 3's dated decree, so it is true.
highlights: cultivated it from thousands of wild tuber varieties over roughly 8,000 years
a freeze-drying process known as chuño, which allowed potatoes to be stored for years
Because the plant belonged to the nightshade family, whose relatives include several toxic species
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
Frederick the Great of Prussia issued a formal "Potato Order" in 1756 mandating cultivation

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's middle claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Potatoes are described as yielding roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions.
One influential study attributed up to 25% of urban population growth in relevant regions to potato adoption.
The Irish Lumper is described as one of many genetically diverse varieties cultivated in Ireland at the time.
The Great Famine, triggered by Phytophthora infestans, began in 1845.
The famine's death toll and emigration together contributed to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25%.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Potatoes are described as yielding roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions.**

Paragraph 4 gives the economic appeal in just those terms: potatoes "could yield roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions." Ratio, comparator, and caveat all survive the paraphrase. Keep the "under comparable conditions" hedge; without it the claim would sound absolute in a way the text does not. The fourfold figure is about land productivity versus wheat, not a claim about every crop or every climate.

The caloric-yield claim matches Paragraph 4, so it is true.

**B) One influential study attributed up to 25% of urban population growth in relevant regions to potato adoption.**

The same paragraph credits "one influential study attributing up to 25% of urban population growth in those areas to the crop's adoption." Ceiling percentage, urban growth focus, and attribution to the potato remain intact. "Up to 25%" is a ceiling, not a guarantee that every region hit that share, and the focus is urban growth in the areas where cultivation spread. Do not broaden the study into a claim about all population growth everywhere.

The 25% urban-growth attribution is explicit, so the statement is true.

**C) The Irish Lumper is described as one of many genetically diverse varieties cultivated in Ireland at the time.**

Paragraph 5 says much of the rural population was "dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper," and that this "genetic uniformity" left the crop vulnerable. The statement invents diversity where the text stresses dangerous sameness. Naming the Irish Lumper does not imply a crowded menu of co-equal staples; the passage's point is near-monoculture. Watch for claims that turn a single named variety into evidence of genetic breadth.

**Trap:** Naming a variety is not the same as calling it one among many co-equal staples.

The claim fails: Ireland relied almost exclusively on one variety, not a diverse mix.

**D) The Great Famine, triggered by Phytophthora infestans, began in 1845.**

Paragraph 5 names Phytophthora infestans and says it "triggered repeated harvest failures beginning in 1845," producing the famine. Pathogen and start year both appear. The passage frames the pathogen as the trigger for those harvest failures, so linking it to the famine's onset is fair. Stick to the dated start the text gives rather than inventing an earlier or later outbreak.

The outbreak-and-date framing matches Paragraph 5, so the statement is true.

**E) The famine's death toll and emigration together contributed to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25%.**

Paragraph 5 pairs roughly 1 million deaths and a further 1 million emigrants, "contributing to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25% within just a few years." The statement keeps the combined demographic result. It does not claim that deaths alone produced the whole decline, and it keeps the passage's approximate band. Treat the 20–25% figure as the joint outcome of starvation, disease, and emigration as the text presents them.

The 20–25% decline figure is stated outright, so the claim is true.
highlights: potatoes could yield roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions
one influential study attributing up to 25% of urban population growth in those areas to the crop's adoption
dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper
Phytophthora infestans triggered repeated harvest failures beginning in 1845
contributing to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25% within just a few years

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's later claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Global potato production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually.
The International Potato Center's gene bank in Lima is described as containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties.
Cooling a cooked potato is described as converting some of its resistant starch into ordinary digestible starch.
The size of the glycemic-response effect from cooling potatoes is described as consistent and identical across all preparation methods.
The passage concludes by presenting the potato's role in population growth as a genuinely debated question among historians.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Global potato production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually.**

Paragraph 6 opens with that exact scale: "Global production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually." Volume, annual framing, and approximating hedge all match. Extra details in the same paragraph about China, India, or six continents are not required for this claim to hold. When a statement reprints a headline production figure with the same "approximately," treat it as a direct hit.

The production total matches Paragraph 6, so the statement is true.

**B) The International Potato Center's gene bank in Lima is described as containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties.**

Paragraph 7 says "the International Potato Center in Lima maintains a gene bank containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties." Institution, city, and count line up. The "more than 4,000" floor is enough; the statement does not invent a smaller or exact closed count. Tie the figure to the Lima gene bank the passage names, not to Ireland's nineteenth-century fields.

The gene-bank figure is stated in Paragraph 7, so the claim is true.

**C) Cooling a cooked potato is described as converting some of its resistant starch into ordinary digestible starch.**

Paragraph 8 runs the chemistry the other way: cooling "converts a portion of its digestible starch into so-called resistant starch." The statement reverses which form becomes which. Cooling moves starch toward the resistant form that passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down, not back into ordinary digestible starch. On process claims, check the arrow of conversion before you accept shared vocabulary.

**Trap:** Direction flips on technical processes are classic true/false bait.

The claim fails: cooling turns digestible starch into resistant starch, not the reverse.

**D) The size of the glycemic-response effect from cooling potatoes is described as consistent and identical across all preparation methods.**

After noting a possible glycemic lowering, Paragraph 8 adds that "the magnitude of this effect varies considerably depending on preparation method." "Consistent and identical across all" invents uniformity the text denies. The passage allows a meaningful lowering in lab studies while still stressing that effect size is not fixed. Absolute sameness across methods is the opposite of "varies considerably."

The claim fails: the passage says the effect size varies considerably by preparation method.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting the potato's role in population growth as a genuinely debated question among historians.**

Paragraph 9 ends on open disagreement: whether the potato was a "primary driver" or "merely one contributing factor… remains a genuinely debated question among economic historians." The statement mirrors that unresolved framing. The text does not close with a settled verdict that the potato alone drove growth; it leaves the dispute open. Match the ending to that debate language rather than forcing a one-sided conclusion.

The closing debate is explicit in Paragraph 9, so the claim is true.
highlights: Global production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually
the International Potato Center in Lima maintains a gene bank containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties
converts a portion of its digestible starch into so-called resistant starch
the magnitude of this effect varies considerably depending on preparation method
remains a genuinely debated question among economic historians studying the period

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since potatoes yielded roughly four times the calories per unit of land compared to wheat, it can be inferred that a given plot could support meaningfully more people when planted with potatoes rather than wheat.
If the famine killed roughly 1 million people and a further 1 million emigrated, then approximately 2 million people were removed from Ireland's population through these two combined causes.
Because Parmentier's guarded fields were deliberately left unattended at night, it can be inferred that this was intended to make the crop seem more, not less, valuable to onlookers.
Because the potato offered a higher caloric yield, the passage implies this factor alone fully and conclusively explains all population growth observed in adopting regions.
Since resistant starch passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down, it can be inferred that it behaves differently in digestion than ordinary digestible starch.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since potatoes yielded roughly four times the calories per unit of land compared to wheat, it can be inferred that a given plot could support meaningfully more people when planted with potatoes rather than wheat.**

Paragraph 4 states the fourfold caloric yield and immediately glosses the consequence: "allowing considerably more people to be fed from the same amount of farmland." The inference is the passage's own next step, not a leap. "Meaningfully more people" tracks "considerably more people" without inventing a precise headcount. Stay inside that land-to-calories-to-people chain rather than claiming other social causes.

**Tip:** When the text itself draws the people-fed consequence, the inference is safe.

The more-people inference follows Paragraph 4's own yield argument, so the statement is true.

**B) If the famine killed roughly 1 million people and a further 1 million emigrated, then approximately 2 million people were removed from Ireland's population through these two combined causes.**

Paragraph 5 gives both figures side by side. Adding them is arithmetic on stated quantities, not a new historical claim. "Removed from Ireland's population" fairly covers deaths plus emigration. The statement does not invent a third cause or change either million into a different order of magnitude. When both inputs are explicit, summing them is a permitted inference.

The combined ~2 million figure follows cleanly from the paired Paragraph 5 totals, so the claim is true.

**C) Because Parmentier's guarded fields were deliberately left unattended at night, it can be inferred that this was intended to make the crop seem more, not less, valuable to onlookers.**

Paragraph 3 says fields were "guarded loudly by day while deliberately left unguarded at night, tricking suspicious peasants into believing the crop was valuable enough to steal." Day noise plus night vulnerability is the value signal. Leaving the fields unattended at night is not carelessness in the passage; it is part of the staged temptation. Read the trick as raising perceived worth, not as proof the crop was worthless.

The intentional "look valuable" reading is the text's own motive, so the inference is true.

**D) Because the potato offered a higher caloric yield, the passage implies this factor alone fully and conclusively explains all population growth observed in adopting regions.**

Paragraph 4 attributes only "up to 25%" of urban growth in one study, and Paragraph 9 still treats sole-driver status as debated versus "one contributing factor among several." "Alone… all" overclaims certainty. A strong caloric advantage can matter without exhausting every demographic cause. Absolute words like "alone," "fully," and "all" are the giveaway that the inference has gone past the text.

**Trap:** A strong contributing cause is not a complete exclusive explanation.

The claim fails: the passage never says yield alone fully explains all growth, and later calls that question debated.

**E) Since resistant starch passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down, it can be inferred that it behaves differently in digestion than ordinary digestible starch.**

Paragraph 8 contrasts digestible starch converted into resistant starch that "passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down," with implications for glycemic response versus a hot, freshly cooked potato. Different digestive behaviour is the point of the contrast. Ordinary digestible starch is what gets converted away from; resistant starch is defined by that incomplete breakdown. The inference stays inside the passage's digestive distinction rather than inventing a new nutrient claim.

Different digestive behaviour follows from Paragraph 8's breakdown contrast, so the statement is true.
highlights: allowing considerably more people to be fed from the same amount of farmland
killed roughly 1 million people through starvation and disease, while a further 1 million emigrated
deliberately left unguarded at night, tricking suspicious peasants into believing the crop was valuable enough to steal
or merely one contributing factor among several simultaneous agricultural and economic changes, remains a genuinely debated question
resistant starch, which passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The genetic uniformity created by reliance on the Irish Lumper helps explain why a single pathogen was able to devastate Ireland's food supply so severely.
The vulnerability exposed by the Irish famine is presented as a motivating factor behind the later genetic-diversity preservation efforts described toward the end of the passage.
Because 25% of urban population growth in some regions was attributed to potato adoption, the passage implies the remaining 75% must be entirely unexplained by any other historical factor.
The caloric-yield advantage described earlier in the passage is consistent with the same crop later becoming central to a catastrophic single-variety dependency in Ireland.
