Because the gene bank preserves more than 4,000 varieties, the passage implies Ireland's nineteenthcentury food supply relied on a similarly large number of varieties.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The genetic uniformity created by reliance on the Irish Lumper helps explain why a single pathogen was able to devastate Ireland's food supply so severely.**

Paragraph 5 links "almost exclusively" dependence on the Irish Lumper to "genetic uniformity" that "left the crop dangerously vulnerable" when Phytophthora infestans hit. Uniformity → one pathogen can wreck the food base is the passage's causal chain. Extreme reliance on one variety means there was little genetic backup when harvest failures began. The synthesis does not invent a new pathogen; it uses the vulnerability the text already states.

The vulnerability synthesis matches Paragraph 5's uniformity–pathogen link, so the statement is true.

**B) The vulnerability exposed by the Irish famine is presented as a motivating factor behind the later genetic-diversity preservation efforts described toward the end of the passage.**

Paragraph 7 opens "Partly in response to the vulnerability so starkly illustrated by the Irish famine," then describes gene-bank work to preserve diversity. Cross-section motive is explicit, not guessed. "Partly in response" is enough to count the famine as a motivating factor without claiming it was the only reason. Connect the early crisis section to the later Lima gene bank without inventing a different motive.

The famine-to-gene-bank motivation is stated in Paragraph 7, so the claim is true.

**C) Because 25% of urban population growth in some regions was attributed to potato adoption, the passage implies the remaining 75% must be entirely unexplained by any other historical factor.**

Paragraph 4's study attributes "up to 25%" to potato adoption; it never audits the residual share or declares it unexplained. Treating the leftover as "entirely unexplained" adds a claim the text never makes. An attributed percentage does not invent a vacuum for whatever remains. Watch for math that turns a partial attribution into a claim that other causes do not exist.

**Trap:** An attributed share does not invent a theory about whatever is left.

The claim fails: the passage says nothing that forces the remaining 75% to be unexplained.

**D) The caloric-yield advantage described earlier in the passage is consistent with the same crop later becoming central to a catastrophic single-variety dependency in Ireland.**

Paragraph 4's fourfold yield advantage explains why potatoes could dominate diets; Paragraph 5 then shows Ireland dependent almost exclusively on one variety for daily calories, with disastrous results. High appeal and extreme reliance belong to the same crop story. Consistency here means the middle sections can sit together without contradiction, not that yield alone caused the famine. Keep the synthesis modest: caloric payoff helps explain how a crop could become diet-central, which later turned dangerous under uniformity.

**Tip:** Consistency across sections is not the same as claiming yield caused the famine.

The yield-to-dependency arc fits the passage's middle sections, so the statement is true.

**E) Because the gene bank preserves more than 4,000 varieties, the passage implies Ireland's nineteenthcentury food supply relied on a similarly large number of varieties.**

Paragraph 5 stresses almost exclusive reliance on one variety; Paragraph 7's large modern collection is a corrective response to that vulnerability, not a mirror of nineteenth-century Irish practice. The statement reverses the contrast. A present-day diversity bank does not rewrite the earlier monoculture crisis. Do not project today's 4,000+ holdings backward onto Ireland's Lumper-dependent countryside.

The claim fails: Ireland's crisis came from near single-variety dependence, while the 4,000+ bank is a later diversity safeguard.
highlights: This genetic uniformity left the crop dangerously vulnerable when the fungus-like pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Partly in response to the vulnerability so starkly illustrated by the Irish famine
one influential study attributing up to 25% of urban population growth in those areas to the crop's adoption
dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper, for daily caloric intake
dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the pathogen not spread so rapidly, the famine's death toll would likely have been considerably lower."
"Officials recommended that farmers diversifies their planted varieties to reduce future risk."
"The number of preserved potato varieties continue to grow as new specimens are catalogued."
"Neither the soil conditions nor the climate were fully suited to reliable wheat cultivation in that region."
"Having subsisted largely on potatoes as a prisoner, Parmentier later championed the crop publicly."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the pathogen not spread so rapidly, the famine's death toll would likely have been considerably lower."**

This is a clean third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + past participle in the if-clause, and would have + past participle in the result. No missing auxiliary, no tense mix-up. The inverted Had… form is standard for a counterfactual past condition, and would likely have been keeps the result in the same past-perfect conditional zone. Potato-famine vocabulary does not change the grammar test: check the conditional scaffolding.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… is just If… had… with the if dropped.

The conditional pattern is well formed, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "Officials recommended that farmers diversifies their planted varieties to reduce future risk."**

After recommend that, English needs the mandative subjunctive (base form): farmers diversify, not diversifies. The -s ending wrongly treats the verb as a present-tense finite form agreeing with farmers. Recommendations, demands, and similar verbs after that take the bare base form even with a plural subject. Spot the -s on diversifies as the error, not the surrounding crop vocabulary.

**Trap:** Recommend/insist/require + that → bare infinitive base form.

The sentence fails: repair to "recommended that farmers diversify…".

**C) "The number of preserved potato varieties continue to grow as new specimens are catalogued."**

The number of is a singular head: the number… continues. Continue agrees with the plural noun varieties instead of with number, which is the classic agreement trap. Ignore the nearest plural noun and ask what the real subject is: number, not varieties. Once that head is clear, the plural continue is the fault.

The sentence fails: repair to "The number of preserved potato varieties continues to grow…".

**D) "Neither the soil conditions nor the climate were fully suited to reliable wheat cultivation in that region."**

Neither… nor joins a plural noun phrase (the soil conditions) and a singular one (the climate). When one conjunct is plural, plural agreement with were is an accepted choice; the coordinated subjects are treated as a joint unsuitable pair. The sentence does not force singular was just because climate is singular; the plural first conjunct supports were. Focus on the neither… nor agreement pattern rather than the farming content.

**Tip:** Mixed-number neither… nor is contested in pedantic rules, but plural were is standard enough here with a plural first conjunct.

The agreement choice is acceptable, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**E) "Having subsisted largely on potatoes as a prisoner, Parmentier later championed the crop publicly."**

The -ing absolute Having subsisted… correctly attaches to Parmentier, the subject of the main clause. There is no dangling modifier naming the wrong agent. The person who subsisted is the same person who later championed the crop, so the participle is anchored. A dangler would appear only if a different subject opened the main clause.

The participle and main-clause subject match, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the blight appeared than harvests began failing across the region."
"The gene bank, along with several partner institutions, were responsible for preserving the collection."
"Each of the surveyed farmers have reported declining yields in recent seasons."
"By the time the famine ended, emigration will have already reshaped the country's population."
"The findings, which were compiled across multiple studies, suggest a meaningful glycemic difference."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the blight appeared than harvests began failing across the region."**

No sooner… than correctly triggers inversion (had the blight appeared) and pairs past perfect with a simple-past sequel (began failing). The correlative pair is complete. Do not swap than for when, and do not drop the inversion after No sooner. The blight vocabulary is flavour; the grammar win is the finished No sooner… than frame.

**Tip:** No sooner pairs with than, not when.

The inversion correlative is well formed, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "The gene bank, along with several partner institutions, were responsible for preserving the collection."**

Along with several partner institutions is an aside, not a second subject for plural agreement. The true subject is singular the gene bank, so the verb should be was responsible. Phrases like along with, as well as, and together with do not turn a singular head into a plural subject. Strip the aside mentally and check agreement with gene bank alone.

**Trap:** Along with / as well as / together with does not pluralise a singular head.

The sentence fails: repair to "The gene bank… was responsible…".

**C) "Each of the surveyed farmers have reported declining yields in recent seasons."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when the of-phrase is plural. Have reported wrongly agrees with farmers instead of each. The magnet noun after of is a common trap; the real controller is each. Change have to has and the sentence locks into standard agreement.

The sentence fails: repair to "Each of the surveyed farmers has reported…".

**D) "By the time the famine ended, emigration will have already reshaped the country's population."**

By the time the famine ended anchors a past reference point, so the result needs past perfect (had already reshaped). Will have… projects a future-perfect result from now, which clashes with a finished past frame. Once the time clause is past, keep the main result in past perfect rather than jumping to will have. The mismatch of timeline is the error, not the emigration topic.

The sentence fails: repair to "…emigration had already reshaped…".

**E) "The findings, which were compiled across multiple studies, suggest a meaningful glycemic difference."**

Plural findings correctly takes were compiled in the relative clause and suggest in the main clause. Singular/plural agreement stays consistent throughout. The non-restrictive which-clause does not change the plural head, and both verbs follow that head. Treat this as a clean agreement check across clause and main verb.

Subject–verb agreement holds, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "domesticated" means bred and cultivated by humans over generations, rather than remaining wild.
As used in Paragraph 2, "suspicion" means confident trust and immediate acceptance, rather than doubt or wariness.
As used in Paragraph 3, "accelerated" means slowed down considerably, rather than sped up.
As used in Paragraph 5, "vulnerable" means resistant to harm or unlikely to be affected by disease.
As used in Paragraph 7, "safeguarding" means deliberately exposing something to greater risk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "domesticated" means bred and cultivated by humans over generations, rather than remaining wild.**

Paragraph 1 uses domesticated for the potato's shift from wild Andean tubers to human cultivation over roughly 8,000 years. That is precisely "bred and cultivated by humans… rather than remaining wild." The contrast with wild stock is built into the origin story the paragraph tells. Keep the gloss tied to human cultivation history, not to a later European marketing campaign.

The gloss matches Paragraph 1's usage, so the statement is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 2, "suspicion" means confident trust and immediate acceptance, rather than doubt or wariness.**

Paragraph 2 says the potato "was initially met with deep suspicion" before Europeans blamed nightshade kinship and delayed eating it. Suspicion here is doubt/wariness — the opposite of confident trust. Immediate acceptance would erase the two-century ornamental delay the same section describes. Antonym definitions are a common vocabulary trap on these items.

**Trap:** Vocabulary items often offer the antonym dressed as a definition.

The claimed meaning is inverted, so the statement is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 3, "accelerated" means slowed down considerably, rather than sped up.**

Paragraph 3 says "Adoption accelerated dramatically during the eighteenth century," describing a ramp-up via government campaigns. Accelerated means sped up, not slowed down. Frederick's order and Parmentier's publicity stunts are evidence of push and uptake, not of braking. Reject the slowdown gloss as a straight antonym of the passage's verb.

The antonym gloss fails against Paragraph 3, so the statement is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 5, "vulnerable" means resistant to harm or unlikely to be affected by disease.**

Paragraph 5 says genetic uniformity "left the crop dangerously vulnerable" to Phytophthora infestans. Vulnerable means exposed to harm, not resistant to it. "Dangerously" intensifies exposure, which cannot mean disease-proof. Flip the gloss back to susceptibility and the claim collapses. Resistance would contradict the harvest failures that follow from that vulnerability.

The claimed meaning reverses Paragraph 5, so the statement is false.

**E) As used in Paragraph 7, "safeguarding" means deliberately exposing something to greater risk.**

Paragraph 7's gene bank is "safeguarding traits such as disease resistance for future breeding programmes" — protecting desirable traits, not exposing them to risk. The whole point of the bank is preservation against loss, the opposite of deliberate exposure. Antonym bait again: safeguarding ≠ endangering.

The antonym definition fails, so the statement is false.
highlights: the potato was domesticated in the high Andean plateaus
it was initially met with deep suspicion
Adoption accelerated dramatically during the eighteenth century
This genetic uniformity left the crop dangerously vulnerable
safeguarding traits such as disease resistance for future breeding programmes

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "staple" (in "staple crop") means a basic, regularly consumed food forming a major part of a diet.
As used in Paragraph 5, "reliance" means active avoidance of something, rather than dependence on it.
As used in Paragraph 4, "measurably" means to a degree too small to detect or confirm.
As used in Paragraph 8, "meaningfully" (in "meaningfully lower") means to a degree substantial enough to matter, not negligibly.
As used in Paragraph 5, "uniformity" means a wide, varied range of different forms, rather than sameness.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "staple" (in "staple crop") means a basic, regularly consumed food forming a major part of a diet.**

Paragraph 1 contrasts the potato's later status as "a staple crop on nearly every continent" with its Andean origins. Staple crop = basic dietary mainstay, not a rare garnish. The global, everyday-food sense is what makes the opening contrast work. Keep that diet-core reading rather than treating staple as a mere synonym of "interesting plant."

The diet-core gloss matches Paragraph 1, so the statement is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 5, "reliance" means active avoidance of something, rather than dependence on it.**

Paragraph 5 opens "Ireland's reliance eventually became extreme," then explains almost exclusive dependence on the Irish Lumper. Reliance = dependence; "active avoidance" is the opposite. Extreme reliance is what made the food supply fragile, which only makes sense if people depended on the crop. Reject the avoidance gloss as inverted vocabulary.

The antonym gloss fails, so the statement is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 4, "measurably" means to a degree too small to detect or confirm.**

Paragraph 4 says population growth "measurably outpaced" comparable regions — i.e., to a detectable, confirmable degree. "Too small to detect" inverts the adverb. Historians would not cite a measurable outpace if the difference were invisible. Stick to detectable difference, not negligible noise.

The claimed meaning contradicts Paragraph 4, so the statement is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "meaningfully" (in "meaningfully lower") means to a degree substantial enough to matter, not negligibly.**

Paragraph 8 says cooling can "meaningfully lower the food's glycemic response," contrasting a non-trivial effect with mere noise, while still allowing preparation-dependent magnitude. Substantial-enough-to-matter is the right reading. The later note that magnitude varies does not shrink "meaningfully" into "negligibly"; it only says the size is not fixed. Keep the adverb tied to a real glycemic difference, not to a claim of identical results across every cooking method.

The gloss fits Paragraph 8's glycemic claim, so the statement is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 5, "uniformity" means a wide, varied range of different forms, rather than sameness.**

Paragraph 5's "genetic uniformity" follows from relying on a single variety and explains vulnerability to one pathogen. Uniformity = sameness, not diversity. Later gene-bank variety counts describe a modern corrective, not the meaning of uniformity in this sentence. Antonym bait again: do not redefine sameness as variety.

**Trap:** Gene-bank diversity elsewhere does not redefine uniformity here.

The antonym gloss fails against Paragraph 5, so the statement is false.
highlights: Long before it became a staple crop on nearly every continent
Ireland's reliance eventually became extreme
population growth measurably outpaced that of comparable regions
this can meaningfully lower the food's glycemic response
This genetic uniformity left the crop dangerously vulnerable

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Below is one short sentence taken directly from the passage. Each numbered option is a paraphrase claiming to preserve its original meaning. Decide whether each one actually does. Original sentence: "For roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food."
statements: For a long stretch of time, the plant was cultivated more as a decorative curiosity than as a common part of people's diets.
For roughly two centuries, the plant was widely eaten as food rather than grown as an ornamental.
The plant was, for a long period, largely dismissed as inedible rather than grown for any purpose at all.
During this period, the plant's decorative appeal outweighed its role as a food source for most people.
The plant was grown almost exclusively as food, with any ornamental use being extremely rare.
tactical_explanations:
**A) For a long stretch of time, the plant was cultivated more as a decorative curiosity than as a common part of people's diets.**

The original says it was "grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food" for roughly two centuries. Decorative/curiosity use ahead of dietary use is preserved; only the wording softens. "Long stretch of time" covers the two-century span without changing which use dominated. A true paraphrase keeps the ornamental-over-food ranking intact.

**Tip:** Faithful paraphrase keeps the same unequal comparison, not just shared keywords.

The paraphrase keeps the ornamental-over-food imbalance, so it is true.

**B) For roughly two centuries, the plant was widely eaten as food rather than grown as an ornamental.**

This swaps both sides of the rather than contrast: food becomes primary, ornamental secondary. That is the reverse of "mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten." Keeping "roughly two centuries" does not rescue a flipped ranking. On rather-than lines, check which side is majority before you accept the paraphrase.

**Trap:** Keeping the time span while flipping the comparison still fails.

The paraphrase inverts the original contrast, so it is false.

**C) The plant was, for a long period, largely dismissed as inedible rather than grown for any purpose at all.**

The original never claims the potato was thought inedible or unused. It was grown — chiefly as decoration — not abandoned as purposeless. "Inedible" and "for any purpose at all" are smuggled-in distortions. Shared ideas of early European reluctance are not enough if the paraphrase invents total non-use. Stick to ornamental-over-food; do not upgrade suspicion into a claim that nobody grew the plant.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the shortage not disrupted automotive supply chains, vehicle production would have remained substantially higher."
"Regulators recommended that the company diversifies its supplier base to reduce risk."
"The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continue to increase each year."
"Neither the equipment nor the expertise required were easily replicated by new entrants."
"Having invested heavily in domestic capacity, the government sought greater supply chain independence."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the shortage not disrupted automotive supply chains, vehicle production would have remained substantially higher."**

This is a third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + past participle replaces If… had. The result clause correctly uses would have + past participle (would have remained). The negation sits on the inverted had-clause without breaking the pattern.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… not… pairs with would have + V3 — same timeline as If… had not…

The conditional architecture is sound, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Regulators recommended that the company diversifies its supplier base to reduce risk."**

After recommend that, formal English wants the mandative subjunctive — base form diversify, not present-tense diversifies. The -s ending treats the verb as an ordinary present instead of a subjunctive.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Recommend that + indicative -s is a frequent near-miss.

The line fails; the repaired wording is "Regulators recommended that the company diversify its supplier base to reduce risk."

**C) "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continue to increase each year."**

The number of is grammatically singular, so the verb must be continues, not plural continue. The plural countries after of does not control agreement.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** A plural noun after of does not make "the number of" plural.

Agreement breaks here; the sound version is "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continues to increase each year."

**D) "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required were easily replicated by new entrants."**

With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here that subject is the expertise required — singular uncountable expertise — so the verb should be was, not were.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Two nouns before the verb tempt a plural even when the nearer head is singular.

Proximity agreement fails, so the sentence doesn’t hold — "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required was easily replicated by new entrants."

**E) "Having invested heavily in domestic capacity, the government sought greater supply chain independence."**

The perfect participle Having invested modifies the government, the same agent that sought independence afterward. No dangling or mismatched subject — the investor and the seeker are one.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

The participle attaches cleanly to the government, so the wording is sound.

No sooner… than correctly triggers inversion (had the shortage begun) with past perfect in the first clause and simple past (started) in the second. The correlative pair is than, not when.

The No sooner… than pattern is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The programme, along with several related subsidies, were announced the same year."**

Along with several related subsidies is a parenthetical add-on; the real subject is singular the programme, so the verb must be was announced, not were. The plural noun inside the aside does not take over agreement.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Along with + plural looks like a plural subject, but the head noun still governs the verb.

Agreement fails; repair to "The programme, along with several related subsidies, was announced the same year."

**C) "Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported ongoing supply constraints."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when the of-phrase is plural. Have reported should be has reported.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

**Trap:** Manufacturers after of invites plural have, but Each keeps the verb singular.

The plural verb after Each is wrong — "Each of the surveyed manufacturers has reported ongoing supply constraints."

**D) "By the time the new fab opens, competitors will have already expanded their own capacity."**

By the time + present (opens) sets a future reference point; will have expanded is future perfect for completion before that point. Already sits naturally inside the perfect.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

Future perfect before a future By the time marker is the right tense pairing, so the line holds.

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across several fiscal years, indicate a persistent cost increase."**

Plural figures takes were compiled in the non-restrictive which-clause and plural indicate in the main clause. Relative and main verbs both track the same plural head.

Check the trigger pattern in isolation — agreement, mood, or modifier attachment — before trusting how the sentence sounds. A single wrong form is enough to flip the item even when the vocabulary feels familiar.

Plural subject and plural verbs align throughout, so the sentence is sound.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**E) As used in Paragraph 8, "outsized" means smaller than would normally be expected.**

Paragraph 8 says disruptions need not involve cutting-edge tech "to produce outsized economic consequences." Outsized means disproportionately large, not smaller than expected.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Out- as a size prefix is misread as undersized.

The meaning claim fails; outsized here means larger than normal, not smaller.

Paragraph 3 talks about competing "at the cutting edge" of chip manufacturing after describing denser, more expensive fabs. Cutting-edge means at the technological forefront — the opposite of outdated or behind.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

The gloss fails; cutting-edge here means leading-tech, not behind the curve.

**B) As used in Paragraph 4, "idle" (as in "idle assembly lines") means to keep running continuously at full capacity.**

Paragraph 4 says the shortage "forced automakers worldwide to idle assembly lines," then cut vehicle output by millions. Idle here means shut down or leave unused — not run at full capacity.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Everyday "idle" as "not working" is flipped into continuous full production.

The claimed meaning reverses the verb; idle here means stop or pause the lines, so the identification fails.

**C) As used in Paragraph 7, "replicating" means copying or reproducing something that already exists elsewhere.**

Paragraph 7 says closing the gap needs more than capital, "without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise." Replicating there means copying / reproducing that expertise — matching the offered gloss.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "unremarkable" means ordinary or unexceptional, not attracting special notice.**

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "concentration" (in this economic sense) means being spread evenly and widely across many locations.**

Paragraph 9 asks whether economics will "continue to favour concentration" versus geographic diversification. Concentration here means clustering production narrowly — the opposite of even, wide distribution.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

The gloss fails; concentration means gathering in few places, not spreading evenly.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Below is one short sentence taken directly from the passage. Each numbered option is a paraphrase claiming to preserve its original meaning. Decide whether each one actually does. Original sentence: "Critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one."
statements: Critics argue the same situation might instead make Taiwan especially attractive to attack, not especially safe from it.
Critics agree that this dynamic clearly makes Taiwan the most protected location in the region, with no plausible alternative interpretation.
Critics suggest this dynamic could be interpreted either way, making Taiwan both unusually vulnerable and unusually secure at the same time.
According to critics, the same circumstances might just as easily mark Taiwan out as a prime target as they might mark it out as being shielded.

tactical_explanations:
**A) Critics argue the same situation might instead make Taiwan especially attractive to attack, not especially safe from it.**

The original says critics counter that the silicon-shield dynamic "could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one." "Attractive to attack" ↔ "tempting target" and "not especially safe" ↔ "rather than… protected" preserve that reversal.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

The paraphrase keeps the critics' target-not-shielded flip, so it stands.

**B) Critics agree that this dynamic clearly makes Taiwan the most protected location in the region, with no plausible alternative interpretation.**

Critics do not agree with the protective reading; they counter it. "Clearly… most protected" and "no plausible alternative" erase both the countering stance and the "could equally be read" hedge.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Critics' challenge is rewritten as endorsement of the shield.

The paraphrase fails; the original is an alternative reading (tempting target), not critics affirming unique protection.

**C) Critics suggest this dynamic could be interpreted either way, making Taiwan both unusually vulnerable and unusually secure at the same time.**

"Could equally be read as… rather than…" presents the target reading as a rival that displaces the protected reading, not as critics holding both vulnerability and security simultaneously. "Both… at the same time" invents a both/and stance the sentence does not claim.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

**Trap:** Rather than (replacement) is misheard as both/and.

The paraphrase fails; critics offer an alternative target reading, not simultaneous dual endorsement.

**D) According to critics, the same circumstances might just as easily mark Taiwan out as a prime target as they might mark it out as being shielded.**

"Might just as easily… as…" restates "could equally be read as… rather than…": same hedge, same target-versus-shielded contrast, without adding certainty or dropping the critics' frame.

Read the claim against the exact wording in the source rather than against a remembered paraphrase. On the exam, that closer reading is what separates a faithful restatement from a near-miss twist.

The equal-possibility target-vs-shielded wording matches the original, so the paraphrase holds.

**E) Critics dismiss the idea that Taiwan's situation carries any strategic risk or protection whatsoever.**

Critics do not dismiss strategy altogether; they argue the silicon-shield story can be read as greater temptation, not that risk and protection are nonexistent. Total dismissal invents a claim the sentence never makes.

Name the precise mismatch: chronology, quantity, certainty, or a swapped subject. Once that distortion is visible, the false label follows without needing extra invention.

The paraphrase fails; critics reframe the dynamic as a tempting target, they do not deny strategic stakes entirely.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.
Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.
Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.
The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.
Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.**

Paragraph 1 opens with a direct size comparison: a glacier "roughly the size of Great Britain" sits in West Antarctica. The statement simply repeats that explicit scale, without adding numbers or geography the text never gives. Do not confuse this Britain-scale analogy with the later Manhattan cavity or the 65-centimetre sea-level figure—those are separate measurements. The wording "roughly the size of Great Britain" is the exact anchor you need for a bare size claim.

**Tip:** Treat bare size or place analogies as true when they echo the passage word-for-word or with a light paraphrase.

The size match is stated outright in Paragraph 1, so the claim is true.

**B) Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.**

Still in Paragraph 1, the text says that if Thwaites were to "disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres." The statement's "full disintegration" is just a clean rephrase of that total-collapse scenario, and the centimetre figure is unchanged. Watch that you do not swap this 65 cm Thwaites-only figure for Paragraph 4's additional three metres from surrounding glaciers. The phrase "disintegrate entirely" plus "roughly 65 centimetres" is the precise pairing the statement restates.

The 65-centimetre rise is the passage's own number for complete loss, so the claim matches.

**C) Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: once retreat begins, warmer water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, "accelerating melting rather than slowing it." The statement flips that causal direction—from acceleration to slowing—so it fails against the stability mechanism the text names. The trap is the verb "slows": the passage insists the feedback speeds melt, not brakes it. Match the claim against the exact contrast "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" and the reverse becomes obvious.

**Trap:** Watch for verbs that reverse the marine ice-sheet feedback; the passage insists melt speeds up, not cools down.

The claim reverses Paragraph 2's accelerating feedback, so it fails.

**D) The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.**

Paragraph 2 locates the danger in bedrock that "slopes downward inland," not upward. An upward slope would block warm-water intrusion; a downward one enables the self-reinforcing retreat the paragraph describes. The statement simply swaps the slope direction. "Upward" is a one-word antonym trap of "downward inland," so any slope claim must keep that direction intact. The passage's wording "slopes downward inland" is the fact that kills this rewrite.

Downward inland, not upward, is the bedrock fact, so the claim is false.

**E) Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.**

Paragraph 2 ends by labelling that self-reinforcing melt loop: "a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability." The statement faithfully restates that definition—name and mechanism line up. Nothing in the label invents a different process or a different technical name. The clause that equates "self-reinforcing process" with "marine ice sheet instability" is the definitional match the statement copies.

The term and the feedback process are equated in Paragraph 2, so the claim is true.
highlights: a glacier roughly the size of Great Britain
were it to disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres
accelerating melting rather than slowing it
bedrock that slopes downward inland
a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.
The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.
Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.
Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.
That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.**

Paragraph 3 reports that in 2019 radar found a cavity "roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan." The statement's hyphenated "two-thirds" is the same fraction; it does not invent a larger or later cavity. Spelling or hyphenation differences ("two-thirds" vs "twothirds") do not change the fraction the passage gives. Anchor on "roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan" as the cavity's stated scale.

The Manhattan-scale comparison is Paragraph 3's own measure, so the claim is true.

**B) The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.**

The same sentence says the cavity was "large enough to have once contained approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice that had already melted away." "About" fairly covers "approximately," and the tonne count is unchanged. Softeners like "about" and "approximately" are interchangeable paraphrases, not new quantities. The figure "approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice" is the exact number the statement echoes.

The 14-billion-tonne figure is stated in Paragraph 3, so the claim matches.

**C) Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.**

Paragraph 3 stresses the opposite: warm-water erosion was "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested." Radar, not surface surveys, revealed the cavity's scale. The statement credits surface data with a discovery the text withholds from them. The word "already" falsely pretends surface methods had finished the job before radar. Compare the claim with "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested" and the understatement becomes clear.

**Trap:** "Already" + surface methods is a common flip—Paragraph 3 says surface data understated the problem.

Surface observations alone missed this extent, so the claim fails.

**D) Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.**

Paragraph 4 estimates that if the buttressing effect were entirely lost, surrounding glaciers "could eventually contribute an additional three metres of sea-level rise." The statement correctly ties that three-metre add-on to loss of the ice shelf's buttress role. Do not confuse this additional three metres with Paragraph 1's roughly 65 centimetres for Thwaites alone. The wording "additional three metres of sea-level rise" after lost buttressing is the exact estimate restated here.

The three-metre estimate is Paragraph 4's figure for lost buttressing, so the claim is true.

**E) That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.**

Paragraph 4 immediately times the extra rise as "unfolding over centuries rather than years." A single decade is far shorter than that multi-century window, so the statement invents a rapid timetable the text rejects. "Years" already rules out a decade-scale sprint; "centuries" stretches the window even further. Match any timing claim against "unfolding over centuries rather than years" before accepting a fast calendar.

Centuries, not a decade, is the span given, so the claim is false.
highlights: roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan
approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice
far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested
an additional three metres of sea-level rise
unfolding over centuries rather than years

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.
This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.
The joint research collaboration began in 2018.
All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.
Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.**

Paragraph 5 reports that satellite measurements show Thwaites "has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss" since the 1990s. The statement repeats that doubling without inventing a steeper surge or a different start year. "Roughly doubled" is already a softener, so do not treat the claim as demanding an exact 2.00 multiplier. The phrase "roughly doubled its rate of ice loss" since the 1990s is the statistic the statement copies.

The doubled-loss claim is Paragraph 5's own statistic, so it is true.

**B) This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.**

The same paragraph cautions that acceleration "has not proceeded smoothly"; sections have "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." "Without any pauses" erases those temporary stabilisations the text explicitly records. Overall doubling and stop-start local behaviour can both be true; the trap is treating them as mutually exclusive. The wording "has not proceeded smoothly" plus periodic stabilisation directly kills a no-pause claim.

**Trap:** Doubling overall does not mean a smooth, unbroken climb—Paragraph 5 flags stop-start behaviour.

Pauses and restabilisations contradict "smoothly," so the claim fails.

**C) The joint research collaboration began in 2018.**

Paragraph 6 introduces the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration as a U.S.–U.K. venture "beginning in 2018." The statement names that start date accurately and invents no earlier founding year. A founding year is not a claim that all scientific uncertainty ended that year—later paragraphs still show divergent models. The exact anchor is "beginning in 2018" for the joint U.S.–U.K. collaboration.

The 2018 start is stated in Paragraph 6, so the claim is true.

**D) All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 opens with projections that "remain strikingly divergent"—decades in some runs, centuries in others. "Agree closely" is the exact opposite of that advertised mismatch. "All" plus "agree closely" is a unanimity rewrite the paragraph never supports. The opening line "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent" is enough to reject close agreement.

Striking divergence overturns close agreement, so the claim is false.

**E) Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.**

Paragraph 8 says current projections "span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult." Coastal engineers, planners, and insurers all work under that spread. The statement's "genuinely wide" tracks the passage's own wording. The difficulty is about the width of the range, not about planners ignoring sea-level risk altogether. Echo "span a range wide enough" and "genuinely difficult" when checking this synthesis of planning trouble.

The wide projection span for coastal planning is Paragraph 8's point, so the claim matches.
highlights: Since the 1990s, satellite measurements show Thwaites has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss
this acceleration has not proceeded smoothly; certain sections have periodically stabilised
beginning in 2018
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
current projections span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether an inference is actually supported, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.
If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.
Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.
Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.
Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.**

Paragraph 2 links bedrock that "slopes downward inland" to ever-deeper warm water and "accelerating melting," which glaciologists call "marine ice sheet instability." The inference is not a stretch: the slope is offered as the mechanism behind the self-reinforcing speed-up. "Helps explain" only asks for a causal link the paragraph already draws, not for a claim that slope is the sole cause of all ice loss. Re-read "slopes downward inland, meaning that… accelerating melting" as the mechanism chain the inference restates.

The bedrock geometry and the feedback are tied together in Paragraph 2, so the inference holds.

**B) If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.**

Paragraph 5's doubling of the ice-loss rate since the 1990s is already framed as acceleration (even with intermittent pauses). A higher loss rate is a straightforward worsening of retreat intensity relative to that earlier baseline. Temporary local stabilisations do not cancel the overall rate increase the satellites show. "Clearly worsened" here means a worse ice-loss rate than the 1990s baseline, which "roughly doubled" supports.

**Tip:** "Clearly worsened" here tracks rate of ice loss, not a claim that every section is always retreating at once.

Doubled loss since the 1990s supports a worse retreat rate, so the inference is true.

**C) Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 calls the projections "strikingly divergent" and traces that gap to uncertainty and hard-to-model ice physics. Divergence is evidence of disagreement about timing, not of "full agree[ment]." The inference flips the logical force of the word. "Imply…fully agree" is an illicit leap from disagreement-language to unanimity. Keep "strikingly divergent" as proof that timing consensus is missing, not present.

**Trap:** "Divergent" never licenses unanimous timing; it blocks it.

Divergence contradicts full agreement, so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.**

Paragraph 4 says Thwaites' ice shelf "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland," and that losing that buttress could unlock metres of extra rise from surrounding glaciers. Dependence of inland ice on Thwaites' buttress is exactly what that relationship implies. "Partly" is the safe hedge: the shelf holds ice back, so inland mass is not wholly independent of Thwaites. The phrase "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland" is the dependence clue the inference uses.

The inland buttressing role supports partial dependence, so the inference is true.

**E) Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.**

Paragraph 5 notes only that certain sections "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." Temporary pauses before restarting do not prove that overall retreat has ended; they complicate a simple future path while retreat continues. "Prove…has ended" overclaims from local, temporary pauses to a finished glacier-wide story. The sequence "stabilised before resuming retreat" shows pauses are interruptions, not an ending.

Stabilisation then "resuming retreat" overturns an "ended" verdict, so the claim is false.
highlights: bedrock that slopes downward inland, meaning that once retreat begins, warmer ocean water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, accelerating melting rather than slowing it
Thwaites has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
its ice shelf currently holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland
certain sections have periodically stabilised before resuming retreat

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across sections, with one numeric statement included.
statements: The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.
Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.
Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.
Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.
Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.**

Paragraph 3's cavity shows warm water eroding the underside far more than surface clues suggested; Paragraph 5 records roughly doubled ice loss since the 1990s. Linking underside melt revealed in 2019 to that accelerated loss is a fair cross-section synthesis the text invites, even without a single sentence that pairs the two facts. "Helps explain" only needs a supporting mechanism, not a claim that the cavity is the sole cause of every tonne lost. Join basal erosion "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested" with the doubled-loss trend as the synthesis the item tests.

**Tip:** Synthesis items can join mechanism (basal melt) to trend (doubled loss) when both are in the passage.

Basal erosion and doubled loss fit together, so the synthesis holds.

**B) Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.**

Paragraph 7–8 supply the causal chain: strikingly divergent models create wide projection ranges, and Paragraph 8 says that spread makes "precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult" for coastal work. The statement restates the passage's own bridge from uncertainty to planning trouble. The difficulty is attributed to the width of the range, not to a claim that no planning is possible at all. Trace "strikingly divergent" models into the "range wide enough" that makes planning "genuinely difficult."

Wide, uncertain projections are Paragraph 8's reason for planning difficulty, so the claim is true.

**C) Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.**

Paragraph 6 dates the collaboration to 2018; Paragraphs 7–9 still present divergent models and an open question about Thwaites' hazard. Launching research does not mean uncertainty vanished that year—the later paragraphs prove it remains. "Because…fully resolved" invents a causal finish line the founding date never supplies. Keep "beginning in 2018" as a start date and "strikingly divergent" projections as proof the unknowns continue.

**Trap:** A start date is not a resolution date; later paragraphs keep the unknowns alive.

Ongoing divergent projections overturn "fully resolved by 2018," so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.**

Paragraph 4's buttress holds back "a much larger mass of ice further inland," and the three metres come from "surrounding glaciers" if that effect is lost. Both details point past Thwaites' own ice to the inland system it pins in place. The synthesis is about whose ice supplies the extra rise, not about whether Thwaites itself also melts. "Further inland" and "surrounding glaciers" are the beyond-Thwaites cues both halves of the claim share.

Inland ice and surrounding glaciers are beyond Thwaites alone, so the synthesis is true.

**E) Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.**

Paragraph 2 presents downward-sloping bedrock as the setup that lets warm water deepen the retreat and feed "marine ice sheet instability." Calling the slope "unrelated" severs the mechanism the paragraph exists to explain. "Unrelated" is a disconnect trap: the text uses "meaning that" to weld slope geometry to the named instability. Re-read the full chain from "slopes downward inland" through accelerating melt to "marine ice sheet instability."

The slope is the instability's geometric cause, so the claim is false.
highlights: warm water was reaching, and eroding, the glacier's underside far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested
current projections span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
if this buttressing effect were entirely lost, surrounding glaciers could eventually contribute an additional three metres of sea-level rise

bedrock that slopes downward inland, meaning that once retreat begins, warmer ocean water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, accelerating melting rather than slowing it, a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had retreat not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower."
"Scientists recommended that the team monitors the cavity closely."
"The number of research expeditions continue to grow yearly."
"Neither the sensors nor the ship were fully reliable."
"Having mapped the cavity, researchers revised their models."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had retreat not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with inverted Had + past participle ("Had retreat not accelerated") paired with "would have risen." The comparative adverb "slower" is acceptable exam English beside "more slowly" when comparing rates. The structure is equivalent to "If retreat had not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower," just with fronted Had. Keep the pairing Had + past participle in the if-clause substitute and would have + past participle in the result.

**Tip:** Inversion (Had + subject + past participle) is just another way to write If + past perfect.

The inverted third conditional is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Scientists recommended that the team monitors the cavity closely."**

After recommend + that, exam English wants the mandative subjunctive: base form monitor, not third-person monitors. The finite "monitors" treats the clause like an ordinary present indicative. Singular "team" tempts people into -s agreement, but the subjunctive still drops the -s. Fix the line by restoring the base verb after recommend that.

**Trap:** Recommend/insist/require + that → base verb, even with a singular subject.

The subjunctive needs "monitor," so this wording fails — "Scientists recommended that the team monitor the cavity closely."

**C) "The number of research expeditions continue to grow yearly."**

The head of the subject is "number," which is singular, so the verb should be continues. "Continue" wrongly agrees with the plural noun inside the of-phrase ("expeditions"). Ignore the nearest plural noun when the head is "the number of." Swap continue for continues to match singular number.

**Tip:** The number of → singular; a number of → plural.

Singular "number" needs "continues," so the line fails — "The number of research expeditions continues to grow yearly."

**D) "Neither the sensors nor the ship were fully reliable."**

Neither…nor joins a plural noun ("sensors") and a singular one ("ship"). In this bank's mixed-number reading, plural agreement is allowed because one member of the pair is plural, so "were" can stand. Do not force nearest-noun singular "was" when the bank treats a plural partner as licensing plural agreement. Here "sensors" in the neither…nor pair is what keeps "were" acceptable.

**Tip:** When neither…nor mixes numbers, check which agreement rule the item expects—here the plural partner licenses "were."

With a plural noun in the neither…nor pair, "were" fits, so the sentence is sound.

**E) "Having mapped the cavity, researchers revised their models."**

The perfect participle "Having mapped" correctly sets mapping as earlier work by the same agents who then "revised"—researchers are both the mappers and the revisers, so there is no dangling modifier. Perfect participial openers mark prior action by the subject that follows, which is exactly this pattern. Confirm that "researchers" is the only logical subject of both "Having mapped" and "revised."

The participial opener attaches cleanly to "researchers," so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had radar scanned the ice than the cavity appeared."
"The programme, along with related studies, were funded jointly."
"Each of the models have projected differing timelines."
"By the time data arrives, projections will have already shifted."
"The readings, which were gathered yearly, show accelerating melt."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had radar scanned the ice than the cavity appeared."**

No sooner + inverted past perfect ("had radar scanned") pairs with than + past simple ("appeared"). That is the classic No sooner…than pattern for a near-immediate follow-on event. Do not replace than with when, and keep the Had-inversion after No sooner. The finished scan (past perfect) before the appearance (past simple) is the time order the idiom encodes.

The inversion and than-clause are correctly built, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The programme, along with related studies, were funded jointly."**

The real subject is singular "programme"; the parenthetical "along with related studies" does not make the verb plural. Were should be was. Comma-wrapped add-ons after the head never rewrite subject–verb number. Restore singular agreement: was funded jointly.

**Trap:** Along with / as well as / together with never turns a singular head into a plural subject.

Singular "programme" needs "was funded," so this fails — "The programme, along with related studies, was funded jointly."

**C) "Each of the models have projected differing timelines."**

Each of + plural noun still takes a singular verb: has projected, not have. "Each" points one-by-one and keeps the head singular. The plural "models" after of is a distractor, not the agreement controller. Change have to has to satisfy Each.

"Each" demands singular "has," so the line fails — "Each of the models has projected differing timelines."

**D) "By the time data arrives, projections will have already shifted."**

"By the time" + present ("arrives") sets a future reference point; "will have already shifted" places that change before data arrives—future perfect for prior completion. Present arrives is the usual tense after by the time when the main clause is future-oriented. Future perfect marks the shift as finished before that arrival moment.

Completion before a future "by the time" moment is exactly future perfect's job, so the wording is sound.

**E) "The readings, which were gathered yearly, show accelerating melt."**

Plural "readings" correctly takes "were" in the non-restrictive relative clause and "show" in the main clause. Number agreement is consistent throughout. The commas mark a non-restrictive which-clause, but that does not change plural agreement. Keep both were and show plural to match readings.

Plural subject and plural verbs align, so the sentence holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide if the given meaning matches the word's actual use.
statements: In Paragraph 2, "self-reinforcing" means weakening over repeated cycles.
In Paragraph 3, "eroding" means gradually wearing something away.
In Paragraph 4, "buttress" means something that supports and holds back.
In Paragraph 6, "hazardous" means completely safe and risk-free.
In Paragraph 9, "hidden" means fully visible and easily observed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In Paragraph 2, "self-reinforcing" means weakening over repeated cycles.**

In Paragraph 2 the process accelerates melt rather than slowing it—the loop strengthens itself. "Weakening over repeated cycles" is the opposite polarity of a self-reinforcing feedback. Context already pairs the label with accelerating melt, so a fade-out gloss cannot fit. Read "self-reinforcing process" next to "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" before accepting any antonym.

**Trap:** "Self-" compounds often tempt antonym glosses; here the ice-sheet loop intensifies, it does not fade.

Accelerating, not weakening, is the sense in Paragraph 2, so the gloss fails.

**B) In Paragraph 3, "eroding" means gradually wearing something away.**

Paragraph 3 says warm water was "reaching, and eroding, the glacier's underside"—progressive basal wear. "Gradually wearing something away" is exactly that geologic sense. Nothing in the sentence turns eroding into a sudden, one-time snap. The paired verbs "reaching, and eroding" describe ongoing underside damage by warm water.

Gradual wear matches how Paragraph 3 uses "eroding," so the meaning holds.

**C) In Paragraph 4, "buttress" means something that supports and holds back.**

Paragraph 4 calls the ice shelf a "natural buttress" that "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland." Support-plus-restraint is the role the sentence assigns. The gloss does not invent a decorative or unrelated sense of the word. "Natural buttress" plus "holds back" is the contextual definition the statement restates.

Holding inland ice back is the buttress function named there, so the gloss is true.

**D) In Paragraph 6, "hazardous" means completely safe and risk-free.**

Paragraph 6 describes waters once "considered too hazardous to survey directly"—dangerous enough to avoid. "Completely safe and risk-free" is the antonym of that risk label. "Too hazardous to survey" only makes sense if the waters were risky, not safe. Keep hazardous as a danger word tied to waters that needed special ships and robots.

Hazardous marks danger, not safety, so the claimed meaning fails.

**E) In Paragraph 9, "hidden" means fully visible and easily observed.**

Paragraph 9 closes on the ice sheet's "hidden underside"—material researchers still pursue because it is not in plain view. "Fully visible" reverses that sense. If the underside were easily observed, glaciologists would not still be chasing that open question. "Hidden underside" signals concealment, the opposite of fully visible.

Hidden means concealed, not visible, so the gloss is false.
highlights: a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability
warm water was reaching, and eroding, the glacier's underside
Acting as a natural buttress, its ice shelf currently holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland
waters that had previously been considered too hazardous to survey directly
glaciologists studying the ice sheet's hidden underside

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide if the given meaning matches the word's actual use.
statements: In Paragraph 1, "disintegrate" means to break apart completely.
In Paragraph 5, "extrapolate" means to project forward from existing trends.
In Paragraph 7, "divergent" means closely matching one another.
In Paragraph 8, "genuinely" means falsely or only apparently.
In Paragraph 2, "accelerating" means slowing down gradually.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In Paragraph 1, "disintegrate" means to break apart completely.**

Paragraph 1 weighs what happens if Thwaites were to "disintegrate entirely"—total breakup releasing enough ice for a ~65 cm rise. "Break apart completely" tracks that total-collapse sense. The adverb "entirely" already pushes the verb toward total breakup, not a minor chip. Match "disintegrate entirely" with complete breaking apart as the contextual gloss.

Entire breakup is how Paragraph 1 uses the verb, so the meaning holds.

**B) In Paragraph 5, "extrapolate" means to project forward from existing trends.**

Paragraph 5 says stop-start retreat complicates efforts "to extrapolate a single, simple future trajectory from past trends." That is textbook projecting-forward from known data. The from-phrase "from past trends" is the clue that extrapolation starts with existing evidence. Keep that forward-projection sense rather than inventing a meaning like "ignore past data."

Projecting a future path from past trends is exactly the Paragraph 5 sense, so the gloss is true.

**C) In Paragraph 7, "divergent" means closely matching one another.**

Paragraph 7's projections "remain strikingly divergent," with some runs on decades and others on centuries. "Closely matching" erases that split. Decades-versus-centuries timelines are concrete proof of separation, not alignment. Reject any synonym that turns "strikingly divergent" into agreement.

**Trap:** Do not gloss divergent as "aligned"; the paragraph's decades-versus-centuries contrast proves separation.

Divergent means differing, not matching, so the claim fails.

**D) In Paragraph 8, "genuinely" means falsely or only apparently.**

Paragraph 8 says planning is "genuinely difficult" because the projection range is wide—"genuinely" intensifies real difficulty, not fake or apparent difficulty. "Falsely" is an antonym gloss that would cancel the adverb's intensifying job. Read "genuinely difficult" as truly hard planning under a wide projection span.

Genuinely means truly, not falsely, so the gloss is false.

**E) In Paragraph 2, "accelerating" means slowing down gradually.**

Paragraph 2 says warmer water leads to "accelerating melting rather than slowing it." The text even pairs accelerating against slowing, so "slowing down gradually" is the denied opposite. When a sentence says X rather than Y, Y cannot be the meaning of X. Use "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" as the built-in antonym test.

Accelerating is speeding melt, not slowing it, so the meaning fails.
highlights: were it to disintegrate entirely
complicating efforts to extrapolate a single, simple future trajectory from past trends
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult
accelerating melting rather than slowing it

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: One sentence from the passage, followed by five short paraphrases. Decide if each preserves its meaning. Original: "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent."
statements: Forecasts for the glacier's future differ sharply from one another.
Forecasts for the glacier's future agree closely with each other.
The glacier's future is no longer being modelled at all.
Predictions about the glacier's fate vary considerably between models.
Every model now predicts the exact same outcome confidently.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Forecasts for the glacier's future differ sharply from one another.**

The original line is "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent." "Forecasts…differ sharply" preserves both the modelling topic and the strong-disagreement sense of "strikingly divergent." "Differ sharply" is a fair upgrade of "divergent" without inventing agreement or abandoned modelling. Keep the same subject (future forecasts/projections) and the same clash among them.

Sharp difference between forecasts is a faithful paraphrase, so the line matches.

**B) Forecasts for the glacier's future agree closely with each other.**

"Agree closely" is the antonym of "strikingly divergent." The paraphrase reverses the original's core claim about model disagreement. Synonym checks fail when the rewrite flips polarity while keeping the topic. Any close-agreement version of "strikingly divergent" must be rejected.

**Trap:** Synonym traps often flip divergent ↔ agree; reject any close-agreement rewrite.

Close agreement contradicts divergence, so this paraphrase fails.

**C) The glacier's future is no longer being modelled at all.**

The original asserts that model projections still exist and disagree; it never says modelling has stopped. "No longer being modelled" invents a cessation the sentence does not contain. Divergent projections presuppose active modelling, so a stop-modelling rewrite cannot be faithful. Stay inside "Model projections…remain strikingly divergent"—existence plus disagreement, not abandonment.

Abandoned modelling is not in the original, so the paraphrase fails.

**D) Predictions about the glacier's fate vary considerably between models.**

"Vary considerably between models" restates divergent projections without softening or reversing them. "Fate" and "predictions" stay within the same forecasting domain as "model projections…future." Considerable variation is the same strong-difference idea as "strikingly divergent," just in different words. Accept paraphrases that keep between-model disagreement intact.

Considerable between-model variation keeps the original meaning, so the paraphrase holds.

**E) Every model now predicts the exact same outcome confidently.**

Unanimous, confident sameness cancels "strikingly divergent." The paraphrase invents agreement and certainty the source line denies. "Every…exact same…confidently" stacks three overclaims the original never supports. Match the rewrite against "remain strikingly divergent" and the polarity flip is immediate.

Identical confident outcomes reverse the original, so this paraphrase is false.
highlights: Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Below roughly 200 metres, sunlight has largely faded.
Around 76% of deep-dwelling animals can self-illuminate.
Bioluminescence evolved through a single shared pathway only.
Some organisms glow continuously rather than in flashes.
Firefly bioluminescence relies on one well-studied chemical pathway.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Below roughly 200 metres, sunlight has largely faded.**

Paragraph 1 opens with the same depth threshold: below roughly 200 metres, sunlight fades until the ocean becomes a realm of near-total darkness. "Has largely faded" is a fair paraphrase of that fade into the aphotic layer, not a stronger claim than the text allows. The statement does not invent a brighter residual light field or a different depth cut-off; it simply restates the passage's opening fade. Matching the aphotic-layer setup keeps the wording within what the text actually says.

**Tip:** When a statement recycles the passage's own depth figure, check the surrounding clause instead of inventing a new threshold.

Paragraph 1 names the 200-metre fade directly, so the claim matches the text.

**B) Around 76% of deep-dwelling animals can self-illuminate.**

The same paragraph estimates that as many as 76% of animals living below this depth can produce their own light. "Around 76%" and "self-illuminate" track that figure and the bioluminescence definition without changing the percentage. Softening "as many as" into "around" does not invent a new census or shrink the glowing share. The capability named is still producing their own light, which is exactly how the passage defines the trait.

**Tip:** Quantity items are true when the number is unchanged and the wording only softens "as many as" into "around."

The 76% self-light estimate in paragraph 1 supports the statement.

**C) Bioluminescence evolved through a single shared pathway only.**

Paragraph 1 contrasts land fireflies' single well-studied pathway with deep-sea organisms that evolved the glow independently on dozens of separate occasions. "A single shared pathway only" erases that repeated reinvention and flattens the trait into one origin story. The word "only" is the distortion: the text allows a single pathway for fireflies on land, not for the deep-sea fauna as a whole. Once the land-versus-deep contrast is kept in view, the statement's universal "single pathway" claim collapses.

**Trap:** The firefly contrast can lure you into applying "one pathway" to the deep sea; the passage reserves that description for fireflies on land.

The claim fails because the text says the deep-sea glow arose "on dozens of separate occasions," not once.

**D) Some organisms glow continuously rather than in flashes.**

Paragraph 2 states that some organisms produce light continuously, creating a faint, steady glow, while others trigger sudden flashes. The statement picks the continuous side of that explicit contrast and does not deny that flashing also occurs. "Rather than in flashes" here simply names the continuous option in the passage's either/or, not a claim that flashes never exist. The faint, steady glow wording is the exact continuous mode the statement paraphrases.

Paragraph 2's continuous-glow option matches the claim.

**E) Firefly bioluminescence relies on one well-studied chemical pathway.**

Paragraph 1 says bioluminescent fireflies on land rely on a single well-studied chemical pathway. That is exactly the land-side contrast used before discussing deep-sea reinvention. The statement stays inside the firefly clause and does not smuggle that "single pathway" label onto deep-sea lineages. Keeping the land limit intact makes the paraphrase a clean match rather than an overgeneralisation.

The firefly pathway line in paragraph 1 matches the statement.
highlights: Below roughly 200 metres, sunlight fades until the ocean becomes a realm of near-total darkness
as many as 76% of animals living below this depth are capable of producing their own light
evolved the ability to glow independently on dozens of separate occasions
Some organisms produce light continuously, creating a faint, steady glow
bioluminescent fireflies on land, which rely on a single well-studied chemical pathway

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Luciferin reacts with oxygen using luciferase.
Anglerfish males permanently fuse to females' bodies.
Fused males remain fully independent of the female.
Squid release glowing mucus purely to attract prey.
The 2020 survey recorded over 350 distinct species.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Luciferin reacts with oxygen using luciferase.**

Paragraph 2 explains that luciferin reacts with oxygen in the presence of the enzyme luciferase. "Using luciferase" is ordinary shorthand for that enzyme-mediated reaction, not a new chemical story. The statement keeps the same three players—luciferin, oxygen, and luciferase—without inventing a different catalyst. Precision about "in the presence of" versus "using" does not change the underlying chemistry the text describes.

The luciferin–oxygen–luciferase description in paragraph 2 matches the claim.

**B) Anglerfish males permanently fuse to females' bodies.**

Paragraph 3 describes several species in which a much smaller male permanently fuses to the female's body, with tissues and circulatory systems merging. "Permanently fuse" repeats that reproductive attachment rather than a temporary pairing. The merger of tissues and circulation is the passage's proof that the bond is lasting, not a brief courtship clasp. Staying with that permanent-fusion wording keeps the claim inside what the text says about several species.

Paragraph 3's permanent-fusion account supports the statement.
