The concessive opener "Despite this extraordinary speed" also depends on the speed being impressive, since there would be nothing to concede otherwise.

Extraordinary and ordinary are opposites, so the claimed gloss is **false**.

**B) In Paragraph 5, "robust" means fragile and easily damaged.**

Paragraph 5 says engineers chose "robust, non-digital analogue encoding" so the record could survive and be reconstructed later. Robust means sturdy and durable, not fragile. The stated purpose settles it: an encoding meant to outlast the mission and be decoded by unknown finders has to be resilient by design. A fragile format would defeat the very reason the passage gives for the choice.

**Trap:** Analogue can sound "old" and therefore fragile, but the text pairs it with robustness on purpose.

Robust means durable here, so fragile is **false**.

**C) In Paragraph 7, "proximity" means the state of being nearby or close to something.**

Paragraph 7 calls the Gliese 445 pass "a proximity that, while still enormous by any everyday standard, counts as a genuinely close stellar encounter." Proximity is nearness — exactly the offered gloss. The concession "while still enormous" shows that nearness is being judged on an astronomical scale, not an everyday one. That relative framing does not change the word's meaning; it only changes the yardstick.

Proximity as nearness matches the stellar-encounter wording, so the meaning is **true**.

**D) In Paragraph 9, "dwindling" (as in "dwindling power") means power that is steadily decreasing.**

Paragraph 9 wonders whether "dwindling power will silence both spacecraft" before the fiftieth launch anniversary. That use is power steadily falling away — the definition given. The verb "silence" confirms the direction of travel, since only a shrinking supply could shut the probes down. The word carries the same sense here as it does in Paragraph 4, so the two uses reinforce each other.

Dwindling power as steadily decreasing fits Paragraph 9, so the claim is **true**.

**E) In Paragraph 1, "overtake" means to fall behind something rather than pass it.**

Paragraph 1 says Voyager 1's faster trajectory "allowed it to overtake its sibling" and become more distant. Overtake means to catch up and pass — the opposite of falling behind. The outcome clause seals the reading, since becoming "the more distant of the two probes" is only possible if Voyager 1 moved ahead. A faster trajectory as the stated cause points the same direction.

Overtake is passing ahead, so "fall behind" is **false**.
highlights: Despite this extraordinary speed
Engineers deliberately selected robust, non-digital analogue encoding
a proximity that, while still enormous by any everyday standard, counts as a genuinely close stellar encounter
whether dwindling power will silence both spacecraft before that milestone arrives
a faster trajectory that allowed it to overtake its sibling

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: One sentence from the passage, followed by five short paraphrases. Decide if each preserves its meaning. Original: "…meaning any single command-and-confirmation exchange with mission control necessarily spans nearly two full days."
statements: A complete round-trip exchange with mission control takes close to two entire days.
Sending and confirming a single command takes only a few brief minutes.
Any full exchange of a command and its confirmation requires almost two full days.
Mission control receives instant confirmation the moment any command is sent.
Communicating a command and receiving confirmation takes nearly two days combined.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A complete round-trip exchange with mission control takes close to two entire days.**

The source line says a "command-and-confirmation exchange … necessarily spans nearly two full days." "Complete round-trip" and "close to two entire days" keep the same exchange idea and the same near-two-day duration. Every substitution here is a synonym swap rather than a change of quantity: complete for full, close to for nearly, entire for full. A valid paraphrase may change the words freely so long as the measurable claim underneath stays fixed.

The paraphrase preserves both exchange and duration, so it is **true**.

**B) Sending and confirming a single command takes only a few brief minutes.**

"A few brief minutes" collapses the passage's "nearly two full days" into a tiny interval. That is not a soft rewording — it contradicts the stated timescale outright. The first half of the statement is a faithful restatement of command-and-confirmation, which is what makes the swapped duration easy to miss. Always locate the number in a paraphrase item and compare it before judging the sentence as a whole.

**Trap:** "Single command" can tempt a mini-second mental picture; the text's delay is light-travel distance, not laptop latency.

Minutes replace nearly two days, so the paraphrase is **false**.

**C) Any full exchange of a command and its confirmation requires almost two full days.**

"Full exchange of a command and its confirmation" restates command-and-confirmation, and "almost two full days" tracks "nearly two full days." Scope and duration both survive. The quantifier "any" also matches the source's "any single … exchange," so the breadth of the claim is unchanged. Neither the hedge nor the scope has been tightened or loosened in the rewrite.

Same exchange-plus-duration claim in new clothes stays **true**.

**D) Mission control receives instant confirmation the moment any command is sent.**

"Instant confirmation the moment any command is sent" erases the multi-hour one-way delay and the nearly two-day exchange. The passage's whole point is the opposite of instant feedback. The 22-hour one-way figure alone rules out instantaneity, before the round trip is even considered. Words like "instant" and "the moment" are absolute time markers, and absolutes rarely survive a passage built on enormous distances.
